knowledge_statements.title: Feasible Demand Routing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc-flow feasibility for fixed commodities in a capacitated directed network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with capacities \(u_a\ge 0\), and let \(K\) be a finite commodity set. For every \(k\in K\), let \(s_k,t_k\in V\) satisfy \(s_k\ne t_k\), and let \(d_k\ge0\). A feasible demand routing is a family \(x^k\in\mathbb R_+^A\) satisfying, for every \(v\in V\) and \(k\in K\),
\[\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a^k-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a^k=\begin{cases}d_k,&v=s_k,\\-d_k,&v=t_k,\\0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\]
and, for every \(a\in A\), \(\sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\le u_a\). Thus all prescribed demands are routed simultaneously without violating shared arc capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every commodity sends its prescribed amount between distinct source and sink vertices, conserves flow elsewhere, and all commodities together respect each arc capacity.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,A)\text{ is finite and directed}
K\text{ is finite}
u\in\mathbb R_+^A
s_k,t_k\in V,\ s_k\ne t_k\text{ for every }k\in K
d\in\mathbb R_+^K
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists (x^k)_{k\in K}\text{ satisfying conservation and }\sum_k x_a^k\le u_a

notation.meaning: arcs leaving and entering vertex v
flow of commodity k on arc a

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance-criterion characterization of multicommodity-flow feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact feasibility characterization for directed and undirected multicommodity flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every directed or undirected multicommodity-flow instance $(G,H,u,b)$, a feasible solution exists if and only if, for every $z:E(G)\to\mathbb R_+$, $$\sum_{f=(t,s)\in E(H)}b(f)\operatorname{dist}_{(G,z)}(s,t)\leq\sum_{e\in E(G)}u(e)z(e),$$ where demand edges are written $f=\{s,t\}$ in the undirected case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed or undirected multicommodity-flow instance is feasible exactly when it satisfies the distance criterion for every nonnegative supply-edge length assignment.
assumptions_latex: $(G,H,u,b)$ is a directed or undirected multicommodity-flow instance.
$z:E(G)\to\mathbb R_+$ ranges over all nonnegative edge-length functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (G,H,u,b)\text{ is solvable}\iff\sum_{f=(t,s)\in E(H)}b(f)\operatorname{dist}_{(G,z)}(s,t)\leq\sum_{e\in E(G)}u(e)z(e)\quad\forall z:E(G)\to\mathbb R_+.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Multicommodity Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-cost routing of fixed demands under shared capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the feasible-routing model with arc-commodity costs \(c_a^k\in\mathbb R\), the minimum-cost multicommodity-flow problem is
\[\min_{(x^k)_{k\in K}}\ \sum_{k\in K}\sum_{a\in A}c_a^k x_a^k\]
subject to commodity-wise flow conservation with net supply \(d_k\) at \(s_k\) and net demand \(d_k\) at \(t_k\), nonnegativity \(x_a^k\ge0\), and shared capacities \(\sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\). If the feasible set is empty, the problem is infeasible; otherwise any minimizing feasible family is an optimal multicommodity flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among all simultaneous routings of the fixed demands, choose one minimizing total arc-commodity cost while respecting shared capacities.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,A)\text{ is finite and directed}
u\in\mathbb R_+^A
c\in\mathbb R^{A\times K}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\text{ feasible}}\sum_{k,a}c_a^k x_a^k

notation.meaning: unit cost for commodity k on arc a

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partial Dualization of Shared Arc Capacities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that optimal multicommodity flows separate into commodity-wise uncapacitated minimum-cost flows after shared capacities are priced.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $y$ be an optimal multicommodity flow and let $w_{ij}$ be optimal arc prices. Then, for every commodity $k$, $y^k$ solves
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{(i,j)\in A}(c_{ij}^k+w_{ij})x_{ij}^k:\;\mathcal N x^k=b,\;x_{ij}^k\ge0\ \forall(i,j)\in A\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At optimal shared-capacity prices, each commodity component of an optimal multicommodity flow solves an uncapacitated minimum-cost flow problem with adjusted arc costs equal to its original costs plus the shared arc prices.
assumptions_latex: y\text{ is optimal for the multicommodity-flow problem}
w_{ij}\text{ are optimal arc prices for that problem}
k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y^k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\mathcal N x^k=b,\;x^k\ge0}\sum_{(i,j)\in A}(c_{ij}^k+w_{ij})x_{ij}^k\quad\forall k.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Multicommodity Flow Problems and Their Separable Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines continuous convex multicommodity flow models, distinguishing total-arc-flow cost separability, constraint separability, and shared arc-capacity coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)$ be a directed graph and let $x=(x(1),\ldots,x(M))$ collect finitely many commodity-flow vectors. Each commodity satisfies $\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal A}x_{ij}(m)-\sum_{j:(j,i)\in\mathcal A}x_{ji}(m)=s_i(m)$ for every node $i$ and commodity $m$. Given a constraint set $X$, define $F=\{x\in X:x\text{ satisfies all commodity conservation equations}\}$. If $F$ is convex and $f$ is convex on $F$, the general convex multicommodity flow problem is $\min_{x\in F}f(x)$. In the convex separable variant, $X=\{x:x_{ij}(m)\in X_{ij}(m)\}$ for real intervals $X_{ij}(m)$ and $f(x)=\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}f_{ij}(y_{ij})$, where $y_{ij}=\sum_{m=1}^M x_{ij}(m)$ and each $f_{ij}:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is convex; thus the objective is separable by total arc flow, not by commodity flow. A constraint-separable variant retains the product-form set $X$ without requiring this objective form. Shared arc capacities may instead be included through $y_{ij}\le c_{ij}$, yielding the arc-capacitated convex separable variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multicommodity flow consists of finitely many commodity flows on one directed graph, each satisfying its own conservation equations, with a common constraint set and objective providing any coupling. Minimizing a convex objective over the resulting convex feasible set defines the general convex multicommodity flow problem. In the convex separable version, commodity-specific arc flows lie in intervals and each convex arc cost depends on the total flow of all commodities on that arc—not separately on individual commodity flows. Constraint-separable and shared-capacity variants respectively retain only the product-form constraints or add upper bounds on total arc flows.
assumptions_latex: M\in\mathbb N
\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal A}x_{ij}(m)-\sum_{j:(j,i)\in\mathcal A}x_{ji}(m)=s_i(m)\quad\forall i\in\mathcal N,\ \forall m\in\{1,\ldots,M\}
F=\{x\in X:x\text{ satisfies all commodity conservation equations}\}\text{ is convex}
f\text{ is convex on }F
\text{For the convex separable variant, each }X_{ij}(m)\subseteq\mathbb R\text{ is an interval and each }f_{ij}:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\text{ is convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in F}f(x);\qquad f(x)=\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}f_{ij}\!\left(\sum_{m=1}^M x_{ij}(m)\right)\text{ in the cost-separable variant, optionally subject to }\sum_{m=1}^M x_{ij}(m)\le c_{ij}\ \forall(i,j)\in\mathcal A.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence of the resource-directive and original multicommodity-flow formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility and objective value are preserved under projection to the flow variables and under the lifting r=x.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The resource-directive formulation and the original multicommodity-flow formulation are equivalent in the following sense: (i) if $(x,r)$ is feasible for the resource-directive formulation, then $x$ is feasible for the original formulation and has the same objective value; (ii) if $x$ is feasible for the original formulation, then setting $r=x$ makes $(x,r)$ feasible for the resource-directive formulation with the same objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting a feasible resource-directive solution onto its flow variables preserves feasibility and cost. Conversely, any feasible original flow can be lifted by setting its resource allocation equal to the flow itself.
assumptions_latex: (x,r)\text{ is feasible for the resource-directive formulation in direction (i).}
x\text{ is feasible for the original multicommodity-flow formulation in direction (ii).}
r=x\text{ in the reverse construction.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_x(F_{RD})=F_{MCF}\quad\text{with objective values preserved in both directions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum-Cost Multicommodity Flow Formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc-indexed linear formulation with commodity-wise conservation, shared arc capacities, and optional commodity-specific bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given commodities \(k=1,\ldots,K\) on a directed network with node--arc incidence matrix \(\mathcal N\), the minimum-cost multicommodity flow problem is
\[
\min_x \sum_{k=1}^{K}(c^k)^\top x^k
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{K}x_{ij}^k\le u_{ij}\quad((i,j)\in A),\qquad \mathcal N x^k=b^k\quad(k=1,\ldots,K),
\]
and
\[
0\le x_{ij}^k\le u_{ij}^k\quad((i,j)\in A,\ k=1,\ldots,K).
\]
The bounds \(u_{ij}^k\) may be \(+\infty\). Equivalently, each shared-capacity constraint may be written as \(\sum_k x_{ij}^k+s_{ij}=u_{ij}\) with \(s_{ij}\ge0\), where \(s_{ij}\) measures unused capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize total commodity cost subject to separate flow-balance equations for each commodity, shared arc capacities limiting their total flow, and optional commodity-specific arc bounds. A nonnegative slack converts a shared-capacity inequality into an equality and measures unused capacity.
assumptions_latex: k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}
(i,j)\in A
u_{ij}\ge0
u_{ij}^k\in[0,+\infty]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\left\{\sum_{k=1}^{K}(c^k)^\top x^k:\ \sum_{k=1}^{K}x_{ij}^k\le u_{ij},\ \mathcal N x^k=b^k,\ 0\le x_{ij}^k\le u_{ij}^k\right\}

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum Multiflow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted total-throughput multiflow for specified terminal pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with capacities \(u\in\mathbb R_+^A\), and let \(K\) be a finite set of terminal pairs \((s_k,t_k)\) satisfying \(s_k,t_k\in V\) and \(s_k\ne t_k\). A multiflow consists of nonnegative arc flows \(x^k\in\mathbb R_+^A\) and routed values \(z_k\ge0\), where \(x^k\) has divergence \(z_k\) at \(s_k\), divergence \(-z_k\) at \(t_k\), and zero divergence elsewhere. Under shared capacities \(\sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\le u_a\), the maximum-multiflow problem is
\[\max\left\{\sum_{k\in K}z_k:(x,z)\text{ satisfies these conservation and capacity constraints}\right\}.\]
No prescribed proportions among the terminal-pair values are imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose independently routed amounts for finitely many distinct terminal pairs to maximize their unweighted sum under shared network capacities.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,A)\text{ is finite and directed}
K\text{ is finite}
u\in\mathbb R_+^A
s_k,t_k\in V,\ s_k\ne t_k\text{ for every }k\in K
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\sum_{k\in K}z_k\text{ over capacity-feasible multiflows}

notation.meaning: value routed for terminal pair k

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Multiflow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-utility multiflow with commodity-specific nonnegative weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In the multiflow model, assign each terminal pair \(k\in K\) a weight \(w_k\ge0\). The weighted-multiflow problem is
\[\max\left\{\sum_{k\in K}w_k z_k:(x,z)\text{ is a capacity-feasible multiflow}\right\}.\]
Here \(x^k\) routes value \(z_k\ge0\) from \(s_k\) to \(t_k\), obeys flow conservation at other vertices, and the aggregate flow satisfies \(\sum_k x_a^k\le u_a\) on each arc. Equal positive weights recover maximum multiflow up to a constant scaling of the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximize a weighted sum of independently chosen terminal-pair throughputs, subject to commodity conservation and shared capacities.
assumptions_latex: w\in\mathbb R_+^K
u\in\mathbb R_+^A
G=(V,A)\text{ is finite and directed}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\sum_{k\in K}w_kz_k\text{ over capacity-feasible multiflows}

children.title: Objective-Regime Comparison
children.top_down_role: Structural relationships, equivalence regimes, plus separation boundaries between the two objective families.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Regime Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of total-throughput, weighted-utility, and proportional-throughput objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a common multiflow feasible region \(F\subseteq\mathbb R_+^K\) of routed-value vectors, maximum multiflow optimizes \(\mathbf1^Tz\), weighted multiflow optimizes \(w^Tz\), and maximum concurrent flow for demand vector \(d\in\mathbb R_{++}^K\) optimizes \(\lambda\) subject to \(z=\lambda d\). Consequently, maximum multiflow is the weighted model with \(w=\mathbf1\), whereas concurrency restricts candidate values to the ray \(\{\lambda d:\lambda\ge0\}\). In general these objectives select different feasible vectors; they coincide only when an optimizer of the unrestricted linear objective lies on the prescribed demand ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total and weighted throughput optimize over all feasible value vectors; concurrent flow restricts values to fixed demand proportions, so their optima generally differ.
assumptions_latex: F\subseteq\mathbb R_+^K\text{ is the common feasible value region}
d\in\mathbb R_{++}^K
w\in\mathbb R_+^K
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{z\in F}\mathbf1^Tz,\quad \max_{z\in F}w^Tz,\quad \max\{\lambda:\lambda d\in F\}\text{ are distinct regimes}

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the three-way comparison. Moreover, the coincidence sentence is ambiguous across the two unrestricted objectives and fails for degenerate weights such as w=0; a source-backed statement must specify which optimizers are compared and any positivity condition on the objective along the demand ray.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum Concurrent Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum common scaling of a strictly positive demand vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let commodity \(k\in K\) have demand \(d_k>0\). The maximum concurrent-flow value is
\[\lambda^*=\max\{\lambda\ge0:\text{there exist flows routing }\lambda d_k\text{ from }s_k\text{ to }t_k\text{ for all }k,\ \sum_kx_a^k\le u_a\ \forall a\in A\}.\]
Equivalently, every commodity receives the same satisfaction ratio \(z_k/d_k=\lambda\). The variables obey nonnegativity and commodity-wise conservation with net source outflow and sink inflow equal to \(\lambda d_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale every positive demand by one common factor and maximize that factor while routing all scaled demands within shared capacities.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,A)\text{ is finite and directed}
u\in\mathbb R_+^A
d\in\mathbb R_{++}^K
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda^*=\max\{\lambda\ge0:\lambda d\text{ is routable under }u\}

notation.meaning: actual routed value of commodity k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation is standard, but no inspectable source is supplied. It should also require a finite nonempty commodity set; with K empty, the displayed maximization is unbounded.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Path-Flow Formulation and Cut Bound for Maximum Concurrent Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path-based linear formulation, demand-scaling interpretation, LP-duality identity, and elementary cut upper bound for maximum concurrent flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given commodities with demands \(d(i)\), maximum concurrent flow maximizes the common routed fraction \(\alpha\) over path flows satisfying \[\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_i}f(P)\ge \alpha d(i)\quad(i=1,\ldots,k),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^k\sum_{\substack{P\in\mathcal P_i\\e\in P}}f(P)\le c(e)\quad(e\in E),\qquad f(P)\ge0.\] Its optimum \(\alpha^*\) equals the optimum of the dual fractional sparsest-cut relaxation and satisfies \(\alpha^*\le\rho(S)\) for every cut \(S\), hence \(\alpha^*\le\min_S\rho(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum concurrent flow maximizes the common fraction of all commodity demands routable under shared edge capacities. Its value equals the fractional sparsest-cut relaxation value and is no greater than the sparsity of any cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha^*=\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{fractional\ sparsest\ cut}}\quad\text{and}\quad\alpha^*\le\rho(S)\ \text{for every cut }S

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Congestion Routing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum uniform capacity augmentation needed to route fixed demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed demands \(d_k\ge0\) and capacities \(u_a>0\), the minimum-congestion value is
\[\rho^*=\min\left\{\rho\ge0:\begin{array}{l}(x^k)_{k\in K}\text{ routes every }d_k,\\ \sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\le \rho u_a\quad\text{for all }a\in A\end{array}\right\}.\]
Equivalently, \(\rho^*=\min_x\max_{a\in A}(\sum_kx_a^k/u_a)\), where the minimum is over nonnegative flows satisfying commodity-wise conservation. The original capacities admit all demands exactly when \(\rho^*\le1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Route all fixed demands while minimizing the largest capacity-utilization ratio; feasibility under the original capacities is equivalent to optimum congestion at most one.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,A)\text{ is finite and directed}
u\in\mathbb R_{++}^A
d\in\mathbb R_+^K
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho^*=\min_x\max_{a\in A}\frac{\sum_kx_a^k}{u_a}

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the stated convention. The definition also needs either an assumption that the demands are routable after some finite uniform augmentation or an extended-value convention rho*=+infinity when no conservation-feasible routing exists.

knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise Terminal Demands
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Commodity specification by ordered terminal pairs and scalar demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a directed network. A pairwise terminal-demand instance is a finite indexed family \(\{(s_k,t_k,d_k):k\in K\}\), where \(s_k,t_k\in V\), \(s_k\ne t_k\), and \(d_k\ge0\). Commodity \(k\) requires net outflow \(d_k\) at \(s_k\), net inflow \(d_k\) at \(t_k\), and zero net flow at every other vertex. Distinct indices may share a source, a sink, or the same ordered terminal pair unless the instance convention aggregates duplicates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each commodity is identified by an ordered source-sink pair and a nonnegative amount, with conservation at every nonterminal vertex.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,A)\text{ is finite and directed}
K\text{ is finite}
d_k\ge0\text{ for all }k
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal D=\{(s_k,t_k,d_k):k\in K\}\text{ specifies pairwise commodities}

notation.meaning: ordered terminal pair of commodity k

children.title: Single-Source Demands
children.top_down_role: Commodity systems sharing one source across multiple destinations.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Source Demands
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise commodities sharing one common source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A pairwise terminal-demand family \(\{(s_k,t_k,d_k):k\in K\}\) is single-source if there exists \(r\in V\) such that \(s_k=r\) for every \(k\in K\). Its aggregate balance vector \(b\in\mathbb R^V\), under the convention that positive balance denotes supply, is
\[b_r=\sum_{k\in K}d_k,\qquad b_v=-\sum_{k:t_k=v}d_k\quad(v\ne r),\]
provided no commodity has sink \(r\). Individual commodity identities may still be retained even though all flow originates at the same vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All commodities originate at one common vertex and may terminate at different vertices with independently specified amounts.
assumptions_latex: K\text{ is finite}
d_k\ge0\text{ for all }k
t_k\ne r\text{ for all }k
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists r\in V\ \forall k\in K:\ s_k=r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source establishes the intended single-source convention. This record requires every indexed commodity to have source r, while Source-Structure Transition ignores zero-demand commodities; the convention must be resolved consistently before acceptance.

children.title: Multiterminal Demands
children.top_down_role: Commodity systems involving broader terminal sets without a universal source.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiterminal Demands
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Demand systems permitting multiple source and sink terminals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A multiterminal demand is a balance vector \(b^k\in\mathbb R^V\) for each commodity \(k\in K\) satisfying \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v^k=0\), with source set \(S_k=\{v:b_v^k>0\}\) and sink set \(T_k=\{v:b_v^k<0\}\). A routing \(x^k\in\mathbb R_+^A\) realizes the demand when
\[\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a^k-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a^k=b_v^k\quad\text{for every }v\in V.\]
It is genuinely multiterminal when \(|S_k|+|T_k|>2\) for at least one commodity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A commodity may have several supplying and demanding terminals, encoded by a zero-sum vertex balance vector and realized by flow divergence.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,A)\text{ is finite and directed}
K\text{ is finite}
\sum_{v\in V}b_v^k=0\text{ for every }k
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{div}(x^k)=b^k\text{ with possibly }|S_k|+|T_k|>2

notation.meaning: net supply of commodity k at vertex v
source and sink terminal sets of commodity k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The balance-vector formulation is coherent, but multiterminal demand has multiple established meanings, including single-commodity multi-source balance demands and terminal-set connectivity demands. An explicit source is needed to establish the intended local convention.

children.title: Source-Structure Transition
children.top_down_role: Modeling consequences when source-centered structure is relaxed.

knowledge_statements.title: Source-Structure Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact boundary between common-source and general pairwise demand families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty pairwise demand family \(\mathcal D=\{(s_k,t_k,d_k):k\in K\}\), define the active-source set \(S(\mathcal D)=\{s_k:d_k>0\}\). Then \(\mathcal D\) is single-source exactly when \(|S(\mathcal D)|\le1\). Adding a positive-demand commodity \((s,t,d)\) preserves the single-source property precisely when the current active-source set is empty or \(s\) equals its unique member. Introducing a commodity with a different source changes the instance to a multiple-source pairwise-demand regime, while zero-demand commodities do not affect the classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A demand family remains single-source exactly while every positive-demand commodity uses the same source; the first distinct active source crosses the boundary.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal D\ne\varnothing
d_k\ge0\text{ for all }k
\mathcal D\text{ is pairwise}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal D\text{ is single-source}\iff |S(\mathcal D)|\le1

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The active-source characterization is correct only under a convention that discards zero-demand commodities for classification. That convention conflicts with the supplied Single-Source Demands definition and lacks a supporting citation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry of a real-valued function on ordered vertex pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(r:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}\) is symmetric if \(r(u,v)=r(v,u)\) for every \(u,v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued function on pairs of vertices is symmetric when interchanging its arguments does not change its value.
assumptions_latex: r:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall u,v\in V,\quad r(u,v)=r(v,u).

children.title: All-Pairs Demands
children.top_down_role: Demand systems with commodities spanning every relevant terminal pair.

knowledge_statements.title: All-Pairs Demands
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Demand support containing every distinct ordered terminal pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\subseteq V\) be a finite terminal set. An ordered all-pairs demand family specifies a value \(d_{st}\ge0\) for every \((s,t)\in T\times T\) with \(s\ne t\), treating each ordered pair as a commodity. It has full all-pairs support when \(d_{st}>0\) for every distinct \(s,t\in T\). For an undirected or symmetric convention one instead indexes unordered pairs \(\{s,t\}\) and requires \(d_{st}=d_{ts}\); the ordered and unordered conventions must not be mixed without an explicit conversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every distinct terminal pair is a commodity; directed models use ordered pairs, while undirected symmetric models may use unordered pairs.
assumptions_latex: T\subseteq V\text{ is finite}
|T|\ge2
d_{st}\ge0\text{ for distinct }s,t\in T
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal D=\{(s,t,d_{st}):s,t\in T,\ s\ne t\}

notation.meaning: demand from terminal s to terminal t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The available all-pairs locators concern shortest paths rather than demand families. A relevant source must establish whether this leaf uses ordered directed commodities, unordered symmetric commodities, and whether zero entries count as supported all-pairs demands.

children.title: Uniform Demands
children.top_down_role: Demand systems with common magnitudes across the selected commodity pairs.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Demands
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniformity concerns demand magnitudes on a fixed symmetric commodity support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T\) be a finite terminal set, let \(K\subseteq\{\{s,t\}:s,t\in T,\ s\ne t\}\), and let \(d:K\to\mathbb{R}_{+}\) be a symmetric demand family. The family is uniform if there exists \(q\ge 0\) such that
\[
d_{\{s,t\}}=q\qquad\text{for every }\{s,t\}\in K.
\]
Equivalently, its symmetric demand matrix \(D\) satisfies \(D_{st}=q\) on the prescribed support \(K\), \(D_{st}=0\) off that support, and \(D_{ss}=0\). Uniformity alone does not require \(K\) to contain every terminal pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A demand family is uniform when every commodity in its fixed symmetric support has the same nonnegative demand; the support need not contain all terminal pairs.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is finite.
\(K\) is a fixed set of unordered terminal pairs.
\(d_k\ge 0\) for every \(k\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\) is uniform exactly when \(d_k=q\) for some \(q\ge 0\) and every \(k\in K\).

children.title: Product Demands
children.top_down_role: Demand systems whose pair values arise from terminal-specific factors.

knowledge_statements.title: Product Demands
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric product demands factor into one nonnegative weight per terminal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T\) be a finite terminal set and let \(w\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{T}\). The symmetric product-demand family generated by \(w\) is the matrix \(D\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{T\times T}\) defined by
\[
D_{st}=w_s w_t\quad(s\ne t),\qquad D_{ss}=0.
\]
If only a support \(K\) is admitted, its commodity demands are \(d_{\{s,t\}}=w_s w_t\) for \(\{s,t\}\in K\), with all other pairs excluded or assigned zero demand according to the model convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Product demands assign each distinct terminal pair the product of its terminals' nonnegative weights, optionally restricted to a prescribed commodity support.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is finite.
\(w_t\ge 0\) for every \(t\in T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{st}=w_s w_t\) for distinct terminals and \(D_{ss}=0\).

children.title: Demand-Family Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Containment, specialization, plus separation across symmetric demand families.

knowledge_statements.title: Demand-Family Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates restrictions on commodity support from restrictions on demand magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a finite terminal set \(T\), an all-pairs family specifies the complete support \(K=\{\{s,t\}:s\ne t\}\) but imposes no equality among positive magnitudes. A uniform family imposes \(d_k=q\) on its chosen support. A product family imposes \(d_{\{s,t\}}=w_s w_t\). Consequently, complete-support uniform demands with \(q>0\) are product demands by taking \(w_t=\sqrt q\) for every \(t\in T\); conversely, a positive complete-support product family is uniform exactly when all terminal weights are equal, except that when \(|T|=2\) the single pair is automatically uniform.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All-pairs constrains support, while uniform and product constrain magnitudes. Equal terminal weights produce uniform all-pairs demands; with at least three terminals, uniform positive products force equal weights.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is finite.
Product weights and demands are nonnegative.
For the converse equality claim, product weights are positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(|T|\ge 3\), positive complete-support product demands are uniform if and only if \(w_t\) is constant on \(T\).

knowledge_statements.title: Demand-Graph Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A demand graph records commodities independently of the routing network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite terminal set \(T\) and a finite commodity set \(K\), a demand graph is a weighted undirected multigraph \(H=(T,K,d)\). Each commodity \(k\in K\) is an edge with distinct endpoints \(s_k,t_k\in T\) and weight \(d_k\ge 0\). Parallel edges permit distinct commodities with the same endpoint pair. When at most one commodity joins each pair, \(H\) is equivalently represented by the symmetric matrix \(D\) satisfying \(D_{st}=d_{\{s,t\}}\), \(D_{ss}=0\), and \(D_{st}=0\) for absent pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A demand graph is a weighted terminal multigraph whose edges are commodities and whose edge weights are required traffic volumes; a simple demand graph has an equivalent symmetric matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) and \(K\) are finite.
Every commodity has two distinct terminals.
\(d_k\ge 0\) for all commodities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H=(T,K,d)\) encodes commodity endpoints and magnitudes separately from the routing network.

knowledge_statements.title: Commodity-Indexed Arc-Flow Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard splittable multicommodity formulation with one arc-flow vector per commodity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with capacities \(u_a\ge 0\), and let commodity \(k\in K\) have source \(s_k\), sink \(t_k\), and demand \(d_k\ge 0\). A commodity-indexed arc-flow representation uses variables \(x_a^k\ge 0\) satisfying
\[
\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a^k-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a^k=b_v^k\quad(v\in V,k\in K),\qquad
\sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\le u_a\quad(a\in A),
\]
where \(b_{s_k}^k=d_k\), \(b_{t_k}^k=-d_k\), and \(b_v^k=0\) otherwise. These constraints represent feasible splittable routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each commodity has nonnegative flow on every arc, obeys its own source-to-sink balance equations, and shares each arc's capacity with all other commodities.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) and \(K\) are finite.
Capacities and demands are nonnegative.
Routing is splittable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed balance and shared-capacity system represents feasible commodity-indexed arc routings.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with capacities \(u_a\ge 0\), and let \(K\) be a finite commodity set. For each \(k\in K\), let \(s_k,t_k\in V\) be distinct terminals, let \(d_k\ge 0\), and let \(\mathcal P_k\) be the admitted set of simple directed \(s_k\)-to-\(t_k\) paths. A path-flow representation uses variables \(z_P^k\ge 0\) satisfying
\[
\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_k}z_P^k=d_k\quad(k\in K),\qquad
\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_k:a\in P}z_P^k\le u_a\quad(a\in A).
\]
Thus each demand is split among admitted paths, while the total flow on paths using an arc respects that arc's capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A path-flow model assigns nonnegative flow to each admitted source-to-sink path, routes each commodity's full demand, and limits the total flow on paths using an arc by that arc's capacity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circuit-variable polytope representation of multicommodity flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path-flow representation for directed or undirected capacitated multicommodity-flow feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(G,H,u,b)$ be a directed or undirected multicommodity-flow instance. Let $\mathcal C$ be the circuits of $G+H$ containing exactly one demand edge, and define incidence matrices $M\in\{0,1\}^{E(G)\times\mathcal C}$ and $N\in\{0,1\}^{E(H)\times\mathcal C}$ by $M_{eC}=1\iff e\in C$ and $N_{fC}=1\iff f\in C$. Every feasible multicommodity-flow solution has at least one representing vector in $\{y\in\mathbb R^{\mathcal C}:y\geq0,\ My\leq u,\ Ny=b\}$, and every vector in this polytope determines a unique feasible multicommodity-flow solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using nonnegative variables for circuits containing exactly one demand edge, every feasible multicommodity flow has at least one representation satisfying the supply capacities and demands, while each such circuit-variable vector determines one unique flow solution.
assumptions_latex: $(G,H,u,b)$ is a directed or undirected multicommodity-flow instance.
$\mathcal C=\{C:C\text{ is a circuit of }G+H\text{ containing exactly one edge of }H\}$.
$M_{eC}=\mathbf 1[e\in C]$ for $e\in E(G)$ and $N_{fC}=\mathbf 1[f\in C]$ for $f\in E(H)$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Each flow solution has at least one }y\geq0\text{ with }My\leq u,\ Ny=b,\text{ and each such }y\text{ determines a unique flow solution.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with capacities \(u_a\ge 0\), and let \(K\) be a finite commodity set. Suppose nonnegative commodity flows \(x_a^k\) have signed supplies \(b_v^k\), satisfy their commodity-wise balance equations, and obey \(\sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\le u_a\). Define
\[
y_a=\sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\quad(a\in A),\qquad b_v=\sum_{k\in K}b_v^k\quad(v\in V).
\]
The fully aggregated arc representation retains only
\[
y_a\ge 0,
\qquad
\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}y_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}y_a=b_v\quad(v\in V),
\qquad y_a\le u_a\quad(a\in A).
\]
Every feasible commodity-indexed routing projects to this system. The converse need not hold because aggregate balance does not preserve the prescribed pairing of commodity sources and sinks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Summing commodity flows gives a nonnegative aggregate arc flow that satisfies aggregate balance and capacity constraints. This projection discards commodity identity, so aggregate feasibility need not imply feasible routing for each prescribed source-sink pair.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with capacities \(u_a\ge 0\), let \(K\) be a finite commodity set, and let \(\Pi\) be a partition of \(K\). Given commodity arc flows \(x_a^k\) with signed supplies \(b_v^k\), define for every \(B\in\Pi\)
\[
z_a^B=\sum_{k\in B}x_a^k\quad(a\in A),\qquad b_v^B=\sum_{k\in B}b_v^k\quad(v\in V).
\]
A partially disaggregated arc representation retains the constraints
\[
z_a^B\ge 0,
\qquad
\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}z_a^B-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}z_a^B=b_v^B\quad(v\in V,B\in\Pi),
\qquad
\sum_{B\in\Pi}z_a^B\le u_a\quad(a\in A).
\]
The singleton partition recovers commodity indexing, while the one-block partition \(\{K\}\) gives full aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partition of the commodity set defines one nonnegative arc flow and one balance equation per block. Singleton blocks give commodity indexing, while a single block gives complete aggregation.

children.title: Aggregation Granularity
children.top_down_role: Intermediate grouping choices across the representation hierarchy.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation Granularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partition refinement orders block-flow relaxations by retained commodity information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Pi'\) refine a partition \(\Pi\) of \(K\). Every feasible \(\Pi'\)-block flow projects to a feasible \(\Pi\)-block flow through
\[
z_a^B=\sum_{B'\in\Pi':B'\subseteq B}z_a^{B'}
\qquad(a\in A,B\in\Pi).
\]
Hence, after projection to common design and total-load variables, the feasible region produced by the finer partition is contained in that produced by the coarser partition. For a minimization model whose objective depends only on those common variables, the relaxation value for \(\Pi\) is no greater than the relaxation value for \(\Pi'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refining commodity blocks preserves more information and yields a tighter projected relaxation; coarsening blocks enlarges the relaxation and cannot improve a minimization lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(\Pi'\) refines \(\Pi\).
Both models use identical network and capacity constraints.
The compared objective depends only on common design or total-load variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}(F_{\Pi'})\subseteq\operatorname{proj}(F_{\Pi})\), and therefore \(v_{\Pi}\le v_{\Pi'}\) for minimization relaxations.

notation.meaning: feasible region of the partition-based model

children.title: Representation-Fidelity Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Fidelity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate balance cannot generally certify prescribed source–sink pairings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the directed graph on \(\{s_1,s_2,t_1,t_2\}\) having only arcs \((s_1,t_2)\) and \((s_2,t_1)\), each of capacity one. Let two unit commodities require routing from \(s_1\) to \(t_1\) and from \(s_2\) to \(t_2\). Assigning one unit to each arc satisfies aggregate capacity and aggregate balance: each \(s_i\) has net outflow one and each \(t_i\) has net inflow one. Nevertheless, neither required source–sink path exists. Thus complete aggregation is a strict relaxation once distinct commodity pairings matter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Crossed arcs satisfy total source and sink balances but connect each source to the wrong sink, proving that fully aggregated feasibility need not preserve commodity pairings.
assumptions_latex: Flows are directed and splittable.
Each of the two demands and arc capacities equals one.
No arcs other than the two displayed crossed arcs exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The aggregate model is feasible, but the commodity-indexed routing model is infeasible.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph and let \(K\) be a finite commodity set. For each \(k\in K\), let \(\mathcal P_k\) be a set of directed \(s_k\)-to-\(t_k\) paths and let \(z_P^k\ge 0\) for \(P\in\mathcal P_k\). Define the arc-path projection by
\[
x_a^k=\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_k}\mathbf 1_{\{a\in P\}}z_P^k
\qquad(a\in A,k\in K).
\]
If \(\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_k}z_P^k=d_k\) for every \(k\in K\), then \(x^k\) satisfies commodity \(k\)'s flow-balance equations with value \(d_k\). Moreover,
\[
\sum_{k\in K}x_a^k=\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_k:a\in P}z_P^k\qquad(a\in A),
\]
so the shared path-capacity inequalities project to the corresponding shared arc-capacity inequalities with identical arc loads.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite directed graph and commodity set, summing each commodity's path weights over the paths containing an arc defines its arc flow. This map preserves commodity balances and total capacity usage on every arc.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite nonnegative directed flow decomposes into source–sink paths and circulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, and let \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{A}\) have divergence \(d>0\) at \(s\), divergence \(-d\) at \(t\), and zero divergence elsewhere. Then there exist simple directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) paths \(P_i\), directed simple cycles \(C_j\), and positive coefficients \(\lambda_i,\mu_j\) such that
\[
x=\sum_i\lambda_i\chi^{P_i}+\sum_j\mu_j\chi^{C_j},
\qquad
\sum_i\lambda_i=d.
\]
The total number of paths and cycles can be chosen no larger than the number of arcs on which \(x\) is positive. If \(x\) contains no positive directed circulation, the cycle terms are unnecessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite nonnegative source-to-sink arc flow is a positive combination of simple source-to-sink paths and directed cycles; cycle-free flows need only paths.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and directed.
\(x_a\ge 0\) for every arc.
The divergence of \(x\) is \(d\) at \(s\), \(-d\) at \(t\), and zero elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) admits the displayed path-and-cycle decomposition with \(\sum_i\lambda_i=d\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arc-Flow and Path-Flow Representations of Multicommodity Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent representations of undirected multicommodity flows, with optional shared edge capacities and preservation of integral or half-integral values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph with distinct commodity pairs \(\{r_i,s_i\}\), \(i=1,\ldots,k\). A multicommodity flow can be represented either by an orientation of \(G\) and an \((r_i,s_i)\)-flow \(x_i\) for each commodity, or by terminal-pair paths \(P_j\) with weights \(\lambda_j\in\mathbb Q_+\). Under an edge-capacity function \(c:E\to\mathbb Q_+\), the aggregate load on each edge must not exceed its capacity. The two representations can be converted into one another in polynomial time while preserving every commodity value and feasibility for the same capacity functions. If the values of the \(x_i\) are integral or half-integral, the \(\lambda_j\) may be chosen integral or half-integral, respectively, and conversely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An undirected multicommodity flow can be represented by one oriented terminal-to-terminal flow per commodity or by nonnegative rational weights on terminal-pair paths. The representations are polynomial-time equivalent and preserve commodity values, shared-capacity feasibility, and integral or half-integral structure.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is an undirected graph}
\{r_i,s_i\}\subseteq V\text{ are distinct commodity pairs for }i=1,\ldots,k
c:E\to\mathbb Q_+\text{ when capacities are imposed}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The arc-flow and weighted-path representations are polynomial-time equivalent and preserve values, capacity feasibility, and integral or half-integral structure.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph. For each commodity \(k\), let \(s_k,t_k\in V\) be distinct and let \(x^k\in\mathbb{R}_+^A\) satisfy flow conservation at every vertex in \(V\setminus\{s_k,t_k\}\), with nonnegative net outflow from \(s_k\). Then there are nonnegative weights \(y_P^k\) on directed \(s_k\)-\(t_k\) paths and nonnegative weights \(z_C^k\) on directed cycles such that
\[
x_a^k=\sum_{P\ni a}y_P^k+\sum_{C\ni a}z_C^k\qquad(a\in A).
\]
Conversely, every such collection defines a nonnegative arc flow with the stated conservation equations and source-to-sink value \(\sum_P y_P^k\). If there is no nonzero nonnegative circulation \(c^k\) satisfying \(c^k\le x^k\) componentwise, the cycle weights may all be chosen as zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite nonnegative source-to-sink arc flow decomposes into nonnegative source-to-sink path flows and directed circulations, and every such collection projects back to the corresponding conserved arc flow. Paths alone suffice when the arc flow contains no nonzero dominated circulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a directed cycle, let \(s,t\in V\) be distinct, and define \(x\in\mathbb{R}_+^A\) by \(x_a=1\) for every \(a\in A\). Then \(x\) is a nonzero circulation of zero \(s\)-\(t\) value, and there are no nonnegative weights \(y_P\) on directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths satisfying
\[
x_a=\sum_{P\ni a}y_P\qquad(a\in A).
\]
Consequently, path-only decomposition does not cover arc flows containing an uncancelled circulation; cycle terms must be admitted or the circulation must first be removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit flow around a directed cycle is a nonzero zero-value circulation and has no nonnegative source-to-sink path-only decomposition. Cycle terms or prior circulation removal are therefore necessary.

knowledge_statements.title: Edge Capacities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shared capacities in undirected multicommodity networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph and let \(u_e\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\) be the capacity of edge \(e\). For commodity set \(K\), an edge-indexed multiflow \(x=(x_e^k)\) respects edge capacities when
\[
\sum_{k\in K}x_e^k\le u_e\qquad(e\in E),
\]
where \(x_e^k\ge0\) is the total amount of commodity \(k\) using \(e\), irrespective of traversal direction. In a path formulation with nonnegative path weights \(y_P^k\), the same condition is \(\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{P\ni e}y_P^k\le u_e\). Thus both directions and all commodities consume one shared physical-edge resource.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An undirected edge capacity bounds the combined traffic of every commodity and both traversal directions using that physical edge.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and \(u\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{E}\).
All commodity flows or path weights are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{k\in K}x_e^k\le u_e\) for every \(e\in E\).

notation.meaning: total commodity-k use of edge e

knowledge_statements.title: Arc Capacities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direction-specific capacities in directed multicommodity networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed graph and let \(u_a\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\) be the capacity of arc \(a\). A nonnegative multiflow \(x=(x_a^k)\), indexed by commodities \(k\in K\), respects arc capacities when
\[
\sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\le u_a\qquad(a\in A).
\]
The capacity of \(a=(v,w)\) constrains only traffic traversing from \(v\) to \(w\); traffic on a reverse arc \((w,v)\), when present, is governed by its own capacity. In a path formulation the left-hand side equals \(\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{P\ni a}y_P^k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed arc capacity bounds aggregate commodity flow in that arc’s direction; a reverse arc has a separate constraint and capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is finite and \(u\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{A}\).
Every \(x_a^k\) is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Commodity-Weighted Shared Arc Capacity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalization of homogeneous capacity consumption in an arc-capacitated multicommodity-flow model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If one unit of commodity \(k\) on arc \((i,j)\) consumes \(\rho_{ij}^k\) units of the shared arc resource, the bundle constraint becomes
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{K}\rho_{ij}^k x_{ij}^k\le u_{ij}\qquad((i,j)\in A).
\]
The homogeneous-goods model is the specialization \(\rho_{ij}^k=1\) for every arc and commodity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When commodities consume different amounts of an arc's shared resource, each flow is weighted by its commodity- and arc-specific consumption coefficient. Unit coefficients recover the homogeneous model.

knowledge_statements.title: Node Capacities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shared transit capacities at vertices of a multicommodity network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a network with node capacities \(b_v\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\). For a path multiflow with nonnegative weights \(y_P^k\), the transit load at node \(v\) is
\[
L_v=\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{P:\,v\in\operatorname{int}(P)}y_P^k.
\]
The multiflow respects node capacities if \(L_v\le b_v\) for every capacitated node \(v\). Here only internal occurrences of \(v\) are counted; whether source and sink incidences consume capacity is a separate modeling convention that must be specified. For simple paths, each path contributes its weight at most once to a node’s transit load.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node capacity bounds total multiflow passing internally through that node; endpoint traffic is counted only if the model explicitly adopts that convention.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) and the commodity set \(K\) are finite.
Path weights are nonnegative and paths are simple.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{P:\,v\in\operatorname{int}(P)}y_P^k\le b_v\) for every capacitated \(v\).

notation.meaning: aggregate transit load at node v

children.top_down_role: Scope-preserving transformations among edge-, arc-, plus node-capacitated formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Location Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact node-splitting and edge-subdivision reductions preserving path multiflows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed network, replace each capacitated node \(v\) by \(v^{\mathrm{in}}\), \(v^{\mathrm{out}}\), and an arc \(a_v=(v^{\mathrm{in}},v^{\mathrm{out}})\) of capacity \(b_v\); redirect every entering arc to \(v^{\mathrm{in}}\) and every leaving arc from \(v^{\mathrm{out}}\). Then feasible path multiflows correspond bijectively, and transit load at \(v\) equals flow on \(a_v\). Conversely, for an undirected capacitated edge \(e=\{u,v\}\), subdivide it as \(u-x_e-v\) and give the new node \(x_e\) capacity \(u_e\). Path expansion and contraction preserve commodity values, shared resource loads, and integrality whenever all introduced capacities and original path weights use the same integrality lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Node splitting converts node capacities to arc capacities, while edge subdivision converts undirected edge capacities to node capacities, preserving feasible path multiflows and loads.
assumptions_latex: Paths do not use a split or subdivision gadget more than once.
Endpoint-capacity conventions are preserved when terminals are transformed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated gadget maps give load-preserving bijections between the corresponding feasible path-multiflow sets.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the reduction container and the gadgets are plausible under the stated simple-path and endpoint conventions. No source is supplied for the claimed bijections or preservation of the integrality lattice, so those claims require an authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Multiflows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous path-weight regime for finite multicommodity flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) be a finite network, let \(K\) be a finite commodity set, and let \(\mathcal P_k\) be the admissible paths for commodity \(k\). A fractional multiflow is a family
\[
y=(y_P^k: k\in K,\ P\in\mathcal P_k),\qquad y_P^k\in\mathbb{R}_{+},
\]
whose induced resource loads satisfy the specified capacity constraints. Its routed value for commodity \(k\) is \(r_k=\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_k}y_P^k\). If demands \(d_k\) are prescribed, feasibility additionally requires \(r_k=d_k\), or \(r_k\ge d_k\) when over-routing is allowed. No arithmetic restriction beyond nonnegativity is imposed on path weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fractional multiflow assigns arbitrary nonnegative real weights to admissible commodity paths while satisfying capacities and any prescribed routing requirements.
assumptions_latex: The network, commodity set, and admissible path families are finite.
Resource capacities and demands are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_P^k\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\), the induced loads obey capacity constraints, and prescribed routed-value constraints hold.

notation.meaning: weight of commodity k on path P
total routed value of commodity k

knowledge_statements.title: Half-Integral Multiflows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path-weight half-integrality relative to a fixed unit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a flow unit \(\delta>0\). A feasible path multiflow \(y=(y_P^k)\) is half-integral relative to \(\delta\) if
\[
y_P^k\in (\delta/2)\mathbb{Z}_{+}
\qquad(k\in K,\ P\in\mathcal P_k).
\]
Under the customary normalization \(\delta=1\), every path weight is a nonnegative multiple of \(1/2\). Consequently, induced arc, edge, and node loads and each routed value \(r_k=\sum_P y_P^k\) also lie in \((\delta/2)\mathbb{Z}_{+}\). Half-integrality concerns the chosen path decomposition; an arc-flow vector should be called half-integral only when its arc coordinates satisfy the corresponding lattice condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A half-integral path multiflow uses weights in nonnegative multiples of one-half of the chosen flow unit; its induced loads and routed values share that lattice.
assumptions_latex: A positive flow unit \(\delta\) and finite admissible path families are fixed.
The multiflow satisfies all underlying feasibility constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_P^k\in(\delta/2)\mathbb{Z}_{+}\) for every commodity-path pair.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The path-weight definition and its lattice consequences are internally correct, but no source is given for the selected path-based half-integrality convention or its distinction from coordinatewise arc half-integrality.

children.title: Integral Multiflows
children.top_down_role: Routing regimes requiring integral path or flow values.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Multiflows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path-weight integrality relative to a fixed flow unit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a flow unit \(\delta>0\). A feasible path multiflow \(y=(y_P^k)\) is integral relative to \(\delta\) if
\[
y_P^k\in\delta\mathbb{Z}_{+}
\qquad(k\in K,\ P\in\mathcal P_k).
\]
With the normalization \(\delta=1\), every path carries an integer amount of its commodity. The induced resource loads and routed values are then integral. For unit demands, an integral feasible multiflow may select one path per commodity, but this equivalence requires the demand equality \(\sum_P y_P^k=1\); integrality alone permits a commodity to use several paths with positive integer weights when its routed value exceeds one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral path multiflow assigns nonnegative integer multiples of a chosen unit to paths; unit-demand equality then forces exactly one selected path per routed commodity.
assumptions_latex: A positive flow unit \(\delta\) and finite admissible path families are fixed.
The multiflow satisfies all capacity and routed-value constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_P^k\in\delta\mathbb{Z}_{+}\) for every commodity-path pair.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexamples showing that the implications from fractional to half-integral and from half-integral to integral fail in general for path-weight regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Relative to flow unit \(1\), every integral multiflow is half-integral and every half-integral multiflow is fractional, but neither converse holds in general. On a single edge of capacity \(1\), one commodity with required routed value \(1/2\) has a half-integral feasible path weight that is not integral; required value \(1/3\) instead gives a fractional feasible path weight that is not half-integral. With integral data, let \(G\) be the undirected cycle \(v_1v_2v_3v_4v_1\), give every edge capacity \(1\), and introduce unit-demand commodities \((v_1,v_3)\) and \((v_2,v_4)\). Assigning weight \(1/2\) to each of the two cycle paths available to each commodity is feasible, while no integral path routing is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral multiflows are always half-integral, and half-integral multiflows are always fractional, but the reverse implications fail. children.title: Unsplittable Routing
children.top_down_role: Commodity routing subject to single-path or indivisible-flow requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Unsplittable Routing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-path routing for each positive-demand commodity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let commodity \(k\in K\) have terminals \((s_k,t_k)\), demand \(d_k>0\), and admissible path family \(\mathcal P_k\). An unsplittable routing chooses exactly one path \(P_k\in\mathcal P_k\) and sends all \(d_k\) units on it. Equivalently, binary variables \(z_P^k\in\{0,1\}\) satisfy
\[
\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_k}z_P^k=1,
\qquad
\sum_{k\in K}d_k\sum_{P\ni r}z_P^k\le u_r
\]
for every capacitated resource \(r\). Thus a commodity may not divide its demand among multiple paths, although different commodities may share resources within their capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unsplittable routing assigns every commodity to one admissible path and sends its entire demand there, while aggregate resource loads remain within capacity.
assumptions_latex: The commodity set and each admissible path family are finite.
Each demand is positive and each resource has nonnegative capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one \(z_P^k\) equals \(1\) for each \(k\), and every resource load is at most \(u_r\).

children.title: Congestion-Bounded Routing
children.top_down_role: Routing regimes permitting controlled capacity overload.

knowledge_statements.title: Congestion-Bounded Routing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum normalized resource load under a prescribed congestion allowance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let each capacitated resource \(r\in R\) have capacity \(u_r>0\), and let a routing induce load \(L_r\ge0\). Its congestion is
\[
\operatorname{cong}(L)=\max_{r\in R}\frac{L_r}{u_r}.
\]
For a prescribed factor \(\rho\ge1\), the routing is \(\rho\)-congestion-bounded precisely when \(L_r\le\rho u_r\) for every \(r\in R\), equivalently \(\operatorname{cong}(L)\le\rho\). The case \(\rho=1\) is ordinary capacity feasibility. This predicate applies to fractional, integral, or unsplittable routings once the corresponding resource loads have been defined; it relaxes capacities without changing commodity demands or their routing regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A routing has congestion at most rho when every resource load is at most rho times capacity; rho equal to one recovers ordinary capacity feasibility.
assumptions_latex: The resource set \(R\) is finite and every \(u_r>0\).
The routing induces well-defined nonnegative loads \(L_r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cong}(L)\le\rho\iff L_r\le\rho u_r\) for all \(r\in R\).

knowledge_statements.title: Bicriteria Routing Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost–congestion bicriteria convention for capacitated multicommodity routing and network design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance with edge capacities \(u_e>0\), let \(x\) be a routing-design solution, let \(L_e(x)\) be its load on edge \(e\), and let \(c(x)\ge 0\) be its design cost. Define its congestion by \(\gamma(x)=\max_e L_e(x)/u_e\), and let \(\mathrm{OPT}_1=\inf\{c(z):\gamma(z)\le 1\}\). For factors \(\alpha,\beta\ge 1\), an \((\alpha,\beta)\)-bicriteria solution satisfies \[c(x)\le \alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}_1\qquad\text{and}\qquad \gamma(x)\le\beta.\] A bicriteria routing regime specifies which routing restrictions, such as splittability or integrality, apply to both \(x\) and the benchmark defining \(\mathrm{OPT}_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An (α,β)-bicriteria solution costs at most α times the unit-congestion optimum while using at most β times every edge capacity, under a fixed routing model.
assumptions_latex: \(u_e>0\) for every capacitated edge \(e\).
The comparison solution and benchmark use the same splittability and integrality conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c(x)\le\alpha\mathrm{OPT}_1\) and \(\max_e L_e(x)/u_e\le\beta\).

children.title: Congestion-Repair Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Instances where bounded overload cannot recover desired unsplittable routing quality.

knowledge_statements.title: Congestion-Repair Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp separation between fractional and unsplittable congestion on parallel edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every integer \(k\ge 2\), consider two vertices joined by \(k\) parallel edges, each of capacity \(1/k\), and one unit-demand commodity between the vertices. A splittable routing sends \(1/k\) on each edge and has congestion \(1\). Every unsplittable routing must send the entire unit on one edge and therefore has congestion \(k\). Consequently, converting an arbitrary fractional routing into an unsplittable routing while preserving all demands admits no instance-independent constant congestion-repair factor when individual demand may exceed individual edge capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unit demand split across k edges has congestion one, but every unsplittable routing has congestion k; constant repair is impossible without demand-to-capacity restrictions.
assumptions_latex: One commodity has demand \(1\), and each of the \(k\) parallel edges has capacity \(1/k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{\mathrm{fractional}}=1\) while \(\gamma_{\mathrm{unsplittable}}=k\).

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Cut Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary directed-cut inequalities for fractional multicommodity feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) have arc capacities \(u_a\ge0\), and let commodities \(i\in K\) have ordered terminals \((s_i,t_i)\) and demands \(d_i\ge0\). For \(S\subset V\), write \(\delta^+(S)=\{(v,w)\in A:v\in S,\ w\notin S\}\). The directed cut condition is \[\sum_{i:s_i\in S,\ t_i\notin S}d_i\le\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}u_a\qquad(S\subset V).\] Every feasible fractional directed multicommodity flow satisfies these inequalities. The reverse-oriented inequality is obtained separately by applying the condition to \(V\setminus S\); it is not interchangeable with the displayed inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Across every directed cut, total demand whose source is inside and sink outside cannot exceed the capacity of arcs leaving the cut.
assumptions_latex: Arc capacities and commodity demands are nonnegative.
Each commodity is routed from its ordered source to its ordered sink with flow conservation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i:s_i\in S,\ t_i\notin S}d_i\le u(\delta^+(S))\) for every \(S\subset V\).

knowledge_statements.title: Undirected Cut Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary undirected-cut inequalities for fractional multicommodity feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph with capacities \(u_e\ge0\), and let commodities \(i\in K\) have unordered terminal pairs \(\{s_i,t_i\}\) and demands \(d_i\ge0\). For \(S\subset V\), let \(\delta(S)\) contain the edges with exactly one endpoint in \(S\). The undirected cut condition is \[\sum_{i:\lvert\{s_i,t_i\}\cap S\rvert=1}d_i\le\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}u_e\qquad(S\subset V).\] Every feasible fractional undirected multicommodity flow satisfies this condition because every unit routed between separated terminals crosses \(\delta(S)\) with net amount one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every vertex cut, the total demand separated by that cut cannot exceed the total capacity of edges crossing it.
assumptions_latex: Edge capacities and demands are nonnegative.
Each commodity obeys flow conservation between its terminal pair.

knowledge_statements.title: Orientation-Sensitive Cut Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed sparsest-cut versus maximum-concurrent-flow gap under ordered terminal demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed capacitated graph with ordered demands, define \(d^+(S)=\sum_{i:s_i\in S,\ t_i\notin S}d_i\) and \[\Phi^+=\min_{S:d^+(S)>0}\frac{u(\delta^+(S))}{d^+(S)}.\] Let \(\lambda^*\) be the largest common fraction of every demand routable simultaneously. The orientation-sensitive cut gap is \(g^+=\Phi^+/\lambda^*\) when \(0<\lambda^*<\infty\). Directed cut necessity gives \(\lambda^*\le\Phi^+\), hence \(g^+\ge1\). Both \(\Phi^+\) and \(g^+\) depend on arc orientation and ordered terminals; replacing arcs by undirected edges changes the admissible cut ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directed cut gap is the sparsest directed-cut value divided by maximum concurrent throughput; it is at least one and depends on arc orientation.
assumptions_latex: At least one demand is positive.
\(0<\lambda^*<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g^+=\Phi^+/\lambda^*\ge1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Eulerian Demand–Supply Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected parity convention for Eulerian supply–demand instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E_G)\) be an undirected supply multigraph and \(H=(V,E_H)\) an undirected demand multigraph, where multiplicity represents integral capacity or demand. The pair \((G,H)\) is Eulerian if their multigraph union is Eulerian, equivalently \[\deg_G(v)+\deg_H(v)\equiv0\pmod 2\qquad\text{for every }v\in V.\] For integer-valued capacities and demands, replace each edge by the corresponding number of parallel copies before applying this predicate. This parity condition defines an Eulerian demand–supply regime; it does not by itself assert that the cut condition is sufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An undirected supply–demand pair is Eulerian when supply degree plus demand degree is even at every vertex, counting integer multiplicities.

The regime is undirected.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Condition Sufficiency Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between single-commodity sufficiency and general multicommodity necessity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a capacitated network, the cut condition is always necessary for routing prescribed demands. For one commodity, it is also sufficient: a demand \(d\) from \(s\) to \(t\) is fractionally routable if and only if \[d\le u(\delta^+(S))\quad\text{for every directed }s\text{–}t\text{ cut }S,\] with \(\delta(S)\) in the undirected case. For two or more commodities, the analogous family of aggregate cut inequalities is not sufficient on arbitrary graphs. Thus any multicommodity sufficiency assertion requires additional hypotheses on topology, demand placement, orientation, parity, or the permitted congestion factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut inequalities exactly characterize single-commodity fractional feasibility, but in unrestricted multicommodity networks they are only necessary unless additional structure is imposed.
assumptions_latex: Capacities and demands are nonnegative.
Routing is fractional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{single commodity: cut condition}\iff\text{feasibility};\quad\text{general multicommodity: cut condition}\not\Rightarrow\text{feasibility}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Condition Failure Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd-spindle instance where every cut inequality holds but fractional routing is impossible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the unit-capacity supply graph be \(K_{2,3}\), with hubs \(a,b\) and leaves \(x_1,x_2,x_3\). knowledge_statements.title: Length-Metric Duals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shortest-path length dual of undirected maximum concurrent flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be undirected with capacities \(u_e\ge0\), and let demands \(d_i>0\) join \(s_i\) to \(t_i\). If \(\lambda^*\) is the maximum common fraction of all demands routable fractionally, then linear-programming duality gives \[\lambda^*=\min_{\ell\in\mathbb R_+^E:\,\sum_i d_i\operatorname{dist}_\ell(s_i,t_i)>0}\frac{\sum_{e\in E}u_e\ell_e}{\sum_i d_i\operatorname{dist}_\ell(s_i,t_i)}.\] Equivalently, normalize the denominator to one and minimize \(\sum_eu_e\ell_e\). Thus a nonnegative edge-length assignment, through its induced shortest-path semimetric, is a dual certificate bounding concurrent throughput.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum concurrent flow equals the minimum ratio of capacity-weighted edge length to demand-weighted terminal distance over nonnegative edge lengths.
assumptions_latex: The finite graph admits a path between every positive-demand terminal pair.
Routing is fractional and capacities are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda^*=\min_{\ell\ge0}(\sum_eu_e\ell_e)/(\sum_i d_i\operatorname{dist}_\ell(s_i,t_i))\).

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Cone Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral cone of finite semimetrics on a fixed vertex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite set \(V\), the metric cone is \[\operatorname{MET}(V)=\left\{d\in\mathbb R^{\binom V2}:d_{ij}\ge0,\ d_{ij}=d_{ji},\ d_{ii}=0,\ d_{ij}\le d_{ik}+d_{kj}\ \text{for all distinct }i,j,k\in V\right\}.\] Its elements are semimetrics because distinct vertices may have distance zero. The homogeneous nonnegativity and triangle inequalities make \(\operatorname{MET}(V)\) a closed convex polyhedral cone, and addition or nonnegative scaling of semimetrics remains in the cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The metric cone consists of all nonnegative symmetric finite semimetrics satisfying every triangle inequality; it is a closed convex polyhedral cone.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{MET}(V)\) is the polyhedral cone defined by nonnegativity and triangle inequalities.

notation.meaning: distance coordinate for the unordered pair of vertices i and j

children.title: Cut-Cone Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric structure generated by cut metrics.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Cone Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic hull of two-partition semimetrics on a fixed vertex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each nonempty proper subset \(S\subset V\), define the cut semimetric \(\delta_S\) by \(\delta_S(i,j)=1\) when exactly one of \(i,j\) lies in \(S\), and \(0\) otherwise. The cut cone is \[\operatorname{CUT}(V)=\operatorname{cone}\{\delta_S:\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\}=\left\{\sum_S\alpha_S\delta_S:\alpha_S\ge0\right\}.\] Because every cut semimetric satisfies the triangle inequalities, \(\operatorname{CUT}(V)\subseteq\operatorname{MET}(V)\). The cone is finitely generated and therefore polyhedral; complementary sets define the same generator because \(\delta_S=\delta_{V\setminus S}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cut cone is the conic hull of all two-partition semimetrics; it is finitely generated, polyhedral, and contained in the metric cone.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and has at least two elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{CUT}(V)=\operatorname{cone}\{\delta_S\}\subseteq\operatorname{MET}(V)\).

notation.meaning: semimetric induced by the cut with shore S
