intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cut-cone definition, complementary-shore identity, finite generation, and inclusion in the metric cone are mathematically correct, and definition is the appropriate content kind. An authoritative metric-polyhedra source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Cone Inclusion Relations
children.top_down_role: Containment, projection, plus separation between metric-cone and cut-cone structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone Inclusion Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite semimetric and cut cones on a fixed labeled ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite with \(|V|=n\). For every nonempty proper subset \(S\subset V\), define \(\delta_S(i,j)=1\) exactly when \(|\{i,j\}\cap S|=1\), and define it as \(0\) otherwise. The cut cone and semimetric cone satisfy \[\operatorname{CUT}_n:=\operatorname{cone}\{\delta_S:\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\}\subseteq\operatorname{MET}_n,\] because each cut semimetric obeys nonnegativity, symmetry, zero diagonal, and all triangle inequalities. Moreover, \(\operatorname{CUT}_n=\operatorname{MET}_n\) for \(n\le 4\), whereas \(\operatorname{CUT}_n\subsetneq\operatorname{MET}_n\) for \(n\ge 5\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonnegative combination of cut distances is a semimetric. The two cones coincide through four points and differ from five points onward.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite labeled set with \(|V|=n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{CUT}_n\subseteq\operatorname{MET}_n\), with equality exactly when \(n\le 4\).

notation.meaning: cone of semimetrics on an n-element labeled set
semimetric induced by the cut with shore S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cone inclusion and sharp equality boundary are mathematically standard and fit the property container, but no inspectable source locator is supplied.

children.title: Non-Cut Metric Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Metric regions lacking exact representation through cut combinations.

knowledge_statements.title: Non-Cut Metric Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A five-point semimetric outside the cut cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=A\mathbin{\dot\cup}B\) with \(|A|=3\) and \(|B|=2\), and let \(d\) be the shortest-path metric of the complete bipartite graph \(K_{3,2}\) with unit edges. Thus distinct vertices in the same part have distance \(2\), while vertices in different parts have distance \(1\). Then \(d\in\operatorname{MET}_5\), but \[\sum_{\{i,j\}\subseteq A}d_{ij}+\sum_{\{i,j\}\subseteq B}d_{ij}=8>6=\sum_{i\in A,\,j\in B}d_{ij}.\] Every cut semimetric satisfies the reverse inequality, so \(d\notin\operatorname{CUT}_5\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit shortest-path metric of the complete bipartite graph with parts of sizes three and two is a five-point semimetric that is not cut-decomposable.
assumptions_latex: \(d\) is the unit-edge shortest-path metric of \(K_{3,2}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\in\operatorname{MET}_5\setminus\operatorname{CUT}_5\).

notation.meaning: the two vertex parts of the complete bipartite graph
shortest-path distance between vertices i and j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The five-point K_{3,2} metric and displayed separating inequality are coherent and fit a counterexample container, but the claim has no cited source.

children.title: Distance Realizability
children.top_down_role: Graph-metric structures realizable by the relevant network or terminal configurations.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance Realizability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact realization of a finite semimetric by an \(L_1\) embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A semimetric \(d:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) on a finite set \(V\) is \(L_1\)-realizable if there exist a measure space \((\Omega,\mu)\) and functions \(f_v\in L_1(\Omega,\mu)\) for all \(v\in V\) such that \[d(u,v)=\lVert f_u-f_v\rVert_1\qquad\text{for every }u,v\in V.\] The realization is isometric: no multiplicative distortion or additive error is permitted. Coincident images are allowed precisely when \(d(u,v)=0\) for distinct vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite semimetric is distance-realizable when its pairwise distances are exactly the L1 distances among a collection of representing points.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
\(d\) is a semimetric on \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\) is \(L_1\)-realizable exactly when such \((\Omega,\mu)\) and \((f_v)_{v\in V}\) exist.

notation.meaning: space of integrable functions modulo almost-everywhere equality
point representing vertex v in L1

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is precise and appropriate for finite exact L1 realizability, but no authoritative definition or section locator is cited.

children.title: Cut Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Representation of relevant distances through weighted cut metrics.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite nonnegative representation by elementary cut semimetrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite, and let \(\mathcal R\) contain exactly one member of each complementary pair \(S,V\setminus S\) of nonempty proper subsets of \(V\). A cut decomposition of a semimetric \(d\) is a family \((\lambda_S)_{S\in\mathcal R}\) with \(\lambda_S\ge0\) such that \[d(u,v)=\sum_{S\in\mathcal R}\lambda_S\delta_S(u,v)\qquad\text{for all }u,v\in V.\] Here \(\delta_S(u,v)=1\) when exactly one of \(u,v\) belongs to \(S\), and \(\delta_S(u,v)=0\) otherwise. Equivalently, this is a conic representation of \(d\) in \(\operatorname{CUT}_{|V|}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut decomposition represents each distance as a nonnegative weighted sum of indicators of cuts separating the corresponding pair.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
\(d:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) is a semimetric.
\(\mathcal R\) contains one representative from each complementary pair of nontrivial cuts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d=\sum_{S\in\mathcal R}\lambda_S\delta_S\) with \(\lambda_S\ge0\) for every \(S\in\mathcal R\).

notation.meaning: representative family of complementary pairs of nontrivial cuts
nonnegative weight assigned to the represented cut
elementary cut semimetric associated with S

children.title: Realizability–Decomposition Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural links between realizable distances and cut-based representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Realizability–Decomposition Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite \(L_1\)-metric characterization by cut-cone membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite and let \(d\) be a semimetric on \(V\). The following are equivalent: \(d\) admits an isometric realization in an \(L_1\) space; there are nonnegative coefficients \(\lambda_S\), indexed by nontrivial cuts of \(V\), for which \[d(u,v)=\sum_S\lambda_S\delta_S(u,v)\qquad\text{for all }u,v\in V;\] and \(d\in\operatorname{CUT}_{|V|}\). Thus exact finite \(L_1\)-realizability is identical to nonnegative cut decomposability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite semimetric embeds isometrically into L1 exactly when it is a nonnegative weighted sum of cut semimetrics.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
\(d\) is a semimetric on \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\text{ is }L_1\text{-realizable}\iff d=\sum_S\lambda_S\delta_S\text{ with }\lambda_S\ge0\iff d\in\operatorname{CUT}_{|V|}\).

notation.meaning: cut semimetric of the nontrivial subset S
weight of cut S in the decomposition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite L1-realizability characterization is correctly stated as a theorem and matches the container, but its equivalence requires an authoritative theorem or section locator.

children.title: Nondecomposable Distance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Metric families outside exact cut-decomposition regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Nondecomposable Distance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of exact cut decomposition beyond four points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite set \(V\) with \(|V|\le4\), every semimetric on \(V\) has a nonnegative cut decomposition. For every \(n\ge5\), there exists an \(n\)-point semimetric outside \(\operatorname{CUT}_n\), hence without an isometric \(L_1\) realization. At \(n=5\), the unit shortest-path metric of \(K_{3,2}\) is such an example. For larger \(n\), adjoining duplicate points preserves its nondecomposable five-point restriction. Consequently, exact cut decomposability ceases to be universal precisely at five points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All semimetrics on at most four points decompose into cuts; from five points onward, nondecomposable and non-L1-realizable semimetrics exist.
assumptions_latex: \(n\) is a positive integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{MET}_n=\operatorname{CUT}_n\) for \(n\le4\), while \(\operatorname{MET}_n\setminus\operatorname{CUT}_n\ne\varnothing\) for \(n\ge5\).

notation.meaning: complete bipartite graph with parts of sizes three and two

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sharp five-point failure boundary and restriction argument are coherent and appropriately classified as a failure boundary, but no supporting locator is supplied.

children.title: Sparsest Cut
children.top_down_role: Cut objectives normalized by separated commodity demand.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparsest Cut
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-to-separated-demand formulation for undirected multicommodity instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with capacities \(c_e\ge0\) and symmetric pair demands \(D_{uv}=D_{vu}\ge0\). For \(S\subset V\), define \(c(\delta(S))=\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}c_e\) and \(D(S,V\setminus S)=\sum_{u\in S,\,v\notin S}D_{uv}\). For a cut with positive separated demand, its sparsity is \[\Phi(S)=\frac{c(\delta(S))}{D(S,V\setminus S)}.\] Provided some cut separates positive demand, the sparsest-cut value is \[\Phi^*=\min\{\Phi(S):\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V,\ D(S,V\setminus S)>0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sparsest-cut value is the minimum, over cuts separating positive demand, of crossing capacity divided by separated demand.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
\(c_e\ge0\) and \(D_{uv}=D_{vu}\ge0\).
There exists \(S\subsetneq V\) with \(S\ne\varnothing\) and \(D(S,V\setminus S)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi^*=\min_{S:D(S,V\setminus S)>0}c(\delta(S))/D(S,V\setminus S)\), where the minimum ranges over nontrivial cuts.

notation.meaning: edges with exactly one endpoint in S

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric Dual Characterization of Optimal Throughput
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes optimal multicommodity throughput through a capacity-to-demand metric ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f^*$ denote the optimal throughput. Then
\[
f^*=\min_{\mathbf d\,\mathrm{metric}}\frac{\sum_{e\in E(G)}c_e d_e}{\sum_{e\in E(H)}\operatorname{dem}(e)d_e}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimal throughput equals the minimum over metrics of the capacity-weighted length of the supply graph divided by the demand-weighted length of the demand graph.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ has edge capacities }c_e
H\text{ is the demand graph with edge demands }\operatorname{dem}(e)
f^*\text{ denotes the optimal throughput}
\mathbf d\text{ is a metric on the relevant vertex set}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^*=\min_{\mathbf d\,\mathrm{metric}}\frac{\sum_{e\in E(G)}c_e d_e}{\sum_{e\in E(H)}\operatorname{dem}(e)d_e}.

children.title: Max-Flow–Min-Cut Ratio
children.top_down_role: Ratio-based comparison between concurrent routing value and cut capacity.

knowledge_statements.title: Max-Flow–Min-Cut Ratio
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flow-cut gap for maximum concurrent multicommodity flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected capacitated graph with demands \(D_{uv}\), let \(\lambda^*\) be the largest scalar for which every pair \(\{u,v\}\) can simultaneously route \(\lambda^*D_{uv}\) units while the total flow on each edge \(e\) does not exceed \(c_e\). If \(0<\lambda^*\le\Phi^*\), define the instance flow-cut ratio by \[\operatorname{gap}(G,c,D)=\frac{\Phi^*}{\lambda^*}.\] Weak cut bounds imply \(\operatorname{gap}(G,c,D)\ge1\); equality is the exact max-flow–min-cut relation for that instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The flow-cut ratio divides the sparsest-cut value by the maximum concurrent-flow value and is always at least one.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
\(c\) and \(D\) are nonnegative.
\(0<\lambda^*\le\Phi^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gap}(G,c,D)=\Phi^*/\lambda^*\ge1\).

children.title: Cut–Ratio Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Normalization choices linking sparsest-cut values to flow-cut gap measures.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut–Ratio Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Each cut supplies a concurrent-flow upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider any feasible concurrent routing with common scaling factor \(\lambda\). For every cut \(S\subset V\) with \(D(S,\bar S)>0\), all flow serving separated pairs must cross \(\delta(S)\); therefore \[\lambda D(S,\bar S)\le c(\delta(S)),\qquad \lambda\le\Phi(S).\] Maximizing over feasible routings and then minimizing over cuts gives \(\lambda^*\le\Phi^*\). Hence the sparsest cut is exactly the strongest upper bound on concurrent throughput obtainable from a single cut-capacity inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every cut bounds concurrent throughput by capacity divided by separated demand; minimizing these bounds gives the sparsest-cut value.
assumptions_latex: The routing is feasible for scaling factor \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda^*\le\min_S\Phi(S)=\Phi^*\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The single-cut upper bound and its minimization are correctly formulated as a property, but no multicommodity cut-bound locator is supplied.

children.title: Ratio Separation Instances
children.top_down_role: Instance families exhibiting nonexact flow-cut correspondence.

knowledge_statements.title: Ratio Separation Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expander-based instance families separating sparsest-cut and concurrent-flow values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist an absolute constant \(c>0\) and an infinite family of finite undirected capacitated instances with \(k\) demand terminals and positive maximum concurrent-flow value \(\lambda^*\) such that \[\frac{\Phi^*}{\lambda^*}\ge c\log k.\] Such a family can be obtained from bounded-degree expander supply graphs with all-pairs uniform demands on their vertices. Consequently, no universal constant bounds the multicommodity flow-cut ratio over all undirected instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expander-based multicommodity instances can have sparsest-cut values logarithmically larger than their maximum concurrent-flow values, disproving any universal constant flow-cut bound.
assumptions_latex: \(k\) is the number of endpoints of positive-demand pairs.
The instances are finite and undirected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi^*/\lambda^*=\Omega(\log k)\) along an infinite family of instances.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Leighton–Rao bounded-diameter partition lemma
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-diameter decomposition of an edge-weighted, capacitated undirected graph, including a capacity bound for edges crossing between parts and a runtime guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be an undirected graph, let \(z:E(G)\to\mathbb R_+\) and \(u:E(G)\to\mathbb R_+\), and define \(W:=\sum_{e\in E(G)}u(e)z(e)\), \(n:=|V(G)|\), and \(m:=|E(G)|\). For every \(d>0\), the vertex set can be partitioned as \(V(G)=V_1\dot\cup\cdots\dot\cup V_k\) so that each \(V_i\) has diameter at most \(d\) in the shortest-path metric induced by \(z\), and the total capacity of edges joining distinct parts is at most \(8W\log n/d\). Such a partition can be computed in \(O(m\log n)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every positive diameter threshold, an undirected graph with nonnegative edge lengths and capacities can be partitioned into bounded-diameter parts. The capacity crossing between parts is at most 8W log(n)/d, and the partition is computable in O(m log n) time.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is an undirected graph}
z:E(G)\to\mathbb R_+
u:E(G)\to\mathbb R_+
W:=\sum_{e\in E(G)}u(e)z(e)
n:=|V(G)|,\quad m:=|E(G)|
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,V(G)=V_1\dot\cup\cdots\dot\cup V_k:\ \forall i,\ \operatorname{diam}_{(G,z)}(V_i)\le d,\quad u(E_{\mathrm{cross}})\le\frac{8W\log n}{d},\quad\text{and the partition is computable in }O(m\log n).

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Demand Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Leighton–Rao flow-cut comparison for all-pairs uniform demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with \(|V|=n\ge2\), capacities \(c_e\ge0\), and uniform demand \(D_{uv}=1\) for every unordered pair of distinct vertices. Let \(\lambda^*>0\) be the maximum concurrent-flow value and let \(\Phi^*\) be the corresponding sparsest-cut value. There exists an absolute constant \(C>0\) such that \[\lambda^*\le\Phi^*\le C\log n\,\lambda^*.\] Hence the uniform-demand flow-cut gap is \(O(\log n)\). Moreover, expander-based families attain a gap of order \(\log n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For all-pairs unit demands with positive concurrent throughput, sparsest cut approximates maximum concurrent flow within a logarithmic factor, and expander families show this order is tight.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected with \(|V|=n\ge2\).
\(c_e\ge0\) for every edge.
\(D_{uv}=1\) for every distinct unordered pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(1\le\Phi^*/\lambda^*\le C\log n\) for an absolute constant \(C>0\), and the order \(\log n\) is attained by an infinite family.

notation.meaning: number of vertices and demand terminals

knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniform-Demand Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General-demand flow-cut comparison indexed by terminal count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with capacities \(c_e\ge0\) and symmetric demands \(D_{uv}=D_{vu}\ge0\). Let \(T\subseteq V\) be exactly the set of endpoints of positive-demand pairs, and suppose \(|T|=k\ge2\). If the maximum concurrent-flow value satisfies \(\lambda^*>0\), then there exists an absolute constant \(C>0\) such that \[\lambda^*\le\Phi^*\le C\log k\,\lambda^*.\] Thus the relevant logarithmic parameter is the number of demand terminals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For arbitrary pair demands supported on k terminals and having positive concurrent throughput, sparsest cut is within an order-log-k factor of maximum concurrent flow.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected.
\(c_e\ge0\) and \(D_{uv}=D_{vu}\ge0\).
\(T\) is exactly the set of endpoints of positive-demand pairs and \(|T|=k\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(1\le\Phi^*/\lambda^*\le C\log k\) for an absolute constant \(C>0\).

notation.meaning: set of endpoints of positive-demand pairs

knowledge_statements.title: Expander Gap Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: All-pairs demands on bounded-degree expanders yield the logarithmic undirected flow-cut gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a \(d\)-regular graph on \(n\) vertices with unit edge capacities, edge expansion at least \(h>0\), and average graph distance \(\Omega(\log n)\). Give every unordered pair \(\{u,v\}\) demand \(1/n\). Every cut \(S\subset V\) then has sparsity \[\frac{|\delta(S)|}{|S|(n-|S|)/n}=\Omega(h).\] If all demands are routed concurrently to fraction \(\lambda\), summing path lengths against edge capacities gives \(\lambda=O(d/\log n)\). Hence the ratio between minimum cut sparsity and maximum concurrent-flow value is \(\Omega(\log n)\) for constant \(d,h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constant-degree expanders with scaled all-pairs demands have constant sparsest-cut value but only inverse-logarithmic concurrent-flow value, producing a logarithmic flow-cut gap.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) has constant degree and constant edge expansion.
The average pairwise distance in \(G\) is \(\Omega(\log n)\).
Routing is fractional and paths are undirected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gap}(G)=\Omega(\log n)\).

notation.meaning: Edges with exactly one endpoint in S.
Common routed fraction of every demand.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind and local topic fit, and the normalization appears mathematically plausible, but the logarithmic gap construction has no inspectable citation. A source must confirm the demand scaling, expansion convention, and average-distance argument.

knowledge_statements.title: Embedding-Based Gap Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The standard metric-embedding route from the multiflow dual to a cut certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected capacitated graph with nonnegative pair demands, and let \(d\) be a shortest-path semimetric feasible for the normalized concurrent-flow dual. Suppose there is an embedding \(f:V\to L_1\) and a scale \(a>0\) such that \(a d(u,v)\leq \lVert f(u)-f(v)\rVert_1\leq Da d(u,v)\) for all \(u,v\in V\). Since every finite \(L_1\) metric is a nonnegative combination of cut metrics, some cut has sparsity at most \(D\) times the dual value. Consequently the flow-cut gap is at most \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distortion-D embedding of every feasible dual metric into L1 converts the metric dual into a cut and bounds the flow-cut gap by D.
assumptions_latex: The network and its capacities are undirected.
All capacities and demands are nonnegative.
The displayed embedding inequalities hold for every vertex pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gap}(G)\leq D\).

notation.meaning: A shortest-path semimetric feasible for the normalized dual.
An L1 space whose finite metrics decompose into cut metrics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem needs an authoritative metric-embedding locator. As written, an embedding of one merely feasible dual metric does not by itself bound the flow-cut gap; the metric must be an optimal dual solution for the instance, or the stated distortion guarantee must apply to every relevant feasible dual metric.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Flow-Cut Asymmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed dual distances are quasimetrics, so undirected metric-to-cut arguments do not transfer automatically.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed capacitated graph, assign nonnegative arc lengths \(\ell_a\) and define \(d_\ell(u,v)\) as the shortest directed \(u\)-to-\(v\) path length. Generally \(d_\ell(u,v)\neq d_\ell(v,u)\), although the directed triangle inequality holds. Directed cut constraints use only arcs leaving \(S\), namely \[c(\delta^+(S))\geq \sum_{i:s_i\in S,\ t_i\notin S} r_i.\] Thus the dual objects are quasimetrics rather than symmetric metrics, and an undirected \(L_1\)-metric decomposition alone neither represents the directed dual nor establishes a directed flow-cut bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed shortest-path duals are asymmetric quasimetrics, while directed cuts count only outgoing arcs; symmetric L1 embedding arguments therefore do not directly apply.
assumptions_latex: Arc capacities, arc lengths, and commodity demands are nonnegative.
Commodities have ordered source-sink pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{undirected metric cut decomposition}\not\Rightarrow\text{directed flow-cut exactness}\).

notation.meaning: Directed shortest-path quasimetric induced by arc lengths.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits and the distinction between directed quasimetrics and symmetric L1 metrics is standard, but no citation supports the directed dual and cut formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent exact-multiflow demand-graph regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Five-way characterization of simple demand graphs for which cut conditions universally suffice for fractional, half-integral, and Eulerian integral multiflows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let H=(T,R) be a simple graph without isolated vertices. The following are equivalent: (i) for every graph G=(V,E) with V\supseteq T and every c:E\to\mathbb{R}_+, d:R\to\mathbb{R}_+, the cut condition implies the existence of a fractional multiflow; (ii) for every such G and every c:E\to\mathbb{Z}_+, d:R\to\mathbb{Z}_+, the cut condition implies the existence of a half-integer multiflow; (iii) for every such G and integer-valued c,d, the cut and Euler conditions imply the existence of an integer multiflow; (iv) H contains none of the graphs in Figure 72.1 as a subgraph; (v) H=K_4, H=C_5, or H is the union of two stars.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a simple demand graph without isolated vertices, universal fractional cut sufficiency, half-integral cut sufficiency for integer data, integral sufficiency under the cut and Euler conditions, exclusion of the Figure 72.1 subgraphs, and being K4, C5, or a union of two stars are equivalent.
assumptions_latex: H=(T,R)\text{ is a simple graph}
H\text{ has no isolated vertices}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{(i)}\iff\mathrm{(ii)}\iff\mathrm{(iii)}\iff\mathrm{(iv)}\iff\mathrm{(v)}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Odd-K5-free signed-graph multiflow existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut-condition sufficiency with fractional, half-integral, and integral conclusions under progressively stronger hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph and $R\subseteq E$. If the signed graph $(V,E,R)$ has no odd-$K_5$ minor, then for every $c:E\to\mathbb{R}_+$ the cut condition implies the existence of a fractional multiflow. If $c$ is integer-valued, it implies the existence of a half-integral multiflow; if, additionally, the Euler condition holds, it implies the existence of an integral multiflow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a signed graph with no odd K5 minor, the cut condition guarantees a fractional multiflow. Integer capacities give a half-integral multiflow, and the additional Euler condition gives an integral multiflow.

c:E\to\mathbb{R}_+

knowledge_statements.statement_title: K5-minor characterization by universal multiflow existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forbidden-minor characterization through cut-condition sufficiency for every signing and capacity function, with one-way integrality refinements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Max-Biflow Min-Cut Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum total two-commodity flow with shared edge capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph with terminal pairs $\{s_1,t_1\}$ and $\{s_2,t_2\}$, and let $c:E\to\mathbb R_+$. The maximum total value of a two-commodity flow subject to $c$ equals the minimum capacity of a cut that separates both $s_1$ from $t_1$ and $s_2$ from $t_2$. If $c$ is integral, the maximum is attained by a half-integral multiflow. If $c$ is integral and $c(\delta(v))$ is even for every $v\notin\{s_1,t_1,s_2,t_2\}$, the maximum is attained by an integral multiflow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum total value of a two-commodity flow equals the minimum capacity of a cut separating both terminal pairs. Integral capacities admit a half-integral optimum, while integral capacities having even incident capacity at every nonterminal vertex admit an integral optimum.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a graph}
c:E\to\mathbb R_+
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{\text{total two-commodity flow value}\}=\min\{c(\delta(X)):X\text{ separates both terminal pairs}\};\quad c\in\mathbb Z_+^E\Rightarrow\text{half-integral attainment};\quad c\in\mathbb Z_+^E\ \land\ c(\delta(v))\in2\mathbb Z\ \forall v\notin\{s_1,t_1,s_2,t_2\}\Rightarrow\text{integral attainment}

knowledge_statements.title: Undirected Two-Commodity Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractional path-flow formulation for two terminal pairs in an undirected capacitated graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An undirected two-commodity flow instance consists of an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), capacities \(c_e\geq0\), terminal pairs \((s_1,t_1)\) and \((s_2,t_2)\), and demands \(r_1,r_2\geq0\). A feasible fractional flow is a family \((x_{i,P})\) indexed by \(i\in\{1,2\}\) and undirected \(s_i\)-to-\(t_i\) paths \(P\), satisfying \[x_{i,P}\geq0,\qquad \sum_Px_{i,P}=r_i,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^2\sum_{P\ni e}x_{i,P}\leq c_e\quad(e\in E).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two fractional commodities share undirected edge capacities; each commodity routes its prescribed demand between its own terminal pair.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
Capacities and demands are finite and nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_{i,P})\) is feasible exactly when the displayed demand and capacity constraints hold.

notation.meaning: Amount of commodity i routed along path P.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Commodity Cut Packing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut inequalities give efficiently checkable necessary certificates for prescribed two-commodity feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected two-commodity instance and each \(S\subseteq V\), define the separated demand by \[r(S)=\sum_{i=1}^2 r_i\,\mathbf 1\!\left[|\{s_i,t_i\}\cap S|=1\right].\] Every feasible fractional two-commodity flow satisfies \(c(\delta(S))\geq r(S)\). Therefore any set \(S\) with \(c(\delta(S))<r(S)\) is a verifiable infeasibility certificate; the family of all displayed inequalities is the two-commodity cut relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every cut must carry the total demand of terminal pairs it separates; a violated cut certifies infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: The instance uses undirected shared edge capacities.
Flows are fractional and satisfy the path-capacity formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c(\delta(S))<r(S)\Rightarrow\text{the instance is infeasible}.\)

notation.meaning: Total demand whose terminal pair is separated by S.
Total capacity of the cut induced by S.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Two-Commodity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The undirected cut-exactness regime requires symmetry and cannot be inferred for directed networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For two ordered pairs in a directed graph, feasibility implies every directed cut inequality \[c(\delta^+(S))\geq \sum_{i:s_i\in S,\ t_i\notin S}r_i.\] The converse is not supplied by the undirected two-commodity theorem: directed path incidence and directed-cut incidence are not related by the symmetric metric decomposition used in the undirected case. Accordingly, replacing every undirected edge by an arbitrary orientation moves the instance outside the exactness regime; feasibility must be tested by the directed multicommodity-flow linear program or by additional directed hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed cut inequalities remain necessary, but undirected two-commodity exactness cannot be transferred through arbitrary edge orientations.
assumptions_latex: The two commodities have ordered source-sink pairs.
Capacities are assigned to directed arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{directed cut condition}\not\overset{\mathrm{undirected\ theorem}}{\Longrightarrow}\text{directed feasibility}.\)

notation.meaning: Arcs directed from S to its complement.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but the directed limitation is unsupported. A directed two-commodity theorem or counterexample locator is needed to establish the precise boundary rather than only the failure of one undirected proof method.

knowledge_statements.title: Rothschild–Whinston Feasibility Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path-LP feasibility core; the precise historical Rothschild–Whinston formulation remains source-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an undirected two-pair instance, its fractional feasibility regime is the set of data for which there exist nonnegative path variables \(x_{i,P}\) satisfying \[\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_i}x_{i,P}=r_i\quad(i=1,2),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^2\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_i:e\in P}x_{i,P}\leq c_e\quad(e\in E).\] Equivalently, feasibility holds exactly when the prescribed demand vector \((r_1,r_2)\) belongs to the downward-closed projection of this path-flow polyhedron. No integrality or directed extension is included in this formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The provisional feasibility regime consists precisely of two-pair demands represented by nonnegative path flows obeying every shared edge capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
\(\mathcal P_i\) is the set of undirected paths joining the terminals of commodity \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((r_1,r_2)\text{ is feasible}\iff\exists x\text{ satisfying the displayed system}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Hu Multiflow Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractional undirected two-commodity cut-condition formulation; integrality is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with capacities \(c_e\geq0\), terminal pairs \((s_1,t_1)\), \((s_2,t_2)\), and demands \(r_1,r_2\geq0\). A fractional two-commodity flow routing both demands exists if and only if, for every \(S\subseteq V\), \[c(\delta(S))\geq \sum_{i=1}^2r_i\,\mathbf 1\!\left[|\{s_i,t_i\}\cap S|=1\right].\] The assertion concerns fractional flows with shared undirected capacities; it does not assert an integral routing without additional parity hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the fractional undirected two-pair regime, routing feasibility is equivalent to satisfying every terminal-separating cut inequality.
assumptions_latex: The graph and capacities are undirected.
There are exactly two prescribed terminal pairs.
Flows may be fractional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{feasible two-commodity flow}\iff\text{all cut inequalities hold}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind and fractional-undirected formulation fit the container, but the cut-condition sufficiency claim is substantial. A specific Hu theorem locator must confirm the capacity domain, fractional or half-integral scope, and any omitted hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Commodity Result Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of fractional feasibility, cut certification, integrality, and directionality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For two prescribed pairs, the path-flow formulation applies to both directed and undirected networks, and the appropriate cut inequalities are always necessary. In the fractional undirected Hu regime, those inequalities are also sufficient. This equivalence does not itself provide an integral multiflow, because integrality may require parity or Eulerian hypotheses, and it does not extend merely by orienting the edges, because directed dual distances are asymmetric. Thus fractional versus integral and undirected versus directed are independent boundaries of the two-commodity exactness statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut exactness belongs to the fractional undirected regime; integrality and directed routing require separate hypotheses or results.
assumptions_latex: Exactly two terminal pairs are prescribed.
The Hu statement is interpreted in its fractional undirected form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{fractional undirected cut exactness}\not\Rightarrow\text{integral or directed cut exactness}.\)

notation.meaning: Equivalence between all cut inequalities and multiflow feasibility.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison role is suitable, but its conclusions depend on the unverified Hu formulation and on unsupported claims about parity, integrality, and directed boundaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Sufficient Demand-Graph Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines cut-sufficient supply-demand graph classes without asserting an unverified classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=(T,F)\) be a demand graph whose edge \(ij\in F\) represents a commodity between terminals \(i,j\in T\). For a specified class \(\mathcal G\) of undirected supply graphs, call \(H\) cut-sufficient for \(\mathcal G\) if, for every \(G\in\mathcal G\), every nonnegative capacity vector \(c\), and every nonnegative demand vector \(r\) indexed by \(F\), the inequalities \[c(\delta_G(S))\geq\sum_{ij\in F:\,|\{i,j\}\cap S|=1}r_{ij}\quad(S\subseteq V(G))\] imply the existence of a fractional multiflow routing all demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A demand graph is cut-sufficient for a supply class when every instance satisfying all cut inequalities admits a fractional routing.
assumptions_latex: Every terminal of \(H\) is a vertex of the supply graph.
Supply graphs are undirected and capacities and demands are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\text{ is cut-sufficient for }\mathcal G\iff\text{the displayed implication holds for every instance over }\mathcal G.\)

notation.meaning: Demand graph on terminal set T.
Specified family of undirected supply graphs.
Demand associated with demand edge ij.

knowledge_statements.title: K2,3-Metric Condition Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Five-terminal dual tests generated by shortest-path metrics on weighted complete bipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=U\mathbin{\dot\cup}W\) with \(|U|=2\) and \(|W|=3\). A \(K_{2,3}\)-metric on \(T\) is the shortest-path metric \(m_w\) of the complete bipartite graph between \(U\) and \(W\), with arbitrary nonnegative edge lengths \(w\). For supply capacities \(c_e\) and terminal-pair demands \(r_{ij}\), the associated metric condition is \[\sum_{e=xy}c_e\,m_w(x,y)\geq\sum_{ij}r_{ij}\,m_w(i,j)\] for every nonnegative weighting \(w\), where nonterminal supply vertices, if present, are assigned images in \(T\) before evaluating the left side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The condition compares capacity and demand costs under every nonnegatively weighted shortest-path metric generated by K2,3.
assumptions_latex: The five metric labels split into parts of sizes two and three.
All metric-edge weights, capacities, and demands are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_ec_em_w(e)\geq\sum_{ij}r_{ij}m_w(i,j)\text{ for every weighted }K_{2,3}\text{ metric}.\)

notation.meaning: Complete bipartite graph with parts of sizes two and three.
Shortest-path metric induced by weights w on K2,3.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A specialized source is required. The record does not fully specify how supply vertices outside the five labels are mapped, whether the inequality ranges over every such mapping, or which weighted K2,3 metric convention the named condition uses.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Five-Terminal K2,3-Metric Characterization and Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes fractional multiflow feasibility for a complete demand graph on five terminals and gives conditional half-integrality and integrality conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(V,E), let H=(T,R) be a complete graph with |T|=5 and T\subseteq V, and let c:E\to\mathbb R_+ and d:R\to\mathbb R_+. A fractional multiflow exists if and only if the K_{2,3}-metric condition holds. If these equivalent feasibility conditions hold and c and d are integer-valued, then a half-integer multiflow exists. If, in addition, the Euler condition holds, then an integer multiflow exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a complete demand graph on five terminals, fractional multiflow feasibility is equivalent to the K2,3-metric condition. Given feasibility, integer capacities and demands yield a half-integral multiflow, and the additional Euler condition yields an integral multiflow.

H=(T,R)\text{ is complete},\quad |T|=5,\quad T\subseteq V
c:E\to\mathbb R_+,\quad d:R\to\mathbb R_+

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Γ-Metrics and the Γ-Metric Multiflow Condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines graph-induced metrics and the resulting necessary condition for fractional multiflow feasibility, with the K2,3 condition subsuming the cut condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \Gamma be a graph and V a finite set. A metric \mu on V is a \Gamma-metric if there exists \phi:V\to V(\Gamma) such that \mu(u,v)=\operatorname{dist}_{\Gamma}(\phi(u),\phi(v)) for all u,v\in V. If a fractional multiflow with capacities c:E\to\mathbb R_+ and demands d:R\to\mathbb R_+ is feasible, then every \Gamma-metric \mu on V satisfies \[\sum_{st\in R}d(st)\mu(s,t)\leq\sum_{uv\in E}c(uv)\mu(u,v).\] Every cut yields a K_2-metric and hence a K_{2,3}-metric, so the K_{2,3}-metric condition includes the cut condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Γ-metric is obtained by mapping the finite vertex set into Γ and using graph distances. Every feasible fractional multiflow satisfies the corresponding demand-versus-capacity inequality. Because cut metrics are K2-metrics and therefore K2,3-metrics, the K2,3-metric condition includes the cut condition.

c:E\to\mathbb R_+,\quad d:R\to\mathbb R_+
\text{a feasible fractional multiflow exists}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\,\Gamma\text{-metrics }\mu,\quad \sum_{st\in R}d(st)\mu(s,t)\leq\sum_{uv\in E}c(uv)\mu(u,v)

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Commodity Cut Packing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For three or more commodities, cut inequalities form only a relaxation in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected instance with \(k\geq3\) terminal pairs, define \(r(S)\) as the total demand of pairs separated by \(S\). Feasibility always implies \(c(\delta(S))\geq r(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq V\). In general these inequalities are not sufficient: the multiflow dual ranges over shortest-path metrics, whereas cuts represent only nonnegative combinations of cut metrics. Consequently a metric dual certificate may separate the demand vector even when every single cut inequality is satisfied; the resulting ratio between the cut relaxation and routable concurrent flow is the higher-commodity flow-cut gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With at least three commodities, satisfying every cut can still leave demands unroutable because the full dual contains non-cut metrics.
assumptions_latex: The supply graph is undirected with nonnegative capacities.
There are at least three prescribed terminal pairs.
Flows are fractional.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractional cut-sufficiency form of the Okamura-Seymour single-face regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) have a fixed planar embedding, and let \(H\) consist of demand edges \(s_kt_k\) with values \(d_k\ge 0\). Suppose all endpoints of \(H\) lie on the boundary of one face of \(G\). If the cut condition
\[
 u(\delta_G(S))\ge d(\delta_H(S))\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V
\]
holds, then there are nonnegative path flows \(x_P\), indexed by \(s_k\)-\(t_k\) paths, such that
\[
 \sum_{P\in\mathcal P_k}x_P=d_k\quad\text{and}\quad
 \sum_k\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_k:e\in P}x_P\le u_e
\]
for every commodity \(k\) and edge \(e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For planar supply graphs whose terminals share one face, the cut condition is sufficient for routing all demands fractionally.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) and \(H\) be finite multigraphs on \(V\), where supply and demand multiplicities are integral. Assume \(G+H\) is planar and every vertex has even degree in \(G+H\). Then the demand edges can be replaced by pairwise capacity-feasible paths in \(G\), one path per demand copy, if and only if
\[
 |\delta_G(S)|\ge |\delta_H(S)|
 \qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V.
\]
Necessity follows from any routing crossing each cut; sufficiency is the exact planar-Eulerian conclusion defining this regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the integral supply-demand union is planar and Eulerian, the cut condition exactly characterizes integral routability.

children.title: Multiple-Face Terminal Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Loss of single-face structure when terminals occupy several planar faces.

assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite planar capacitated supply graph.

review_flags: A concrete published counterexample and exact locator are required

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of cut sufficiency when planar terminals occupy multiple faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exist a planar graph \(G=(V,E)\), nonnegative capacities \(u\), and a demand graph \(H\) whose terminals cannot all be placed on one face of the chosen embedding, such that
\[
 u(\delta_G(S))\ge d(\delta_H(S))
 \qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V,
\]
but no nonnegative family of commodity path flows simultaneously routes all demands within \(u\). Thus the common-face hypothesis cannot be deleted from the fractional Okamura-Seymour statement while retaining the cut condition as a sufficient criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With terminals on multiple faces, all cut inequalities may hold even though no feasible fractional multiflow exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Face Terminal Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is an appropriate failure-boundary claim, but no concrete counterexample or authoritative locator supports the asserted failure of fractional cut sufficiency with multiple-face terminals.

children.title: Surface Routing Boundaries

assumptions_latex: \(G\) is cellularly embedded on a compact surface of positive genus.
Capacities and pairwise demands are nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cut feasibility need not imply fractional multiflow feasibility on the surface.
review_flags: Surface-specific homology or metric obstructions are not characterized here
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of planar cut-sufficiency on positive-genus surfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For some compact surface \(\Sigma\) with \(g(\Sigma)>0\), there are a graph \(G\) cellularly embedded in \(\Sigma\), capacities \(u\), and demands \(d\) satisfying
\[
 u(\delta_G(S))\ge d(\delta_H(S))
 \qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V(G),
\]
for which no feasible fractional multiflow exists. Consequently, ordinary cut inequalities do not by themselves extend the planar single-face exactness theorem to arbitrary surface embeddings; additional topological or metric constraints are necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On positive-genus surfaces, ordinary cut inequalities can miss topological obstructions to fractional routing.
knowledge_statements.title: Surface Routing Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind matches the leaf, but both the positive-genus counterexample and the assertion that additional topological or metric constraints are necessary require a surface-routing source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Doubly Odd Closed Curve
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parity obstruction associated with an embedded graph and prescribed pairwise-disjoint simple closed curves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph embedded in a compact surface \(S\), and let \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\) be pairwise disjoint simple closed curves on \(S\). A closed curve \(D\) on \(S\) is doubly odd with respect to \(G,C_1,\ldots,C_k\) if \(D\) is the concatenation of two closed curves \(D_1,D_2\) having a common endpoint not on \(G\), and, for \(j=1,2\), \[\operatorname{cr}(G,D_j)\not\equiv\sum_{i=1}^k\operatorname{mincr}(C_i,D_j)\pmod 2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed curve is doubly odd when it is the concatenation of two closed curves sharing a point outside the graph and each component has graph-crossing parity different from the summed minimum-crossing parity for the prescribed curves.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a graph embedded in a compact surface }S.
C_1,\ldots,C_k\text{ are pairwise disjoint simple closed curves on }S.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ is doubly odd}\iff D=D_1\cdot D_2,\ D_1,D_2\text{ have a common endpoint outside }G,\text{ and }\operatorname{cr}(G,D_j)\not\equiv\sum_i\operatorname{mincr}(C_i,D_j)\pmod 2\text{ for }j=1,2.

Let the supply graph be \(C_4=v_1v_2v_3v_4v_1\), with \(u_e=1\) for every edge, and prescribe one unit of demand for each pair \(v_1v_3\) and \(v_2v_4\). Then

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a restricted-master dual solution \((\alpha,\lambda)\), assign edge length
\[
 \ell_e=c_e+\lambda_e.
\]
For each commodity \(k=(s_k,t_k)\), compute a shortest \(s_k\)-\(t_k\) path \(P_k\) under \(\ell\). Its reduced cost is
\[
 \bar c_{P_k}=\sum_{e\in P_k}(c_e+\lambda_e)-\alpha_k.
\]
If \(\bar c_{P_k}<0\), add \(P_k\) to \(R_k\) and reoptimize the master. Stop when every commodity has nonnegative shortest-path reduced cost; then no omitted path can improve the linear master.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacity dual prices modify edge costs, so each commodity's minimum-reduced-cost column is found by one shortest-path computation.

children.title: Master Stabilization
children.top_down_role: Stability devices for restricted path-master optimization.

assumptions_latex: The restricted master has a dual feasible region \(D_R\) and concave dual objective \(q_R(y)\).
A center \(\bar y\in D_R\) and parameter \(\rho>0\) are maintained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A proximal stabilized dual point maximizes \(q_R(y)-\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert y-\bar y\rVert_2^2\) over \(D_R\).
review_flags: A column-generation stabilization source and locator are required
standard_field_rationale: standard proximal dual stabilization template
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal stabilization of restricted-master dual multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize a dual-feasible center \(\bar y^0\in D_{R^0}\) and choose \(\rho_0>0\). At iteration \(t\), compute
\[
 y^t\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in D_{R^t}}
 \left\{q_{R^t}(y)-\frac{\rho_t}{2}\lVert y-\bar y^t\rVert_2^2\right\}.
\]
Price omitted paths using \(y^t\), add selected negative-reduced-cost columns, and reoptimize. After a prescribed serious-step test showing sufficient dual improvement, set \(\bar y^{t+1}=y^t\); otherwise retain \(\bar y^{t+1}=\bar y^t\) and adjust \(\rho_t\). Output an unstabilized primal-dual optimum once exact pricing certifies nonnegative reduced costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proximal stabilization keeps dual prices near a center, updating that center only after sufficient progress and retaining exact final pricing.
knowledge_statements.title: Master Stabilization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proximal template fits master stabilization, but no stabilization source or locator is supplied. The serious-step update and final exact-certification claims are algorithmic details whose validity cannot be assessed from the record alone.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Maintain \(R_k\) and \(A_k\) for each commodity. After pricing, insert every selected path \(P\) with \(\bar c_P<-	au\) into \(R_k\). If \(|R_k|>M_k\), move to \(A_k\) only paths satisfying
\[
 x_P=0,
 \qquad \bar c_P\ge-	au,

\]
while preserving a feasible basis or the designated artificial feasibility columns. Before invoking a new shortest-path call, rescan \(A_k\) and reactivate any archived path with \(\bar c_P<-	au\). Terminate only after both the archive scan and exact pricing find no negative-reduced-cost path.

children.title: Stabilization–Pool Interaction
children.top_down_role: Effects of path-pool composition on master stability and pricing behavior.

assumptions_latex: A stabilized dual point \(y^s\) is used for column discovery.
An exact restricted-master dual optimum \(y^R\) is available for certification.
Every admissible path belongs to a commodity-specific path set \(\mathcal P_k\), and archived paths can be repriced under either multiplier vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Discovery may use \(y^s\), but exact termination requires nonnegative reduced costs under a dual vector valid for the unstabilized restricted master.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A path generated because \(\bar c_P(y^s)<0\) may be inserted even when \(y^s\) is not optimal for the unstabilized restricted master. Conversely,
\[
 \min\left\{\bar c_P(y^s):k\in K,\ P\in\mathcal P_k\setminus R_k\right\}\ge0
\]
does not certify full-master optimality unless \(y^s\) is an optimal dual vector for the unstabilized restricted master. Before termination, active and archived columns must be repriced and exact shortest-path pricing must be invoked under \(y^R\). The certificate is valid only when
\[
 \bar c_P(y^R)\ge0
 \qquad\text{for every }k\in K\text{ and }P\in\mathcal P_k.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stabilized prices may guide column discovery, but only exact pricing under an optimal dual solution of the unstabilized restricted master certifies full-master optimality.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At each pricing step, first minimize the true reduced cost \(\bar c_P\). Among paths attaining the same minimum within tolerance \(\tau\), select the \(\prec\)-least path not already active. Admit all paths with \(\bar c_P<-	au\), but admit at most a prescribed number of paths satisfying \(|\bar c_P|\le	au\). Reoptimize with a deterministic lexicographic pivot or an equivalent secondary rule. Because the secondary order is applied only among equal primary objective values, the reported solution must minimize the original master objective; the perturbation is not included in the final objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lexicographic tie-breaking and bounded admission of zero-reduced-cost paths reduce cycling while preserving the original optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy Control

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits degeneracy control, but the proposed admission and pivot policies lack a source. The phrase "attaining the same minimum within tolerance" also blends exact lexicographic tie-breaking with approximate tolerance grouping, so the policy's preservation claim needs an authoritative formulation.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite network and \(K\) is a finite commodity set.
Commodity \(k\in K\) has demand \(d_k\ge0\), source \(s_k\), sink \(t_k\), and a nonempty path set \(\mathcal P_k\).
Shared edge capacities are \(u_e\ge0\), path variables satisfy \(\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_k}x_P=d_k\), and edge-flow costs are additive with coefficients \(c_e\).
Capacity constraints are dualized with multipliers \(\lambda_e\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For fixed \(\lambda\), the Lagrangian infimum separates into one shortest-path subproblem per commodity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-price dual decomposition of minimum-cost fractional multicommodity flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Dualizing
\[
 \sum_{k\in K}\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_k:e\in P}x_P\le u_e
 \qquad(e\in E)
\]
with \(\lambda_e\ge0\) gives
\[
 q(\lambda)=-\sum_{e\in E}\lambda_eu_e+
 \sum_{k\in K}d_k\operatorname{dist}_{c+\lambda}(s_k,t_k).
\]
For fixed \(\lambda\), commodity \(k\) independently assigns its demand to paths minimizing \(\sum_{e\in P}(c_e+\lambda_e)\). The Lagrangian dual is
\[
 \max_{\lambda_e\ge0\ (e\in E)}q(\lambda),
\]
a concave, generally nonsmooth optimization problem with commodity-separable shortest-path subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing shared capacities turns the coupled flow problem into independent shortest-path problems linked only through nonnegative edge prices.
knowledge_statements.title: Commodity-Separable Dualization

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Dual Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected subgradient minimization of the capacity-price dual for fractional multiflow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(\lambda^0\in\mathbb{R}_+^E\). At iteration \(t\), solve every commodity subproblem at prices \(\lambda^t\), let \(y^t\) be the resulting aggregate load, and choose \(s^t=u-y^t\in\partial g(\lambda^t)\). Update
\[
\lambda^{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathbb{R}_+^E}\!\left(\lambda^t-\alpha_t s^t\right)=\bigl[\lambda^t+\alpha_t(y^t-u)\bigr]_+.
\]
After a prescribed finite iteration limit \(T\), let \(t^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\le t\le T}g(\lambda^t)\) and return \(\lambda^{t^*}\) with \(g(\lambda^{t^*})\). If the stepsizes satisfy
\[
\alpha_t>0,\qquad \sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\alpha_t=\infty,\qquad \sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\alpha_t^2<\infty,
\]
then the bounded-subgradient and dual-attainment assumptions imply \(\min_{0\le t\le T}g(\lambda^t)\to g^*\) as \(T\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly solve the commodity subproblems, update nonnegative capacity prices by projected subgradient steps, and return the iterate having the smallest recorded dual value. Under dual attainment, bounded subgradients, and the stated diminishing-stepsize conditions, the best recorded values converge to the dual optimum.
assumptions_latex: The primal problem is a convex fractional multicommodity-flow maximization problem with finite edge capacities and a nonempty feasible set.
Capacity constraints are dualized by multipliers \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^E\), every commodity subproblem attains its optimum, and the resulting dual objective \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex.
The dual problem has a minimizer, and the selected subgradients are uniformly bounded along the generated iterates.
A positive stepsize sequence \((\alpha_t)_{t\ge 0}\) and a finite iteration limit \(T\) are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns \(\lambda^{t^*}\), where \(t^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\le t\le T}g(\lambda^t)\); under the stated infinite-run conditions, the best recorded dual values converge to the dual optimum \(g^*\).

notation.meaning: Convex Lagrangian dual objective, expressed as the sum of commodity subproblem values and capacity terms.
Aggregate edge load induced by optimal commodity subproblem solutions at iteration t.
Index attaining the smallest recorded dual objective value.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recovered flow \(\bar x\) is primal feasible, with objective equal to the same convex average of the iterate objectives.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Form the weighted averages
\[
\bar x^k=\sum_{t=1}^T\theta_t x^{k,t}
\]
for every commodity \(k\). Convexity of each commodity's conservation and nonnegativity constraints makes \(\bar x^k\) individually admissible. Test the shared capacities by computing \(\bar y_e=\sum_k\bar x_e^k\). If \(\bar y_e\le u_e\) for all \(e\), output \(\bar x=(\bar x^k)_k\); otherwise no feasible recovery is certified. For a linear primal objective \(c^\top x\), the recovered value satisfies \(c^\top\bar x=\sum_t\theta_t c^\top x^t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Average commodity-feasible iterates and accept the average only when its aggregate edge loads satisfy every shared capacity.

children.title: Bound Certificates
children.top_down_role: Lower or upper bound evidence produced by the decomposition framework.

assumptions_latex: The primal is a maximization problem with optimum \(P^*\), and \(\hat x\) is a feasible recovered multiflow.
The Lagrangian dual is minimized, and \(\hat\lambda\ge 0\) is dual feasible.
Weak duality holds for the primal-dual pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(\hat x)\le P^*\le g(\hat\lambda)\), so the displayed interval is a verifiable bound certificate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A posteriori lower and upper bounds for a maximization-form multiflow.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a recovered flow \(\hat x\), verify commodity conservation, nonnegativity, and \(\sum_k\hat x_e^k\le u_e\) on every edge. Given \(\hat\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^E\), independently solve the commodity subproblems defining \(g(\hat\lambda)\). Weak duality then yields
\[
p(\hat x)\le P^*\le g(\hat\lambda).
\]
Thus \([p(\hat x),g(\hat\lambda)]\) is a bound certificate. If \(p(\hat x)>0\), it additionally certifies relative suboptimality at most \((g(\hat\lambda)-p(\hat x))/p(\hat x)\); equality of the two bounds certifies optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible recovered flow gives a lower bound, while a nonnegative capacity-price vector and solved subproblems give an upper bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Bound Certificates

children.title: Recovery–Certificate Gap
children.top_down_role: Quality differences between recovered primal values and certified bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Recovery–Certificate Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute and relative interpretation of the certified primal-dual interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the recovery-certificate gap by
\[
\Delta=g(\hat\lambda)-p(\hat x).
\]
Weak duality implies \(\Delta\ge 0\) and gives
\[
\Delta=\bigl(g(\hat\lambda)-P^*\bigr)+\bigl(P^*-p(\hat x)\bigr).
\]
Both summands are nonnegative, so each is at most \(\Delta\). Therefore \(\Delta\le\varepsilon\) certifies absolute \(\varepsilon\)-optimality of \(\hat x\) and absolute \(\varepsilon\)-accuracy of the dual bound. When \(p(\hat x)>0\), the inequality \(\Delta/p(\hat x)\le\varepsilon\) implies \(p(\hat x)\ge P^*/(1+\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The certified upper-minus-lower gap bounds both primal suboptimality and dual-bound error; normalization by a positive recovered value gives the stated relative guarantee.
assumptions_latex: The primal is a maximization problem with finite optimal value \(P^*\).
A feasible recovered flow \(\hat x\) and a dual-feasible multiplier \(\hat\lambda\) are available.
Weak duality gives \(p(\hat x)\le P^*\le g(\hat\lambda)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The gap satisfies \(0\le g(\hat\lambda)-P^*\le\Delta\) and \(0\le P^*-p(\hat x)\le\Delta\); if \(p(\hat x)>0\) and \(\Delta/p(\hat x)\le\varepsilon\), then \(p(\hat x)\ge P^*/(1+\varepsilon)\).

children.title: Recovery Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases where strong dual information yields weak or difficult primal recovery.

assumptions_latex: Two unit-capacity parallel edges connect a common source and sink.
Two commodities each require one unit of flow between that source and sink.
At every dual iteration, both commodity subproblems select the same currently shortest edge, with ties resolved identically.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every last iterate violates capacity by one unit, although the equal average of two alternating iterates is feasible.

notation.meaning: Aggregate load on edge e at iteration t.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of last-iterate recovery under synchronized shortest-path choices.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Multicommodity Flow Problems p. 17
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the parallel edges be \(a,b\), with \(u_a=u_b=1\). Suppose the synchronized subproblem solutions alternate: at odd iterations both unit demands use \(a\), and at even iterations both use \(b\). Then every iterate has
\[
(y_a^t,y_b^t)\in\{(2,0),(0,2)\},
\]
so one capacity is violated by \(1\). Consequently, selecting any last or best dual iterate does not guarantee primal feasibility. In contrast, averaging one odd and one even iterate gives aggregate load \((1,1)\), which is feasible. Recovery can also fail when averaging weights concentrate on only one parity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Synchronized commodities can alternate between overloaded routes forever; last-iterate recovery fails even though a balanced average is feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Recovery Failure Regimes

assumptions_latex: The path-flow formulation is a nonnegative packing problem \(\max\{c^\top x:Ax\le u\}\) with \(A\ge 0\) and \(u>0\).
A shortest admissible path can be computed under nonnegative edge lengths.
Parameters \(\eta>0\), augmentation rule \(\delta>0\), and stopping threshold \(L>0\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is the accumulated path flow, scaled if necessary so that \(Ax\le u\).

notation.meaning: Current nonnegative edge lengths or capacity prices.
Incidence coefficient of edge e in path P.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Shortest Path Problems p. 51

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(x=0\) and positive lengths \(\ell_e\). While some admissible path \(P\) has length \(\ell(P)=\sum_e A_{eP}\ell_e<L\), choose a shortest such path, select an augmentation \(\delta>0\), set \(x_P\leftarrow x_P+\delta\), and update every edge by
\[
\ell_e\leftarrow \ell_e\left(1+\eta\,\delta A_{eP}/u_e\right).
\]
Stop when every admissible path has length at least \(L\). Let \(\rho=\max_e(Ax)_e/u_e\); output \(x/\max\{1,\rho\}\). The scaling step makes the output feasible, while the multiplicative lengths penalize repeatedly congested edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Augment along a currently shortest admissible path, multiplicatively increase lengths on used edges, stop at a length threshold, and scale to feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicative-Weight Routing

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximation and Runtime Guarantee for the Multicommodity Flow Scheme
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility, approximation ratio, and running-time guarantee for the Garg–Könemann maximum fractional multicommodity-flow scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the input assumptions of the MULTICOMMODITY FLOW APPROXIMATION SCHEME, the scheme produces a capacity-feasible path flow \(y\) whose total value satisfies \(\operatorname{val}(y)\ge \operatorname{OPT}(G,H,u)/(1+\epsilon)\). If \(k=|E(H)|\), \(n=|V(G)|\), and \(m=|E(G)|\), its running time is \(O\!\left(\epsilon^{-2}km(m+n\log n)\log n\right)\); consequently, it is a fully polynomial approximation scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the scheme's stated inputs, the returned multicommodity path flow respects every edge capacity and has total value at least OPT divided by 1 plus epsilon. The running time is polynomial in the graph dimensions and in 1/epsilon, so the scheme is an FPTAS.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-total-value specialization of path-based multiplicative weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(x_{iP}=0\) and positive lengths \(\ell_e\). At each iteration, compute a shortest \(s_i\)-\(t_i\) path \(P_i\) for every commodity, choose a pair \((i,P_i)\) of minimum path length, and augment
\[
\delta=\min_{e\in P_i}u_e
\]
units on \(P_i\). For each \(e\in P_i\), multiply \(\ell_e\) by \(1+\eta\delta/u_e\). Stop when the minimum commodity path length reaches the prescribed threshold. With \(\rho=\max_e\sum_{i,P\ni e}x_{iP}/u_e\), return \(x/\max\{1,\rho\}\) and its total value \(\sum_{i,P}x_{iP}/\max\{1,\rho\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly augment the globally shortest commodity path, update congestion prices multiplicatively, then scale the accumulated flow to satisfy capacities.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Multiflow Specialization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic specialization has no citation, and its bottleneck augmentation, stopping threshold, scaling, and description as an approximate maximum multiflow cannot be validated without a Garg–Könemann source.

assumptions_latex: Each commodity \(i\) has demand \(d_i>0\), and the objective is maximum concurrent flow.
A path oracle returns a shortest \(s_i\)-\(t_i\) path under current nonnegative edge lengths.
The multiplicative-update parameters and stopping threshold are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scaling by the accumulated congestion yields a feasible concurrent flow with common routed fraction \(\hat\lambda\).

notation.meaning: Target common fraction of every demand.
Accumulated routed amount for commodity i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Demand-proportional specialization for maximum concurrent flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize all path flows and routed amounts \(f_i\) to zero and all edge lengths positively. Process commodities by repeatedly selecting a shortest \(s_i\)-\(t_i\) path \(P\), augmenting
\[
\delta=\min\{d_i-f_i,\min_{e\in P}u_e\},
\]
and replacing \(\ell_e\) by \(\ell_e(1+\eta\delta/u_e)\) on \(P\). Complete a demand-proportional phase when each commodity has received its prescribed phase increment; stop at the length threshold. If \(\rho=\max_e y_e/u_e\), scale all path flows by \(1/\max\{1,\rho\}\) and output \(\hat\lambda=\min_i f_i/(d_i\max\{1,\rho\})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Route commodities in demand-proportional phases along current shortest paths, update edge prices, and scale by congestion to obtain a common feasible fraction.
knowledge_statements.title: Concurrent-Flow Specialization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the proposed phase algorithm. The prescribed phase increment is undefined, while the update d_i-f_i caps each commodity at one demand and may exclude standard maximum-concurrent-flow instances whose optimum multiplier exceeds one.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(G=(V,E)\), lengths \(\ell\in\mathbb{R}_+^E\), and terminal pairs \((s_i,t_i)\), run a nonnegative-length shortest-path algorithm from each required source, recover a path \(P_i\), and compute \(\ell(P_i)=\sum_{e\in P_i}\ell_e\). Return an index \(i^*\) minimizing the reported path length and the path \(P_{i^*}\). An exact oracle satisfies
\[
\ell(P_{i^*})=\min_i d_\ell(s_i,t_i),
\]
whereas a \((1+\xi)\)-approximate oracle must return \(\ell(P_{i^*})\le(1+\xi)\min_i d_\ell(s_i,t_i)\). The routing algorithm uses the returned path for its next augmentation.

children.title: Fleischer Refinements
children.top_down_role: Approximation-scheme refinements associated with the Fleischer framework.

assumptions_latex: The routing problem has a nonnegative path-packing formulation and admits shortest-path augmentation oracles.
Positive edge lengths are updated multiplicatively after each augmentation.
A phase threshold and accuracy parameter \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The refinement returns a congestion-scaled feasible path flow; its exact approximation and complexity guarantees require a dedicated Fleischer source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Candidate phase-based refinement template; attribution-specific guarantees remain unsourced.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x=0\) and positive \(\ell\). In each phase, use shortest-path distances to identify an admissible commodity-path pair whose length is below the current phase threshold. Augment that path by an amount limited by its bottleneck capacity and multiply each used edge length by \(1+\varepsilon\delta/u_e\). Continue within the phase until no admissible pair remains, then increase the threshold and begin the next phase. Stop at the terminal threshold, compute \(\rho=\max_e(Ax)_e/u_e\), and return \(x/\max\{1,\rho\}\). This specifies the refinement mechanism but not an attribution-specific approximation ratio or oracle bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Organize multiplicative shortest-path augmentations into increasing-length phases, then scale accumulated flow to capacity; exact Fleischer guarantees remain source-dependent.
knowledge_statements.title: Fleischer Refinements

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record attributes a particular phase-based mechanism to Fleischer without evidence and leaves its threshold schedule and guarantees unspecified. A dedicated source is necessary to establish the attribution and exact algorithm.

children.title: Commodity-Independent Refinements
children.top_down_role: Refinements reducing or removing explicit commodity-count dependence.

assumptions_latex: A routing instance contains \(k\) commodities and uses a shortest-path oracle under current edge lengths.
The refinement maintains a global admissibility threshold shared by all commodities.
Commodity selection uses stored distance labels or a priority structure rather than a mandatory full scan.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithmic control rule is independent of an obligatory \(k\)-commodity scan per augmentation, subject to correct maintenance of the global minimum.

notation.meaning: Stored shortest-path estimate for commodity i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural meaning of commodity independence, without an unsourced running-time theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Maintain for each commodity a stored distance estimate \(D_i\) and a structure exposing an index with minimum valid estimate. An augmentation is permitted only when the exposed estimate is below \(L\); after edge lengths change, invalidate or refresh precisely those estimates required by the refinement's correctness invariant. Thus the control flow need not recompute all \(k\) shortest paths before every augmentation. Correctness requires that the selected pair \((i,P)\) satisfy the refinement's declared oracle condition, such as
\[
\ell(P)\le(1+\xi)\min_j d_\ell(s_j,t_j).
\]
The term commodity-independent concerns avoidance of a compulsory linear scan, not independence of the solution from commodity data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain a valid global shortest-commodity choice without recomputing every commodity path before every augmentation; the solution still depends on all commodities.
knowledge_statements.title: Commodity-Independent Refinements

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed priority and invalidation principle is not sourced, and the correctness-critical rule determining which distance estimates must be refreshed is left unspecified. The claimed sense of commodity independence therefore cannot yet be validated.

children.title: Complexity-Improvement Regimes
children.top_down_role: Parameter settings where the refinements improve runtime or representation size.

assumptions_latex: A baseline implementation performs \(Q_0(k,m,\varepsilon)\) shortest-path calls and \(H_0(k,m,\varepsilon)\) additional operations.
A refinement performs \(Q_1(k,m,\varepsilon)\) calls and \(H_1(k,m,\varepsilon)\) additional operations.
One shortest-path call costs \(S(n,m)\) in the selected graph model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The refinement improves the certified running-time bound exactly in parameter regimes where \(T_1<T_0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison criterion separating oracle savings from refinement overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
T_j(k,n,m,\varepsilon)=Q_j(k,m,\varepsilon)S(n,m)+H_j(k,m,\varepsilon),\qquad j\in\{0,1\}.
\]
The refined method has a strictly better certified running-time bound on a parameter family precisely when
\[
\bigl(Q_0-Q_1\bigr)S(n,m)>H_1-H_0.
\]
Consequently, fewer shortest-path calls alone do not establish an improvement: their saved cost must dominate any extra maintenance, batching, or scaling overhead. An asymptotic improvement holds when \(T_1=o(T_0)\) along the stated regime. Concrete Fleischer regimes require sourced formulas for \(Q_j\) and \(H_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A refinement is faster only when savings from fewer shortest-path calls exceed its extra maintenance overhead; asymptotic improvement requires the refined bound to be lower order.
knowledge_statements.title: Complexity-Improvement Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic comparison T1<T0 is correct but tautological. It does not identify the Fleischer complexity-improvement regimes named by the leaf because Q_j and H_j have no sourced formulas.

children.title: Refinement Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Problem variants where commodity-independent improvements do not directly carry over.

knowledge_statements.title: Refinement Transfer Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for transferring commodity-independent multiplicative-weight refinements to multiflow packing formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let commodities be indexed by \(h\), let \(x_{hP}\ge 0\) denote path flow, and let edge load be \(\ell_e(x)=\sum_h\sum_{P\ni e}x_{hP}\). A refinement whose analysis accesses \(x\) only through \(\ell(x)\) transfers unchanged when every iteration minimizes the same additive edge-length functional \(\sum_{e\in P}w_e\), with commodity dependence confined to the terminal pair and admissible-path set. This transfer is not justified when feasibility or oracle cost contains nonseparable terms \(q_{hP}\) that cannot be represented by common edge weights, because aggregate edge loads then fail to determine the required update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Commodity-independent refinements transfer when all commodities share an edge-additive oracle and aggregate-load update. Commodity-specific nonseparable path costs cross this boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(w_e\ge 0\) for every edge \(e\).
Each oracle returns a minimum-weight admissible path for its terminal pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Common edge-additive objectives permit the transfer; genuinely commodity-specific nonseparable objectives do not.

notation.meaning: flow assigned to path P of commodity h
