children.title: Width Dependence
children.top_down_role: Runtime and approximation sensitivity to packing or covering width.

knowledge_statements.title: Width Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic bounded-width multiplicative-weights dependence for normalized packing loads.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z^1,\ldots,z^T\in[0,\rho]^m\) be normalized constraint-load vectors supplied to a multiplicative-weights packing routine. The standard exponential-weights estimate gives additive average-load error at most \(\rho\sqrt{2\log(m)/T}\). Consequently, additive error at most \(\varepsilon\) is obtained whenever \[T\ge \frac{2\rho^2\log m}{\varepsilon^2}.\] Thus this bounded-loss analysis is logarithmic in the number of packing constraints but quadratic in the chosen width bound; sharper packing analyses may improve the width dependence only by exploiting additional oracle or update structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For normalized loads bounded by width rho, the generic multiplicative-weights analysis needs order rho-squared log m over epsilon-squared iterations.
assumptions_latex: \(m\ge 2\), \(\rho>0\), and \(0<\varepsilon<\rho\).
Every normalized load coordinate lies in \([0,\rho]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T=O(\rho^2\varepsilon^{-2}\log m)\) iterations suffice for additive error \(\varepsilon\) in the generic bounded-loss analysis.
review_flags: A source matching this normalization and constant is required.
Packing-specific algorithms may use a linear rather than quadratic width bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits, but “average-load error” is not formally defined and no multiplicative-weights update, comparator, or packing guarantee is specified. The normalization and constant therefore require a matching source.

children.title: Scaling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Effects of numerical normalization and capacity magnitude.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariance of a nonnegative packing formulation under positive row and variable scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\ge0\) and \(b>0\). For positive diagonal matrices \(D\) and \(S\), set \(y=S^{-1}x\), \(A'=DAS\), \(b'=Db\), and \(c'=Sc\). Then \(x\mapsto y\) is an objective-preserving bijection between the original and scaled feasible sets, since \(c'^{\mathsf T}y=c^{\mathsf T}x\). Moreover, each normalized constraint load is invariant: \[(A'y)_i/b'_i=(Ax)_i/b_i.\] Hence approximation guarantees expressed through normalized feasibility and relative objective value are invariant under these positive scalings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive row and variable scalings preserve the packing problem, objective values, normalized loads, and relative approximation guarantees.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R_+^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R_{++}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R_+^n\).
\(D\) and \(S\) are positive diagonal matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scaled and unscaled packing programs are equivalent under \(x=Sy\), with identical normalized loads.

knowledge_statements.title: Output Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse path representation of a feasible fractional multicommodity edge flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be directed and let \(f^h\ge0\) be a feasible \(s_h\)-\(t_h\) flow for each commodity \(h\). After deleting nonnegative circulations, each \(f^h\) admits a decomposition \[f^h=\sum_{j=1}^{r_h}\lambda_{hj}\chi^{P_{hj}},\qquad \lambda_{hj}>0,\qquad r_h\le |E|,\] where every \(P_{hj}\) is a simple directed \(s_h\)-\(t_h\) path. Thus a feasible multiflow can be output explicitly using at most \(k|E|\) weighted paths; alternatively, the edge-flow vectors \((f^h)_{h=1}^k\) give an equivalent polynomial-size representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A k-commodity edge flow can be represented by edge-flow vectors or decomposed into at most k times the number of edges weighted paths.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and each \(f^h\) satisfies flow conservation away from \(s_h,t_h\).
Circulation components may be discarded without affecting routed demand.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is an explicit weighted-path representation with \(\sum_h r_h\le k|E|\).

knowledge_statements.title: Complexity–Representation Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-sensitive distinction between implicit oracle solutions and explicit path decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a routing algorithm returns an implicit multiflow representation \(R\) from which each commodity edge-flow vector can be recovered in time \(Q\). If an explicit list of \(L\) positive weighted paths is required, any standard sequential-output model needs \(\Omega(L)\) time merely to write the list. Recovering the edge flows and repeatedly extracting a positive \(s_h\)-\(t_h\) path yields at most \(k|E|\) paths and polynomial additional time. Therefore an oracle-call bound for producing \(R\) is not, by itself, an end-to-end bound for explicit path output; the conversion and output costs must be included.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An implicit routing solution may be computed faster than its path list can be written; explicit complexity must include recovery, decomposition, and output size.
assumptions_latex: The computation model charges constant time per emitted path record.
Recovered edge flows have rational, explicitly manipulable values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Explicit-output running time is at least \(\Omega(L)\) and includes the cost of converting \(R\) into a path decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Disjoint Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision version with prescribed terminal pairs in a finite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\) and terminal pairs \((s_i,t_i)\in V^2\) for \(i=1,\ldots,k\), an edge-disjoint linkage is a family of paths \(P_1,
\ldots,P_k\) such that \(P_i\) joins \(s_i\) to \(t_i\) and \(E(P_i)\cap E(P_j)=\varnothing\) whenever \(i\ne j\). In a directed graph every \(P_i\) must respect arc orientation. The edge-disjoint paths decision problem asks whether such a family exists; vertices, including internal vertices, may be shared unless a separate vertex-disjointness condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The edge-disjoint paths problem asks for one path per terminal pair with no edge used by two paths; vertices may be shared.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) and the ordered list of terminal pairs are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility means the existence of paths satisfying all prescribed pairings and pairwise edge disjointness.

knowledge_statements.title: Disjointness-Model Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex splitting reduces directed vertex-disjoint prescribed linkage to directed edge-disjoint prescribed linkage when all terminals are distinct.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\) with pairwise distinct terminals and prescribed pairs \((s_i,t_i)\), where fully vertex-disjoint directed paths are required. Construct \(G'\) by replacing every vertex \(v\in V\), including every terminal, with vertices \(v^{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(v^{\mathrm{out}}\) joined by a private arc \(a_v=(v^{\mathrm{in}},v^{\mathrm{out}})\). Replace every original arc \((u,v)\in A\) by \((u^{\mathrm{out}},v^{\mathrm{in}})\), and replace each terminal pair by \((s_i^{\mathrm{in}},t_i^{\mathrm{out}})\). Output the resulting directed edge-disjoint-paths instance. The original instance has a vertex-disjoint linkage if and only if the transformed instance has an edge-disjoint linkage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split every vertex, including terminals, into an in-copy and an out-copy joined by a private arc, replace each original arc accordingly, and connect each transformed source in-copy to its sink out-copy. Edge-disjoint paths in the transformed digraph correspond exactly to vertex-disjoint paths in the original digraph.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph.
All \(2k\) terminals are pairwise distinct.
The source problem requires fully vertex-disjoint paths, including disjoint terminal vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The construction has polynomial size and preserves feasibility in both directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Disjointness Separation Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A four-leaf star separates edge-disjoint from internally vertex-disjoint feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be the undirected star with center \(v\), leaves \(a,b,c,d\), and edges \(av,bv,cv,dv\). For terminal pairs \((a,b)\) and \((c,d)\), the unique connecting paths are \(a-v-b\) and \(c-v-d\). Their edge sets are disjoint, so the edge-disjoint instance is feasible. Both paths contain \(v\) as an internal vertex, however, and uniqueness forces every linkage for the two pairs to share \(v\). Hence the corresponding internally vertex-disjoint instance is infeasible.

children.title: Orientation-Sensitive Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Orientation-Sensitive Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical fixed-pair complexity separation between directed and undirected vertex linkage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each fixed \(k\), the undirected prescribed-pair vertex-disjoint paths problem is solvable in polynomial time, with the polynomial degree allowed to depend on \(k\). In contrast, the directed prescribed-pair vertex-disjoint paths problem is NP-complete already for \(k=2\). Thus replacing every undirected edge by two oppositely directed arcs preserves individual walks but does not transfer the fixed-parameter polynomial-time linkage theory: directed orientation can encode ordering constraints absent from the undirected instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fixed k, undirected linkage is polynomial-time solvable, whereas directed linkage is NP-complete already for two prescribed pairs.
assumptions_latex: The number \(k\) of prescribed terminal pairs is fixed for the undirected algorithmic statement.
Inputs are finite graphs with distinct terminals and vertex-disjointness is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Orientation changes the classical complexity boundary: fixed-\(k\) tractability in undirected graphs does not extend to directed graphs.
review_flags: Authoritative locators are required for the fixed-k undirected algorithm and directed two-pair NP-completeness.
Complexity convention should be checked for vertex-disjoint versus internally vertex-disjoint paths.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Splitting Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard directed vertex-capacity-to-arc-capacity transformation, with an explicit terminal-capacity convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed network with arc capacities \(u_a\) and integral vertex capacities \(b_v\). For every vertex \(v\) whose throughput is constrained, create \(v^{\mathrm{in}}\), \(v^{\mathrm{out}}\), and an internal arc \(a_v=(v^{\mathrm{in}},v^{\mathrm{out}})\) of capacity \(b_v\). Replace each original arc \(a=(u,v)\) by an arc from the outgoing copy of \(u\), when \(u\) is split, to the incoming copy of \(v\), when \(v\) is split, retaining capacity \(u_a\); an unsplit endpoint is used directly. Attach supplies and demands according to the declared convention. In particular, split a terminal when its throughput is capacity-constrained and otherwise leave it unsplit. Solving the transformed arc-capacitated instance and contracting every internal arc \(a_v\) gives an exact correspondence with integral flows satisfying the stated vertex capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace each constrained vertex by an entrance and exit joined by a capacity arc, redirect incident arcs consistently, and specify explicitly whether terminal throughput is constrained. Contracting the internal arcs recovers exactly the feasible original flows.

children.title: Reduction-Preservation Criteria

knowledge_statements.title: Reduction-Preservation Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes decision-feasibility preservation from solution-preserving and faithful routing reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a routing instance \(I\), let \(\mathcal F(I)\) denote its feasible route families and let \(T(I)\) be the transformed instance. The transformation \(T\) preserves decision feasibility exactly when \[\mathcal F(I)\ne\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathcal F(T(I))\ne\varnothing.\] A solution-preserving reduction supplies a lifting map \(L:\mathcal F(I)\to\mathcal F(T(I))\) and a projection map \(\pi:\mathcal F(T(I))\to\mathcal F(I)\), each preserving the prescribed terminal pairing, orientation, integrality, and relevant capacity or disjointness constraints. The existence of both maps implies decision-feasibility preservation. The additional identity \(\pi(L(P))=P\) for every \(P\in\mathcal F(I)\) is a stronger faithful-representation condition, not a consequence of decision equivalence. An objective-preserving reduction must additionally preserve the claimed objective value under the applicable lifting and projection maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decision preservation requires equivalence of nonempty feasible-solution sets. Explicit lifting and projection maps give the stronger solution-preserving criterion, while projection after lifting being the identity is stronger still.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a routing instance and \(T(I)\) is its transformed instance.
\(\mathcal F(I)\) and \(\mathcal F(T(I))\) are their respective feasible route-family sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Decision equivalence, solution-preserving maps, and faithful recovery are distinct preservation levels and must not be treated as equivalent conditions.

notation.meaning: lifting map from original to transformed feasible solutions
projection map from transformed to original feasible solutions
feasible route families of instance I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The ordinary split gadget enforces only the aggregate inequality \(\sum_i f_i(v)\le b_v\). It does not by itself encode commodity-dependent permissions, pairwise incompatibilities, turn restrictions, or nonlinear occupancy rules. For example, suppose one unit of either commodity may traverse \(v\) alone, but the two commodities are forbidden from sharing \(v\), even when \(b_v=2\). A split arc of capacity \(2\) admits one unit of each commodity and therefore creates a transformed solution that is infeasible in the original model. Exactness then requires a richer state or conflict gadget, not merely vertex splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single split arc models only additive shared capacity; commodity-specific conflicts, turn rules, and nonlinear occupancy can make the reduction admit spurious routes.

children.title: Edge-Linkage Variants

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and \(S,T\subseteq V\) are disjoint.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An edge linkage of order \(k\) is a family \(\mathcal P=\{P_1,\ldots,P_k\}\) of paths satisfying \(E(P_i)\cap E(P_j)=\varnothing\) whenever \(i\ne j\). In the set-to-set variant, every path has one end in \(S\) and one in \(T\), with distinct ends when required. In the prescribed-pair variant, given \((s_i,t_i)\), path \(P_i\) must join \(s_i\) to \(t_i\). For a digraph, each \(P_i\) must be directed from its designated source to its sink, and disjointness is imposed on arcs rather than underlying undirected edges unless explicitly stated otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edge-linkage variants differ by whether terminal pairing is free or prescribed and whether paths must respect arc orientation.

children.title: Edge-Separator Variants

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Separator Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers undirected edge separators, cut separators, and directed arc separators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For distinct vertices \(s,t\), an \(s\)-\(t\) edge separator is a set \(F\subseteq E\) such that \(G-F\) contains no \(s\)-\(t\) path. For disjoint sets \(S,T\subseteq V\), an \(S\)-\(T\) edge separator destroys every path with one end in \(S\) and the other in \(T\). A cut separator has the form \(\delta(X)\), where \(S\subseteq X\subseteq V\setminus T\). In a digraph \(D=(V,A)\), an arc separator \(F\subseteq A\) destroys every directed path of the specified orientation; a directed cut consists of the arcs leaving a set containing the source side and disjoint from the sink side. Minimum variants minimize \(|F|\), or \(\sum_{e\in F}c_e\) when nonnegative edge or arc costs \(c_e\) are given.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edge-separator variants delete edges or directed arcs to eliminate a specified terminal connection, with cardinality or weighted cost as the usual objective.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph for the edge-separator variants.
\(S,T\subseteq V\) are disjoint terminal sets.
For directed variants, \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite digraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An edge or arc separator is a resource set whose deletion destroys every path of the specified terminal-connection type.

Then \[\lambda_G(s,t)=\kappa'_G(s,t).\] Thus either a family of \(k\) edge-disjoint \(s\)-\(t\) paths exists, or an edge separator of size less than \(k\) certifies that no such family exists. The equality also has a capacitated integral form after replacing cardinality by integral edge capacity.

assumptions_latex: The instance is the cycle \(C_4=(a,b,c,d,a)\) with demand pairs \((a,c)\) and \((b,d)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum number of simultaneously routed demand pairs is \(1\), while the minimum multicut has size \(2\).

notation.meaning: edge set whose deletion separates every demand pair

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of naive multipair Menger equality.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=C_4\) have cyclic order \(a,b,c,d\), and prescribe demand pairs \((a,c)\) and \((b,d)\). Any path joining \(a\) to \(c\) uses two consecutive cycle edges, and every path joining \(b\) to \(d\) shares an edge with it; hence at most one demand pair can be routed in an edge-disjoint family. Conversely, deleting fewer than two edges leaves a connected spanning path, so it cannot separate both demand pairs. Deleting \(F=\{ab,cd\}\) separates both pairs. Therefore the packing value is \(1\) and the minimum multicut value is \(2\), disproving direct multipair equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a four-cycle with opposite demand pairs, only one pair can be routed, but two edges are required to separate both pairs.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vertex linkage of order \(k\) is a family \(\mathcal P=\{P_1,\ldots,P_k\}\) whose paths have pairwise disjoint internal vertex sets: \(\operatorname{int}(P_i)\cap\operatorname{int}(P_j)=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\). A fully vertex-disjoint linkage additionally requires \(V(P_i)\cap V(P_j)=\varnothing\). In a prescribed-pair variant, \(P_i\) joins \(s_i\) to \(t_i\); in a set-to-set variant, pairing between disjoint terminal sets \(S\) and \(T\) may be chosen by the linkage. Directed variants require consistently oriented paths. Whether terminals may occur internally on other paths is part of the variant and must be stated explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertex-linkage variants differ in internal versus full disjointness, prescribed versus free terminal pairing, orientation, and whether terminals may lie inside other paths.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For distinct nonadjacent vertices \(s,t\), an \(s\)-\(t\) vertex separator is a set \(X\subseteq V\setminus\{s,t\}\) such that \(G-X\) contains no \(s\)-\(t\) path. For disjoint terminal sets \(S,T\), an \(S\)-\(T\) separator is usually required to satisfy \(X\subseteq V\setminus(S\cup T)\) and to meet every \(S\)-\(T\) path. In a digraph, the same deletion condition is imposed on directed paths from the specified source side to the sink side. Weighted variants minimize \(\sum_{v\in X}c_v\) for nonnegative vertex costs \(c_v\), while cardinality variants minimize \(|X|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex separator avoids protected terminals and deletes enough vertices to destroy every undirected or directed path of the specified terminal type.

The prescribed terminal pairs are \((v_1,v_3)\) and \((v_2,v_4)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nu_{\mathrm{pair}}=1<2=\tau_{\mathrm{pair}}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: No two vertex-disjoint paths can simultaneously join the alternating pairs \((v_1,v_3)\) and \((v_2,v_4)\), so \(\nu_{\mathrm{pair}}=1\). A single vertex fails to meet all paths for both pairs: after deleting any one vertex, a path remains for at least one pair that avoids it. The set \(\{v_1,v_2\}\) meets every path joining either prescribed pair, hence \(\tau_{\mathrm{pair}}=2\). Thus the naive multipair packing-versus-common-transversal equality fails even on a four-cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For alternating pairs on a four-cycle, at most one pair can be routed vertex-disjointly, while two vertices are required to hit every admissible pair-path.

children.top_down_role: Constructive frameworks for assembling collections of compatible paths.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with distinct nonadjacent terminals \(s,t\).
Every nonterminal vertex has unit capacity.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(M=|V|\). Replace every \(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}\) by \(v^{\mathrm{in}}\), \(v^{\mathrm{out}}\), and an arc \(v^{\mathrm{in}}v^{\mathrm{out}}\) of capacity \(1\). Replace each undirected edge by oppositely directed arcs of capacity \(M\) between the appropriate terminal or split vertices. Starting with \(f=0\), repeatedly augment by one unit along a residual \(s\)-\(t\) path until none exists. Decompose the resulting integral flow into directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths and directed cycles, discard the cycles, and contract every split pair. The resulting paths form a maximum family of pairwise internally vertex-disjoint \(s\)-\(t\) paths in \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonadjacent terminals, split every nonterminal vertex into a unit-capacity arc, compute an integral maximum flow, and decompose it to obtain a maximum internally vertex-disjoint path packing.

children.title: Blocking-Path Methods
children.top_down_role: Obstruction-guided frameworks using paths that prevent further augmentation.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with distinct nonadjacent terminals \(s,t\).
\(D\) is obtained by giving every nonterminal split arc capacity \(1\) and every arc representing an original edge capacity \(M=|V|\).
\(f\) is a feasible integral \(s\)-\(t\) flow in \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Residual search either augments \(f\) by one unit or, when \(t\) is unreachable, returns an \(s\)-\(t\) vertex separator of cardinality \(|f|\).

notation.meaning: vertices reachable from s in the residual network
capacity assigned to arcs representing original edges

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual reachability supplies either an augmenting path or a blocking vertex separator in the explicitly capacitated split network.

source_refs.locator: 8.4 Packing paths p. 277

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct \(D_f\) and search from \(s\). If \(t\) is reached, augment \(f\) by one unit along a residual \(s\)-\(t\) path and repeat. If \(t\) is not reached, let \(R\) be the residual-reachable set. Then every arc leaving \(R\) is saturated, every arc entering \(R\) carries zero flow, and \(c(\delta^+(R))=|f|\). Since \(|f|\le |V|-2<M\), no capacity-\(M\) arc leaves \(R\). Hence every arc in \(\delta^+(R)\) is a unit-capacity split arc. The original vertices represented by these split arcs form an \(s\)-\(t\) vertex separator of cardinality \(|f|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual search either finds an augmenting path or returns a saturated cut consisting of unit split arcs, which identifies a blocking vertex separator of the same size as the current flow.
knowledge_statements.title: Blocking-Path Methods

Consequently, when \(|\mathcal{P}|=|S|\), the family \(\mathcal{P}\) is a maximum internally vertex-disjoint \(s\)-\(t\) path packing and \(S\) is a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) vertex separator. Verification requires checking path endpoints, internal vertex-disjointness, separation in \(G-S\), and the equality of the two cardinalities.

children.title: Packing Stagnation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instances where local blocking structure fails to expose globally useful augmentation.

assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\) and \(k\ge 2\).
\(G_k\) is the finite undirected graph with vertex set \(\{s,t\}\cup\{a_i,b_i:1\le i\le k\}\) and edge set \(\{sa_i,a_ib_i,b_it:1\le i\le k\}\cup\{a_ia_{i+1}:1\le i<k\}\cup\{a_kt\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximal packing \(\{Q\}\) has cardinality \(1\), whereas the maximum packing has cardinality \(k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy maximality without residual rerouting has an unbounded ratio for internally vertex-disjoint path packing.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=s-a_1-a_2-\cdots-a_k-t\). The packing \(\{Q\}\) is maximal because every \(s\)-\(t\) path in \(G_k\) contains at least one vertex \(a_i\). On the other hand, the \(k\) paths \(s-a_i-b_i-t\), for \(1\le i\le k\), are pairwise internally vertex-disjoint. Moreover, \(\{a_1,\ldots,a_k\}\) is an \(s\)-\(t\) vertex separator, so the maximum packing has cardinality exactly \(k\). Thus maximal packing cardinality divided by maximum packing cardinality can equal \(1/k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the explicitly defined graph, choosing the long path first gives a maximal one-path packing, while the maximum packing has k paths; therefore greedy maximality has no constant approximation guarantee.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mader's Disjoint S-Paths Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partition-based min-max characterization for packing vertex-disjoint paths between distinct terminal sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph, let $\mathcal S$ be a collection of pairwise disjoint subsets of $V$, and put $T:=\bigcup\mathcal S$. The maximum number of pairwise vertex-disjoint $\mathcal S$-paths equals
\[
\min_{(U_0,\ldots,U_n)}\left(|U_0|+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\lfloor\frac{|B_i|}{2}\right\rfloor\right),
\]
where the minimum is over all partitions $U_0,\ldots,U_n$ of $V$ such that every $\mathcal S$-path intersects $U_0$ or traverses an edge spanned by some $U_i$, and
\[
B_i:=\{v\in U_i: v\in T\text{ or }v\text{ has a neighbor in }V\setminus(U_0\cup U_i)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum number of pairwise vertex-disjoint S-paths equals the minimum, over qualifying partitions of V, of |U0| plus the sum of floor(|Bi|/2), where Bi contains the terminal or externally adjacent vertices of Ui.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a graph}
\mathcal S\text{ is a collection of pairwise disjoint subsets of }V
T:=\bigcup\mathcal S
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nu_{\mathcal S}(G)=\min_{\substack{(U_0,\ldots,U_n)\text{ partitions }V\\\text{each }\mathcal S\text{-path meets }U_0\text{ or spans an edge in some }U_i}}\left(|U_0|+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\lfloor\frac{|B_i|}{2}\right\rfloor\right)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mader's Edge-Disjoint T-Paths Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut-and-parity min-max characterization of edge-disjoint T-path packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph and let $T\subseteq V$. The maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint $T$-paths equals
\[
\min_{(X_s)_{s\in T}}\frac{1}{2}\left(\sum_{s\in T}d_E(X_s)-\kappa\right),
\]
where the minimum is over pairwise disjoint sets $X_s\subseteq V$ satisfying $s\in X_s$ for every $s\in T$, and $\kappa$ is the number of components $K$ of $G-\bigcup_{s\in T}X_s$ for which $d_E(K)$ is odd.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint T-paths equals the minimum of one half the sum of the terminal-region edge boundaries minus the number of odd-boundary components outside those regions.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a graph}
T\subseteq V
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nu_T^E(G)=\min_{\substack{X_s\subseteq V\ (s\in T)\\s\in X_s\text{ and the }X_s\text{ are pairwise disjoint}}}\frac{1}{2}\left(\sum_{s\in T}d_E(X_s)-\left|\left\{K\in\operatorname{comp}\left(G-\bigcup_{s\in T}X_s\right):d_E(K)\text{ is odd}\right\}\right|\right)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Three-Terminal Edge-Disjoint Path Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes prescribed pairwise edge-disjoint path multiplicities among three terminals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(V,E), let s_1,s_2,s_3\in V, and let d_{12},d_{13},d_{23}\in\mathbb Z_+. Let R be the demand multigraph on \{s_1,s_2,s_3\} having d_{ij} edges between s_i and s_j, and define s(X):=|\delta_E(X)|-d(\delta_R(X)). There are edge-disjoint paths, with exactly d_{ij} paths connecting s_i and s_j for each 1\le i<j\le3, if and only if |\delta_E(X)|\ge d(\delta_R(X)) for every X\subseteq V and, for every choice of pairwise disjoint U_1,U_2,U_3\subseteq V with s_i\in U_i, one has \sum_{i=1}^3s(U_i)\ge\kappa, where \kappa is the number of components K of G-(U_1\cup U_2\cup U_3) such that |\delta_E(K)| is odd.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The prescribed numbers of edge-disjoint paths between each pair of three terminals exist exactly when the cut condition and the stated odd-component inequality both hold.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a graph}
s_1,s_2,s_3\in V
R\text{ has }d_{ij}\text{ demand edges between }s_i\text{ and }s_j
s(X)=|\delta_E(X)|-d(\delta_R(X))
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ the prescribed edge-disjoint paths}\iff\left[\forall X\subseteq V,\ |\delta_E(X)|\ge d(\delta_R(X))\right]\land\left[\forall\text{ admissible }U_1,U_2,U_3,\ \sum_{i=1}^3s(U_i)\ge\kappa\right]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mader's Internally Vertex-Disjoint T-Paths Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Min-max characterization for internally vertex-disjoint T-paths when the terminal set is stable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph and let $T\subseteq V$ be stable. The maximum number of pairwise internally vertex-disjoint $T$-paths equals
\[
\min_{(U_0,\ldots,U_n)}\left(|U_0|+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\lfloor\frac{|B_{G-U_0}(U_i)|}{2}\right\rfloor\right),
\]
where the minimum is over partitions $U_0,U_1,\ldots,U_n$ of $V\setminus T$ such that every $T$-path intersects $U_0$ or traverses an edge spanned by some $U_i$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When T is stable, the maximum number of pairwise internally vertex-disjoint T-paths equals the stated minimum over qualifying partitions of V minus T, using the boundary sets of the parts in G−U0.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a graph}
T\subseteq V\text{ is stable}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nu_T^{\mathrm{int}}(G)=\min_{\substack{(U_0,\ldots,U_n)\text{ partitions }V\setminus T\\\text{each }T\text{-path meets }U_0\text{ or spans an edge in some }U_i}}\left(|U_0|+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\lfloor\frac{|B_{G-U_0}(U_i)|}{2}\right\rfloor\right)

Assign a variable \(x_P\ge 0\) to every \(P\in\mathscr{P}_T\). The unit vertex-capacity fractional \(T\)-path packing number is

\nu_T^*(G)=\max\left\{\sum_{P\in\mathscr{P}_T}x_P:\ \sum_{P\in\mathscr{P}_T:\,v\in V(P)}x_P\le 1\ \text{for every }v\in V\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mader Path-Packing System Is a Matroid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes that the endpoint-subset system induced by disjoint terminal-path packings is a matroid independence system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph, let \(\mathcal S=\{S_1,\ldots,S_k\}\) be a collection of pairwise disjoint subsets of \(V\), set \(T:=\bigcup_{i=1}^k S_i\), and let \(\mathcal I\) consist of all \(I\subseteq T\) contained in \(\operatorname{ends}(\mathcal P)\) for some collection \(\mathcal P\) of disjoint \(\mathcal S\)-paths. Then \(M=(T,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The terminal subsets that can be included among the endpoints of a collection of disjoint S-paths form the independent sets of a matroid on T.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an undirected graph.
\(\mathcal S=\{S_1,\ldots,S_k\}\) is a collection of pairwise disjoint subsets of \(V\).
\(T=\bigcup_{i=1}^k S_i\).
\(\mathcal I=\{I\subseteq T:\exists\mathcal P\text{ a collection of disjoint }\mathcal S\text{-paths with }I\subseteq\operatorname{ends}(\mathcal P)\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M=(T,\mathcal I)\) is a matroid.

children.title: Lockable Collections
children.top_down_role: Terminal or demand collections admitting simultaneous locking behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected with terminal set \(T\).
For \(X\subseteq T\), let \(\lambda(X)\) denote the minimum capacity of an \(X\)-to-\(T\setminus X\) cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A collection is lockable when one multiflow simultaneously attains every prescribed cut bound.

notation.meaning: total multiflow value crossing the terminal bipartition induced by X
minimum capacity separating X from the remaining terminals

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provisional multiflow-cut meaning; integrality and terminal-family conventions remain ambiguous.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A collection \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq 2^T\) is lockable in \(G\) if there exists a feasible multiflow \(f\) such that
\[
f(X,T\setminus X)=\lambda(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal{A}.
\]
Such an \(f\) simultaneously locks all members of \(\mathcal{A}\), meaning that the cut upper bound for paths crossing each terminal bipartition is attained. A complete local definition must additionally choose integral or fractional path weights, vertex or edge capacities, and the convention for complementary members \(X\) and \(T\setminus X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A terminal-set collection is lockable when one feasible multiflow simultaneously saturates the minimum-cut bound associated with every member.
knowledge_statements.title: Lockable Collections

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed lockability formula is plausible but not yet well-defined: the graph assumptions supply no edge or vertex capacity function, feasible multiflow is undefined, and integral versus fractional weights are unresolved. These choices materially change the predicate, and no authoritative source identifies the intended convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lockability Characterization and Multiflow Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes lockable collections and gives conditional half-integral and integral multiflow existence guarantees in the setting of (73.43).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A collection \(\mathcal A\) is lockable if and only if \(\mathcal A\) contains no three pairwise crossing sets. If \(\mathcal A\) is lockable and \(c\) is integer-valued, then there exists a half-integer multiflow satisfying \((73.43)\). If, moreover, \(c(\delta(v))\) is even for every \(v\in V\setminus T\), then there exists an integer multiflow satisfying \((73.43)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A collection is lockable exactly when it contains no three pairwise crossing sets. With integer capacities, lockability guarantees a half-integer multiflow satisfying (73.43); if every nonterminal has even incident capacity, it guarantees an integer multiflow satisfying (73.43).
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is a collection in the multiflow setting of \((73.43)\).
\(c\) is integer-valued for the half-integrality conclusion.
\(c(\delta(v))\) is even for every \(v\in V\setminus T\) for the integrality conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A\text{ is lockable}\iff\mathcal A\text{ contains no three pairwise crossing sets}\), together with the stated conditional half-integer and integer multiflow existence guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlockable Collection Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edge-capacitated Mader terminal paths; nonlockability means simultaneous cut saturation fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) have integer capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), terminal set \(T\subseteq V\), and a collection \(\mathcal A\subseteq 2^T\). For \(A\subseteq T\), let \(\lambda(A)\) be the minimum capacity of an edge cut separating \(A\) from \(T\setminus A\). A feasible integral multiflow \(F\) locks \(A\) when the total multiplicity of its terminal paths having one endpoint in \(A\) and the other in \(T\setminus A\) equals \(\lambda(A)\). The collection \(\mathcal A\) is nonlockable precisely when
\[\nexists F\text{ feasible such that }d_F(A)=\lambda(A)\quad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal A.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A collection is nonlockable when no feasible integral terminal-path packing simultaneously saturates every collection member’s minimum separating-cut bound.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected graph with integral edge capacities.
Every multiflow path has distinct endpoints in \(T\) and no internal terminal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is nonlockable if and only if no feasible \(F\) satisfies \(d_F(A)=\lambda(A)\) for all \(A\in\mathcal A\).

notation.meaning: minimum capacity separating A from the complementary terminals
multiplicity of multiflow paths crossing the terminal bipartition induced by A
collection of terminal subsets required to be locked simultaneously

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, and the statement is internally coherent, but the specialized Mader lockability convention and selected edge-capacitated integral model require an authoritative source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Maximum-Value Multiflows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic optimization over integral terminal-path multiflows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) have capacities \(u_e\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), edge costs \(c_e\in\mathbb R\), terminals \(T\subseteq V\), and terminal-path set \(\mathcal P_T\). An integral multiflow is \(x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{\mathcal P_T}\) satisfying \(\sum_{P
i e}x_P\le u_e\) for every \(e\in E\). Define its value and cost by
\[
u(x)=\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_T}x_P,\qquad C(x)=\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_T}x_P\sum_{e\in P}c_e.\]
A minimum-cost maximum-value multiflow is any \(x^*\) with \(
u(x^*)=\max_x
u(x)\) and \(C(x^*)=\min\{C(x):
u(x)=
u(x^*)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First maximize the number of routed terminal paths subject to capacities; among all maximum-value integral multiflows, choose one having minimum total edge cost.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
Capacities are nonnegative integers and every admissible path has two distinct terminals as endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}\{C(x):x\text{ feasible and }\nu(x)=\max_y\nu(y)\}.\)

notation.meaning: total edge cost of the multiflow

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Pair Undirected Linkage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex-disjoint linkage with a fixed number of prescribed terminal pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every fixed integer \(k\ge1\), there is a polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) and \(k\) pairwise distinct terminal pairs \((s_1,t_1),\ldots,(s_k,t_k)\), decides whether \(G\) contains paths \(P_1,\ldots,P_k\) such that \(P_i\) joins \(s_i\) to \(t_i\) and the paths are mutually vertex-disjoint. Equivalently, for each fixed \(k\), the decision problem has running time \(|V|^{O_k(1)}\); the exponent or hidden constants may depend on \(k\), but not on the input graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any fixed number of prescribed pairs, existence of mutually vertex-disjoint connecting paths in an undirected graph is decidable in polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: \(k\) is fixed independently of the input size.
All \(2k\) terminals are distinct.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\textsc{Undirected-}k\textsc{-Disjoint-Paths}\in\mathrm P\) for every fixed \(k\).

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Pair Undirected Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex-disjoint linkage when the number of prescribed pairs is input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the decision problem whose input is a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), an integer \(k\), and \(k\) prescribed terminal pairs \((s_i,t_i)\) whose \(2k\) terminals are pairwise distinct. The question is whether mutually vertex-disjoint paths \(P_i:s_i\leadsto t_i\) exist for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\). When \(k\) is part of the input, this problem is NP-complete, marking a complexity boundary from the polynomial-time fixed-\(k\) regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Disjoint-Paths Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex-disjoint prescribed-pair paths in general directed graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite digraph \(D=(V,A)\), one prescribed pair \((s,t)\) is feasible exactly when \(t\) is reachable from \(s\), hence is decidable in polynomial time. In contrast, given two distinct source–sink pairs \((s_1,t_1)\) and \((s_2,t_2)\), deciding whether there are mutually vertex-disjoint directed paths \(P_1:s_1\leadsto t_1\) and \(P_2:s_2\leadsto t_2\) is NP-complete. Thus fixing the number of pairs does not yield the undirected fixed-pair tractability boundary: hardness already occurs at \(k=2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed linkage is easy for one pair but NP-complete already for two prescribed pairs, unlike the undirected fixed-pair problem.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a finite directed graph.
All terminals in the two-pair instance are distinct.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The directed problem lies in \(\mathrm P\) for \(k=1\) and is NP-complete for \(k=2\).

notation.meaning: directed path for prescribed pair i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary is mathematically standard and precisely stated, but no citation supports the crucial NP-completeness claim for two prescribed directed vertex-disjoint paths.

knowledge_statements.title: Acyclic-Digraph Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prescribed vertex-disjoint directed paths restricted to directed acyclic graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed acyclic graph with \(k\) prescribed terminal pairs. For every fixed \(k\), feasibility of mutually vertex-disjoint directed paths joining all pairs can be decided in time \(|V|^{O(k)}\), for example by dynamic programming over a topological order and a product state recording the path frontiers. This is polynomial for fixed \(k\). When \(k\) is part of the input, the same feasibility problem on acyclic digraphs is NP-complete, so acyclicity alone does not remove the variable-pair hardness boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a DAG, fixed-pair directed linkage admits polynomial dynamic programming, but the problem remains NP-complete when the pair count varies.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a finite directed acyclic graph.
The prescribed terminals are pairwise distinct.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The DAG problem is solvable in \(|V|^{O(k)}\) time and is NP-complete when \(k\) is unbounded.

notation.meaning: number of prescribed directed terminal pairs
polynomial time for every fixed pair count

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Both the fixed-k runtime and variable-k NP-completeness classification require authoritative sources. The asserted product-state dynamic program is also too specific to accept without inspection.

children.title: Planar Routing Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Planar Routing Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eulerian one-face edge-disjoint paths in a plane supply graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a plane multigraph and let \(H=(V,F)\) be a demand multigraph whose demand-edge endpoints all lie on the boundary of one face of \(G\). Suppose the combined multigraph \(G+H\) is Eulerian. Then the demand edges can be realized by pairwise edge-disjoint paths in \(G\), one path joining the endpoints of each edge of \(H\), if and only if the cut condition
\[|\delta_G(X)|\ge |\delta_H(X)|\qquad\text{for every }X\subseteq V\]
holds. Necessity follows from capacity accounting; the planar one-face and Eulerian hypotheses supply sufficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For Eulerian one-face planar instances, every demand can be routed by edge-disjoint paths exactly when every cut has enough supply edges.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) has a fixed plane embedding and all demand endpoints share one face.
Every vertex has even degree in \(G+H\).
Supply edges have unit capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An edge-disjoint realization of \(H\) in \(G\) exists if and only if \(|\delta_G(X)|\ge|\delta_H(X)|\) for every \(X\subseteq V\).

notation.meaning: supply edges with exactly one endpoint in X
multigraph formed from all supply and demand edges

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind and Eulerian one-face formulation appear appropriate, but the exact integral variant needs a source. The final sentence also gives proof-style commentary that should be removed in any sourced revision.

Suppose \(G\) has two bounded faces \(F_1,F_2\), the vertices \(s_1,\ldots,s_k\) occur in clockwise order along \(\operatorname{bd}(F_1)\), the vertices \(t_1,\ldots,t_k\) occur in clockwise order along \(\operatorname{bd}(F_2)\), and \(G+H\) is Eulerian. Then there are pairwise edge-disjoint paths \(P_{s_it_i}\) joining \(s_i\) to \(t_i\) for all \(i\) if and only if the cut condition holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For correspondingly ordered terminal pairs on two bounded faces of a planar graph, an Eulerian supply-demand union admits simultaneous edge-disjoint paths exactly when the cut condition holds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Three-Face Planar Routing Characterization by the K2,3-Metric Condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral edge-disjoint routing for Eulerian planar instances in which every demand pair is cofacial on one of three specified faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a planar graph, let \(F_1,F_2,F_3\) be three faces of \(G\), and let \(H=(V,R)\) be a graph such that, for every \(r=st\in R\), there is an \(i\in\{1,2,3\}\) for which both \(s\) and \(t\) lie on the boundary of \(F_i\). knowledge_statements.title: Surface Routing Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disjoint-path routing parameterized by surface genus and pair count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix nonnegative integers \(g\) and \(k\). Given an undirected graph \(G\) cellularly embedded in a compact surface of Euler genus at most \(g\), together with \(k\) prescribed pairs of distinct terminals, existence of mutually vertex-disjoint paths joining the pairs is decidable in polynomial time. Its running time may be written \(f(g,k)|V|^{O(1)}\) for some computable function \(f\), when the embedding is supplied with the instance. The assertion treats \(g\) and \(k\) as parameters; it makes no uniform polynomial-time claim when either is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With both surface genus and pair count fixed, prescribed-pair vertex-disjoint routing on an embedded undirected graph is polynomial-time decidable.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is supplied with a cellular embedding of Euler genus at most \(g\).
Both \(g\) and \(k\) are fixed parameters.
All prescribed terminals are distinct.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decision time is \(f(g,k)|V|^{O(1)}\) for fixed \(g\) and \(k\).

notation.meaning: upper bound on the Euler genus of the surface
parameter-dependent factor independent of graph size

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits, but the uniform runtime form \(f(g,k)|V|^{O(1)}\), embedding model, and surface assumptions require a specific algorithmic theorem citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Homotopy-Constrained Routing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Embedded linkage with a prescribed relative homotopy class for each route.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be embedded in a surface \(\Sigma\), let \((s_i,t_i)\) be prescribed terminal pairs, and let \([\gamma_i]\) be a relative homotopy class of curves from \(s_i\) to \(t_i\) in \(\Sigma\setminus Z\), where \(Z\) is a specified obstacle set. A homotopy-constrained routing is a family of graph paths \((P_i)_{i=1}^k\) such that each \(P_i\) joins \(s_i\) to \(t_i\), the paths satisfy the selected vertex- or edge-disjointness convention, and the embedded curve traced by \(P_i\) belongs to \([\gamma_i]\) relative to its endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homotopy-constrained routing connects every prescribed pair by disjoint embedded graph paths lying in specified relative homotopy classes around fixed obstacles.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) has a fixed embedding in \(\Sigma\).
Homotopies fix every route endpoint and avoid \(Z\).
The vertex- or edge-disjointness convention is fixed for the instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((P_i)_{i=1}^k\) is feasible exactly when every \(P_i\) satisfies connectivity, disjointness, and \(P_i\in[\gamma_i]\).

notation.meaning: relative homotopy class prescribed for route i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits, but the selected relative-homotopy model is uncited. A source should also clarify that terminals and admissible embedded routes lie outside the obstacle set and fix one disjointness convention.

children.title: Topology-Sensitive Complexity Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Topology-Sensitive Complexity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why an unrestricted embedding genus does not itself confer tractability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every finite graph \(G=(V,E)\) admits a cellular embedding in some compact orientable surface; an embedding can be obtained by thickening a rotation system and capping its boundary components. Consequently, if the surface and its genus are unrestricted parts of the input, the class of embedded graphs contains all finite graphs. In particular, variable-pair undirected disjoint paths on unrestricted embedded surfaces remains NP-complete: adding an embedding cannot remove hardness of the underlying abstract instance. Thus topology-based tractability statements must bound a topological parameter or impose a genuine embedding restriction such as planarity or fixed genus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unbounded-genus embedded graphs include all finite graphs, so merely supplying an embedding does not eliminate general variable-pair routing hardness.
assumptions_latex: The input surface may have arbitrarily large genus.
Routing feasibility depends on the underlying graph unless additional topological constraints are imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unrestricted-genus embedded disjoint paths inherits NP-completeness from the corresponding abstract-graph problem.

notation.meaning: genus of a supporting surface, not bounded a priori

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is suitable, but the cellular-embedding construction and NP-hardness transfer need sources and an explicit polynomial-size input representation for the embedding and surface.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Path Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent randomized rounding of a fractional path-flow decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each commodity \(i\), let nonnegative path weights \(x_{iP}\) satisfy \(\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_i}x_{iP}=1\). Independently sample one path \(P_i\in\mathcal P_i\) with probability \(\Pr(P_i=P)=x_{iP}\), and output the unsplittable routing \((P_i)_i\). For an edge \(e\), define \(L_e=\sum_i\mathbf1\{e\in P_i\}\). Then
\[\mathbb E[L_e]=\sum_i\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_i:e\in P}x_{iP},\]
so the expected integral load equals the fractional load. Capacity feasibility is not guaranteed in every realization and may require rejection, resampling, or alteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independently sample one path from each commodity’s fractional path distribution; every edge’s expected integral load equals its fractional load.
assumptions_latex: Each commodity has unit demand.
The path weights for each commodity form a probability distribution.
Commodity selections are mutually independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every edge \(e\), \(\mathbb E[L_e]=\sum_i\sum_{P\ni e}x_{iP}\).

notation.meaning: fractional weight and sampling probability of path P for commodity i
number of sampled paths using edge e

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Path formulation and randomized selection for minimum-capacity multicommodity flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path-based integer formulation, its fractional relaxation, and the associated randomized path-selection procedure for undirected minimum-congestion routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$, terminal pairs $(s_i,t_i)$ for $i=1,\ldots,k$, and the set $\mathcal P_i$ of simple $s_i$--$t_i$ paths, minimum-capacity integral routing has the formulation
\[
\min W\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_{P\in\mathcal P_i}x_P=1\ (i=1,\ldots,k),\qquad \sum_{P:e\in P}x_P\le W\ (e\in E),\qquad x_P\in\{0,1\}.
\]
Replacing $x_P\in\{0,1\}$ by $x_P\ge0$ gives a linear relaxation that can be solved in polynomial time and has an optimal solution with only polynomially many nonzero path variables. Given an optimal relaxation solution $x^*$ of value $W^*$, select exactly one path for each pair $i$ according to the distribution $(x_P^*)_{P\in\mathcal P_i}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum-capacity multicommodity routing can be modeled with one path variable per simple terminal-to-terminal path, exactly one selected path per terminal pair, and an edge-load bound W. Its fractional relaxation is polynomial-time solvable and admits a polynomial-support optimum. Randomized selection then chooses one path for each pair using the optimal fractional path values as probabilities.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is an undirected graph}
(s_i,t_i)\in V\times V\quad(i=1,\ldots,k)
\mathcal P_i\text{ is the set of simple }s_i\text{--}t_i\text{ paths}
x^*\text{ is an optimal feasible solution of the path relaxation with value }W^*
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{P\in\mathcal P_i}x_P^*=1,\qquad \Pr[\text{path }P\text{ is selected for pair }i]=x_P^*.

knowledge_statements.title: Alteration Techniques
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Post-rounding deletion repair for edge-capacitated unsplittable routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a family \(S\) of selected unit-demand paths and integer edge capacities \(u_e\). Initialize \(R\leftarrow S\). While some edge \(e\) has load \(L_e(R)=|\{P\in R:e\in P\}|>u_e\), choose any \(L_e(R)-u_e\) paths of \(R\) containing \(e\) and delete them from \(R\). Stop when no edge is overloaded and output \(R\). Each deletion weakly decreases every edge load, so termination occurs after at most \(|S|\) deletions, and the output satisfies \(L_e(R)\le u_e\) for all \(e\). Retention guarantees require a separately specified deletion rule or probabilistic analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly delete selected paths from overloaded edges. The process terminates with a capacity-feasible retained routing, although retention quality needs separate analysis.
assumptions_latex: All selected paths have unit demand.
Every edge capacity \(u_e\) is a nonnegative integer.
Deleting a path is permitted and forfeits its commodity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(R\subseteq S\) satisfies \(L_e(R)\le u_e\) for every edge \(e\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deletion algorithm is coherent, terminates, and guarantees feasibility without claiming retention quality. Nevertheless, the alteration technique has no cited evidence and requires a specific source locator.

children.title: Congestion Repair

knowledge_statements.title: Congestion Repair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deletion-based repair of an already selected unsplittable multicommodity routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given paths \(P_i\), demands \(d_i>0\), edge capacities \(u_e>0\), and a target congestion \(\beta\geq 1\), initialize \(R=I\). While some edge \(e\) satisfies \(\sum_{i\in R:e\in P_i}d_i>\beta u_e\), select such an edge and delete from \(R\) any commodity \(i\) with \(e\in P_i\). Stop when no violated edge remains, and output the retained routing \(\{P_i:i\in R\}\). The procedure terminates after at most \(|I|\) deletions and its output has edge congestion at most \(\beta\); the deletion rule determines the retained value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly delete a routed commodity using an overloaded edge. The process terminates with congestion at most the prescribed threshold, although retention depends on the deletion rule.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite and every \(d_i>0\).
\(u_e>0\) for every usable edge.
\(\beta\geq 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_e u_e^{-1}\sum_{i\in R:e\in P_i}d_i\leq\beta\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deletion algorithm and congestion guarantee are mathematically sound, but no inspectable source supports this alteration rule or any meaningful repair–retention guarantee.

children.title: Repair–Retention Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Balance between congestion reduction and preservation of selected commodities.

knowledge_statements.title: Repair–Retention Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto representation of retained value versus allowed congestion for fixed routed paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For routed commodities \(I\) with weights \(w_i\geq0\), define the retention function at congestion budget \(\beta\geq0\) by \[R(\beta)=\max\left\{\sum_{i\in S}w_i:S\subseteq I,\ \sum_{i\in S:e\in P_i}d_i\leq\beta u_e\text{ for every }e\right\}.\] Then \(R\) is nondecreasing, satisfies \(0\leq R(\beta)\leq\sum_{i\in I}w_i\), and equals the total weight once \(\beta\) reaches the congestion of the original routing. Equivalently, the minimum discarded weight is \(\sum_{i\in I}w_i-R(\beta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The best retention at a congestion budget is the maximum weight of any feasible retained subset. Allowing more congestion cannot reduce this optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\beta_1\leq\beta_2\Longrightarrow R(\beta_1)\leq R(\beta_2)\).

notation.meaning: maximum retained weight under congestion beta

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-subset optimization and monotonicity statement are precise and fit the tradeoff container, but the specialized representation has no cited source.

children.title: Residual Congestion Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instance classes where alteration leaves unavoidable overload or substantial demand loss.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Congestion Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of repaired routings by their remaining capacity violation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a retained routing \(S\), let its load be \(L_e(S)=\sum_{i\in S:e\in P_i}d_i\) and its residual multiplicative congestion be \(C(S)=\max_e L_e(S)/u_e\). The routing is in the exact-feasibility regime when \(C(S)\leq1\), in an additive-residual regime with parameter \(\Delta\geq0\) when \(L_e(S)\leq u_e+\Delta\) for every edge, and in a multiplicative-residual regime with factor \(\beta\geq1\) when \(C(S)\leq\beta\). These labels concern the repaired output, independently of how it was produced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual congestion records whether repaired loads meet capacities exactly, exceed them by a uniform additive amount, or exceed them by a multiplicative factor.
assumptions_latex: \(u_e>0\) for every usable edge.
Each retained commodity uses one path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C(S)\leq1\), or \(L_e(S)\leq u_e+\Delta\), or \(C(S)\leq\beta\), according to the selected regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Demand-to-Capacity Scaling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: No-bottleneck scaling parameter for capacitated multicommodity routing instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For demands \(d_i>0\) and positive capacities on usable edges, define \(d_{\max}=\max_i d_i\), \(u_{\min}=\min_e u_e\), and \(\rho=d_{\max}/u_{\min}\). The global no-bottleneck regime is \(\rho\leq1\); a small-demand regime has \(\rho\leq\varepsilon\) for a specified \(0<\varepsilon<1\); and the large-demand regime has \(\rho>1\). Under uniform demand scaling \(d_i\mapsto t d_i\) with \(t>0\), the parameter scales linearly as \(\rho(t)=t\rho\), so regime thresholds occur at explicit values of \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum demand divided by the minimum usable capacity distinguishes small-demand, no-bottleneck, and large-demand regimes and scales linearly with all demands.
assumptions_latex: The commodity and usable-edge sets are finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho(t)=t\rho\), with no-bottleneck condition \(t\rho\leq1\).

children.title: Integrality-Gap Constructions
children.top_down_role: Instances exhibiting separation between fractional routing quality and integral routing quality.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality-Gap Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instance families separating fractional and integral maximum-throughput routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a capacitated routing instance \(J\) with commodity weights, let \(F(J)\) be the maximum weight accepted by the fractional path-flow relaxation and let \(Z(J)\) be the maximum weight of commodities routable integrally, one path per accepted commodity. A family \(\mathcal J\) is an integrality-gap construction of factor at least \(g\geq1\) if every member has \(Z(J)>0\) and \(F(J)/Z(J)\geq g\). An asymptotic gap \(g(n)\) requires instances \(J_n\) of size parameter \(n\) satisfying this inequality for infinitely many \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrality-gap family has fractional throughput at least a stated factor larger than the best one-path-per-commodity throughput.
assumptions_latex: Fractional and integral models use the same capacities, demands, path families, and weights.
All commodity weights are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(J)/Z(J)\geq g\) for each constructed instance \(J\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ratio defines a plausible routing integrality-gap family, but no source supports the formulation. The construction leaf may ultimately require a counterexample record rather than only a generic definition.

children.title: Congestion-Gap Constructions
children.top_down_role: Instances requiring additional congestion when fractional routings are converted to integral routings.

knowledge_statements.title: Congestion-Gap Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instance families separating fractional and unsplittable minimum congestion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance \(J\) in which all commodities must be routed, let \(C_f(J)\) be the minimum maximum edge load-to-capacity ratio over fractional multicommodity flows, and let \(C_i(J)\) be the corresponding minimum over unsplittable routings using one path per commodity. A family \(\mathcal J\) is a congestion-gap construction of factor at least \(g\geq1\) if \(C_f(J)>0\) and \(C_i(J)/C_f(J)\geq g\) for every \(J\in\mathcal J\). Normalizing \(C_f(J)=1\) makes the lower bound equivalent to \(C_i(J)\geq g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A congestion-gap family forces every unsplittable routing to incur much more congestion than an optimal fractional routing of the same demands.
assumptions_latex: Every commodity is required to be routed.
Fractional and integral models use identical demands, capacities, and admissible paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_i(J)/C_f(J)\geq g\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fractional-versus-unsplittable congestion ratio is mathematically coherent, but no source supports the formulation. The construction leaf may ultimately require a counterexample record rather than only a generic definition.

children.title: Gap Transfer Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural settings relating integrality loss to congestion loss.

knowledge_statements.title: Gap Transfer Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reciprocal correspondence between uniform throughput scaling and minimum congestion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix demands \(d
eq0\), capacities, and admissible paths. For model \(M\in\{f,i\}\), let \(\lambda_M(d)\) be the largest scalar \(\lambda\geq0\) for which demands \(\lambda d\) are routable with unit congestion, and let \(C_M(d)\\) be the minimum congestion for routing \(d\). Because loads scale linearly while the selected fractional flow or integral paths remain fixed, \[C_M(d)=\frac{1}{\lambda_M(d)}.\] Consequently, whenever the quantities are positive and finite, \[\frac{C_i(d)}{C_f(d)}=\frac{\lambda_f(d)}{\lambda_i(d)}.\] Thus a fractional-to-integral uniform-throughput gap transfers exactly to the same-factor congestion gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum congestion is the reciprocal of maximum uniform demand scaling, so fractional-versus-integral gaps transfer exactly between these formulations.
assumptions_latex: The instance is finite and \(d\neq0\).
Loads are linear in uniformly scaled demands.
The relevant optima are positive and finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_i(d)/C_f(d)=\lambda_f(d)/\lambda_i(d)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Survivable Network Design and Its Cut Formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected edge-connectivity requirements, their binary cut formulation, LP relaxation, and pairwise minimum-cut separation oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$, costs $c_e\ge 0$, and requirements $r_{ij}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ for distinct $i,j\in V$, survivable network design seeks a minimum-cost $F\subseteq E$ containing at least $r_{ij}$ edge-disjoint $i$-$j$ paths for every pair. Define $\rho(S)=\max_{i\in S,\,j\notin S}r_{ij}$ for nontrivial cuts, with $\rho(\varnothing)=\rho(V)=0$. By max-flow/min-cut, $F$ is feasible if and only if $|\delta(S)\cap F|\ge\rho(S)$ for every $S\subseteq V$. Thus the binary formulation is $\min\{\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e:\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}x_e\ge\rho(S)\ \forall S\subseteq V,\ x_e\in\{0,1\}\}$, with LP relaxation $0\le x_e\le1$. This relaxation has a polynomial-time separation oracle using an $i$-$j$ minimum cut with capacities $x_e$ for each distinct pair $i,j$. The same cut-LP form may more generally be written with an integer-valued right-hand side $f:2^V\to\mathbb Z$, without thereby asserting the same separation oracle for arbitrary $f$. The generalized Steiner tree problem is the special case $r_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Survivable network design chooses a minimum-cost edge set meeting pairwise edge-connectivity requirements. Max-flow/min-cut makes feasibility equivalent to lower bounds on every cut, yielding a binary cut formulation and a bounded LP relaxation. For the pairwise-maximum requirement function, violated constraints can be found through pairwise minimum cuts. The cut-LP notation also extends to a general integer-valued requirement function, but the stated separation guarantee is specific to the pairwise-connectivity formulation.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is an undirected graph}
c_e\ge0\quad\forall e\in E
r_{ij}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\quad\forall i,j\in V,\ i\ne j
\rho(\varnothing)=\rho(V)=0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is feasible}\iff |\delta(S)\cap F|\ge\rho(S)\quad\forall S\subseteq V,\text{ and the pairwise-connectivity LP admits polynomial-time minimum-cut separation.}

knowledge_statements.title: Rooted Connectivity Design

\(c_e\geq0\) and \(k_v\) are nonnegative integers.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Connectivity Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost spanning subgraph with uniform global edge connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(|V|\geq2\), nonnegative edge costs \(c_e\), and an integer \(k\geq1\), global \(k\)-edge-connectivity design chooses \(F\subseteq E\) minimizing \(\sum_{e\in F}c_e\) such that the spanning subgraph \((V,F)\) remains connected after deletion of any fewer than \(k\) edges. Equivalently, \[|F\cap\delta(S)|\geq k\quad\text{for every }\varnothing\neq S\subsetneq V,\] and every distinct pair of vertices is joined by at least \(k\) edge-disjoint paths.

knowledge_statements.title: Rooted-to-Global Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact equivalence of uniform rooted and global undirected edge-connectivity constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=(V,F)\) be a finite undirected spanning subgraph with \(|V|\geq2\), fix a root \(r\in V\), and let \(k\geq1\) be an integer. Then \[H\text{ is globally }k\text{-edge-connected}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda_H(r,v)\geq k\text{ for every }v\in V\setminus\{r\}.\] Consequently, a global minimum-cost \(k\)-edge-connectivity design instance is equivalent, without changing its edges or costs, to the uniform rooted instance with requirement \(k_v=k\) for every \(v\neq r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any chosen root in a finite undirected graph with at least two vertices, global k-edge-connectivity is equivalent to having k edge-disjoint root-to-vertex paths to every other vertex, giving a cost-preserving reduction.

\(r\in V\).

knowledge_statements.title: Element-Connectivity Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost design protecting terminal connections against edge and nonterminal-vertex failures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be undirected, let \(T\subseteq V\) be terminals, and assign costs \(c_e\geq0\) and integer requirements \(r_{st}\geq0\) for terminal pairs. \(c_e\geq0\) and \(r_{st}\) are nonnegative integers.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cut-requirement realization and exact network synthesis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines realization, exact realization, exact realizability, and the synthesis task for ordered-pair cut requirements; ordinary realization always exists, whereas exact realization need not.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $V$ be finite and let $r:V\times V\to\mathbb R_+$. A realization of $r$ is a directed graph $D=(V,A)$ with capacities $c:A\to\mathbb R_+$ such that every $s$-$t$ cut has capacity at least $r(s,t)$ for all $s,t\in V$. It is exact if, for every distinct $s,t\in V$, the minimum capacity of an $s$-$t$ cut equals $r(s,t)$. Every such function $r$ has a realization, but it is exactly realizable only when an exact realization exists. The network synthesis problem seeks an exact realization or a cheapest realization for $r$, or determines that the requested exact realization does not exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A realization of a nonnegative ordered-pair requirement function is a capacitated directed graph in which every s–t cut has at least the required capacity. It is exact when each distinct pair's minimum-cut value equals its requirement. Every requirement function has some realization, but an exact realization may not exist. Network synthesis seeks an exact or cheapest realization and may need to certify nonexistence of an exact one.
assumptions_latex: V\text{ is finite}
r:V\times V\to\mathbb R_+
D=(V,A)\text{ is directed}
c:A\to\mathbb R_+

knowledge_statements.title: Proper Cut Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard properness predicate for undirected survivable cut requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite ground set \(V\), a requirement function \(r:2^V\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\) is proper when \(r(\varnothing)=r(V)=0\), it is symmetric, \[r(S)=r(V\setminus S)\quad\text{for every }S\subseteq V,\] and it satisfies the disjoint-union maximum condition \[r(A\cup B)\le\max\{r(A),r(B)\}\quad\text{whenever }A\cap B=\varnothing.\] Thus combining two disjoint shores cannot create a requirement exceeding both constituent requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper requirement is normalized, symmetric under complementation, and cannot increase beyond both values when disjoint sets are united.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
\(r\) is nonnegative and integer-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\) satisfies normalization, symmetry, and the disjoint-union maximum inequality.

notation.meaning: complement of S in the ground set V

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is coherent and fits the leaf, but no source is supplied for the exact conjunction of normalization, symmetry, and the disjoint-union maximum property under the name proper. Terminology varies enough that an authoritative definition locator is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proper set functions and 0–1 complementarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines proper set functions and states the complementarity characterization and class boundary for the symmetric 0–1 case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb N\) is proper if \(f(V)=0\), \(f\) satisfies the maximality property, and \(f(S)=f(V\setminus S)\) for every \(S\subseteq V\). For a symmetric function \(f:2^V\to\{0,1\}\), maximality is equivalent to complementarity: for all \(A\subseteq S\subseteq V\), \(f(S)=f(A)=0\) implies \(f(S\setminus A)=0\). The class of 0–1 proper functions and the class of downward-monotone functions are incomparable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper set function vanishes on the full ground set, satisfies maximality, and is symmetric under complementation. For symmetric 0–1 functions, maximality is equivalent to complementarity: if nested sets A and S both have value zero, then S minus A also has value zero. Neither the 0–1 proper class nor the downward-monotone class contains the other.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is proper under the stated defining conditions; in the symmetric 0–1 case, maximality is equivalent to complementarity, and the stated function classes are incomparable.}

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Supermodular Cut Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-crossing version, distinguished here from the all-pairs skew-supermodular predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite. A function \(r:2^V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) is weakly supermodular in the positive-crossing sense if, whenever \(A,B\subseteq V\) cross and \(r(A)>0\), \(r(B)>0\), at least one inequality holds: \[r(A)+r(B)\le r(A\cap B)+r(A\cup B),\] or \[r(A)+r(B)\le r(A\setminus B)+r(B\setminus A).\] Here crossing means that \(A\cap B\), \(A\setminus B\), \(B\setminus A\), and \(V\setminus(A\cup B)\) are all nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every positively required crossing pair, either the intersection-union pair or the two differences preserve the combined requirement.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
\(r:2^V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r(A)+r(B)\le\max\{r(A\cap B)+r(A\cup B),r(A\setminus B)+r(B\setminus A)\}\) for every positively required crossing pair.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed positive-crossing predicate is internally precise, but weakly supermodular is used inconsistently across survivable-design sources and is often synonymous with skew-supermodular under different domains. A source must confirm that the positivity and crossing restrictions define the intended local variant.

knowledge_statements.title: Skew-Supermodular Cut Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: All-pairs two-way uncrossing predicate for a cut-requirement function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite ground set \(V\), a function \(r:2^V\to\mathbb{R}\) is skew-supermodular if every \(A,B\subseteq V\) satisfy at least one of \[r(A)+r(B)\le r(A\cap B)+r(A\cup B)\] and \[r(A)+r(B)\le r(A\setminus B)+r(B\setminus A).\] Equivalently, the left side is at most the maximum of the two displayed right sides. The condition supplies one of the two standard uncrossings for every pair, including pairs for which some of the four regions are empty.

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
\(r\) is real-valued on all subsets of \(V\).
