knowledge_statements.title: Laminar-Support Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Laminar tight-cut basis certificate for an extreme point of a survivable cut relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P(r)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{E}:x(\delta(S))\ge r(S)\text{ for all }S\subset V\}\), where \(r\) is skew-supermodular, and let \(x\) be an extreme point with positive support \(E_x=\{e:x_e>0\}\). A laminar-support certificate is a laminar family \(\mathcal L\) of tight cuts such that \(x(\delta(S))=r(S)\) for every \(S\in\mathcal L\), the restricted incidence vectors \(\chi^{\delta(S)\cap E_x}\) are linearly independent, and they span \(\mathbb{R}^{E_x}\). Consequently \(|\mathcal L|=|E_x|\), so these tight equalities uniquely determine the supported coordinates of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extreme point is certified by a laminar basis of tight cut equations spanning all positive edge coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(r\) is skew-supermodular.
\(x\) is an extreme point of \(P(r)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal L\) is laminar, tight, and \(\{\chi^{\delta(S)\cap E_x}:S\in\mathcal L\}\) is a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^{E_x}\).

notation.meaning: laminar family of tight vertex sets
cut-incidence vector restricted to the support

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role matches the leaf, but the existence of a laminar tight-cut basis is a nontrivial uncrossing theorem. No source establishes that skew-supermodularity alone suffices for the stated polyhedron or confirms the treatment of zero coordinates and redundant cut constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Point Token Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint-token accounting on the inclusion forest of a laminar tight-cut basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal L\) be a laminar tight-cut basis for an extreme point with support \(E_x\). Order \(\mathcal L\) by inclusion and define \(\operatorname{ch}(S)\) as the maximal proper members contained in \(S\), with core \(C(S)=S\setminus\bigcup_{T\in\operatorname{ch}(S)}T\). Assign one half-token for each incidence \((v,e)\) with \(v\) an endpoint of \(e\in E_x\), placing it at the unique core containing \(v\), when such a core exists. The total endpoint-token mass is \(|E_x|\), and the mass initially held by \(S\) is \(\tfrac12\sum_{v\in C(S)}\deg_{E_x}(v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A laminar basis forms an inclusion forest whose disjoint cores support conserved half-token accounting for edge endpoints.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal L\) is laminar.
Every supported edge has two endpoints in \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{S\in\mathcal L}\tfrac12\sum_{v\in C(S)}\deg_{E_x}(v)\le |E_x|\), with equality when the cores cover \(V\).

notation.meaning: children of S in the laminar inclusion forest
portion of S outside all child sets
number of supported edges incident to v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role is plausible, but the statement does not fully reconcile the claimed total token mass with endpoints that belong to no laminar core; equality is separately conditioned on core coverage. Token structures and redistribution rules are application-dependent, so an exact iterative-rounding source is needed before selecting a reliable formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Non-Uncrossable Requirement Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete crossing requirements for which neither standard uncrossing inequality holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{1,2,3,4\}\), \(A=\{1,2\}\), and \(B=\{2,3\}\). Define \(r(A)=r(B)=1\) and \(r(S)=0\) for every other \(S\subseteq V\). The sets \(A\) and \(B\) cross, but \[r(A)+r(B)=2>r(A\cap B)+r(A\cup B)=0\] and \[r(A)+r(B)=2>r(A\setminus B)+r(B\setminus A)=0.\] Thus \(r\) is not skew-supermodular, and the usual replacement of two crossing tight constraints by either standard uncrossed pair has no requirement-value justification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two crossing required sets can violate both uncrossing inequalities, blocking the standard laminarization argument.
assumptions_latex: Only \(A\) and \(B\) have positive requirement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\) violates both skew-supermodular alternatives at \((A,B)\).

notation.meaning: the specified crossing subsets of V

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cut Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of pairwise survivable cut inequalities by repeated minimum-cut computations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), a nonnegative fractional vector \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{E}\), and pair requirements \(r_{st}\ge0\). For each pair with \(r_{st}>0\), compute an \(s\)-\(t\) minimum cut \(S_{st}\) using capacities \(x_e\). If \(x(\delta(S_{st}))<r_{st}\), output the violated inequality \(x(\delta(S_{st}))\ge r_{st}\). If no pair produces a violation, output that all inequalities \(x(\delta(S))\ge\max\{r_{st}:s\in S,t\notin S\}\) are satisfied. Correctness follows because any violated cut separates at least one pair attaining its right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run a capacitated minimum cut for each required pair; return a violated pair cut or certify all pairwise cut inequalities.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
\(x_e\ge0\) and the listed pair requirements are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns a violated cut exactly when one exists for the induced pairwise requirement function.

notation.meaning: shore of a minimum s-t cut under capacities x

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For disjoint sets \(A,B\subseteq V\), define \(E(A,B)=\{uv\in E:u\in A,\ v\in B\}\). Given a nonnegative set-pair requirement \(q\), the associated relaxation is
\[P_{\mathrm{sp}}(q)=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^E:x(E(A,B))\ge q(A,B)\text{ for all }A,B\subseteq V\text{ with }A\cap B=\varnothing\}.\]
The unused vertices \(V\setminus(A\cup B)\) may represent a deleted separator, so this indexing is strictly richer than ordinary two-shore cut indexing when such deletions matter.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the undirected bi-set relaxation used when separator vertices must be represented explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A bi-set is a pair \(\hat S=(S,S^+)\) satisfying \(S\subseteq S^+\subseteq V\); its boundary is \(\Gamma(\hat S)=S^+\setminus S\), and its entering edge set is \(\delta(\hat S)=E(S,V\setminus S^+)\). For a nonnegative requirement function \(f\), define
\[P_{\mathrm{biset}}(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^E:x(\delta(\hat S))\ge f(\hat S)\text{ for every bi-set }\hat S\}.\]
The separate inner, boundary, and exterior regions permit constraints that encode vertex or element separators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bi-set relaxation imposes cut requirements between an inner shore and the exterior of an outer shore, explicitly recording the intervening vertex boundary.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(F=\varnothing\) and \(y_S=0\) for every cut. While some residual requirement \(f_F(S)=\max\{0,f(S)-|F\cap\delta(S)|\}\) is positive, choose an inclusion-minimal active family of violated cuts and increase their dual variables uniformly until an unused edge constraint \(\sum_{S:e\in\delta(S)}y_S\le c_e\) becomes tight; add a tight edge according to the specified augmentation rule. When all residual requirements vanish, optionally delete purchased edges in reverse order whenever feasibility is preserved, and output \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method raises dual prices on unmet cuts, buys edges when their dual constraints become tight, and optionally reverse-deletes redundant edges after all requirements are met.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Dual Growth with Reverse Delete
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual algorithm for feasible binary cut-requirement instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(y=0\), \(A=\varnothing\), and \(\ell=0\). While \(A\) is infeasible, increment \(\ell\), let \(\mathcal V\) be the minimal violated sets, and increase all \(y_S\), \(S\in\mathcal V\), uniformly until an edge \(e_\ell\in\delta(T)\) for some \(T\in\mathcal V\) becomes dual-tight: \[\sum_{S:e_\ell\in\delta(S)}y_S=c_{e_\ell}.\] Add \(e_\ell\) to \(A\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Binary Cut-Requirement Relaxation and Violated Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP-dual representation and structural facts supporting primal-dual algorithms for binary cut requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be undirected and \(f:2^V\to\{0,1\}\). The binary cut model is \[\min\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_{e\in\delta(S)}x_e\ge 1\ \ (S:f(S)=1),\qquad x_e\in\{0,1\}.\] The dual of its LP relaxation is \[\max\sum_{S:f(S)=1}y_S\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_{S:f(S)=1,\ e\in\delta(S)}y_S\le c_e\ \ (e\in E),\qquad y_S\ge0.\] Every edge-minimal feasible solution is a forest. For a current edge set \(A\subseteq E\), \(S\) is violated exactly when \(f(S)=1\) and \(\delta(S)\cap A=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For binary cut requirements, the LP dual packs nonnegative weights on required cuts subject to each edge's cost capacity. Every edge-minimal feasible solution is a forest, and a required set is violated precisely when the current edge set does not cross its cut.

c_e\ge0\quad(e\in E)
A\subseteq E

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb N\) has the maximality property when, for all disjoint \(A,B\subseteq V\), \[f(A\cup B)\le\max\{f(A),f(B)\}.\] For \(f:2^V\to\{0,1\}\), this is equivalent to \[f(A)=f(B)=0\implies f(A\cup B)=0\] for disjoint \(A,B\), and equivalently, if \(f(S)=1\), every partition of \(S\) contains at least one part \(P\) satisfying \(f(P)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut-requirement function has the maximality property when its value on a disjoint union does not exceed the larger value on the pieces. In the binary case, disjoint zero-valued sets have a zero-valued union; equivalently, every partition of a required set contains a required part.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Jain's iterative-rounding algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm specification for capacitated undirected survivable network design with proper cut requirements; its correctness and approximation guarantee are stated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an undirected graph \(G\), costs \(c:E(G)\to\mathbb R_+\), capacities \(u:E(G)\to\mathbb N\), and an oracle-given proper function \(f:2^{V(G)}\to\mathbb Z_+\), initialize \(x_e=0\) if \(c(e)>0\) and \(x_e=u(e)\) if \(c(e)=0\). Repeatedly define \(u'(e)=u(e)-x_e\) and \(f'(S)=f(S)-\sum_{e\in\delta_G(S)}x_e\), find an optimal basic solution \(y\) of the residual LP (20.13), stop if \(y_e=0\) for every edge, and otherwise set \(x_e\leftarrow x_e+\lceil y_e\rceil\) for every edge with \(y_e\geq\tfrac12\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize positive-cost edges at zero and zero-cost edges at capacity. Repeatedly solve an optimal basic residual cut LP and round upward every variable at least one half, stopping when the residual solution is zero.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is an undirected graph}
c:E(G)\to\mathbb R_+
u:E(G)\to\mathbb N
f:2^{V(G)}\to\mathbb Z_+\text{ is proper and oracle-given}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Specified output: }x\in\mathbb Z_+^{E(G)},\quad x_e\leq u(e)\ \forall e,\quad\sum_{e\in\delta_G(S)}x_e\geq f(S)\ \forall S\subseteq V(G).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Half-integral-variable lemma for the skew-supermodular survivable-network cut relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\), and let \(f:2^V\to\mathbb Z_+\) satisfy, for all \(A,B\subseteq V\), at least one of
\[f(A)+f(B)\le f(A\cap B)+f(A\cup B),\qquad f(A)+f(B)\le f(A\setminus B)+f(B\setminus A).\]
If \(x\ne0\) is an extreme point of
\[P(f)=\{z\in\mathbb R_+^E:z(\delta(S))\ge f(S)\text{ for every }S\subseteq V\},\]
then some edge \(e\in E\) satisfies \(x_e\ge\tfrac12\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

\[f_F(S)=\max\{0,f(S)-|F\cap\delta(S)|\}\qquad(S\subseteq V).\]

\[z(\delta(S)\setminus F)\ge f_F(S)\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V.\]

children.title: Edge-Connectivity Consequences
children.top_down_role: Iterative-rounding consequences for edge-connectivity design.

assumptions_latex: The instance is an undirected survivable network design problem with nonnegative edge costs and integer pair requirements.
Feasibility is expressed by the standard skew-supermodular cut requirement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Iterative rounding returns a feasible edge set \(F\) with \(c(F)\le2\,\mathrm{OPT}_{LP}\le2\,\mathrm{OPT}\).

notation.meaning: Optimum value of the cut relaxation
Cost of the selected edge set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical factor-two consequence for undirected edge-connectivity requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Repeatedly solve an extreme-point optimum of the residual cut relaxation, delete every edge with value \(0\), and select an edge whose value is at least \(\tfrac12\). Update the residual integer requirements and continue until they vanish. The large-variable property guarantees progress, and charging the cost of each selected edge against its fractional value yields
\[c(F)\le 2\,\mathrm{OPT}_{LP}\le 2\,\mathrm{OPT}.\]
With a polynomial-time separation oracle for the cut relaxation, the procedure uses polynomially many optimization and update steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jain-style iterative rounding gives a polynomial-time factor-two approximation for undirected survivable edge-connectivity design under the standard cut formulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Connectivity Consequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The factor-two result fits the edge-connectivity consequence leaf, but the theorem, polynomial-time qualification, and charging guarantee have no cited source.

children.title: Element-Connectivity Consequences
children.top_down_role: Iterative-rounding consequences for element-connectivity design.

assumptions_latex: Terminals have integer pairwise element-connectivity requirements and nonnegative edge costs.
Edges and nonterminal vertices are the removable elements; terminals cannot serve as internal vertices of terminal-to-terminal paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For the standard element-connectivity relaxation, iterative rounding yields \(c(F)\le2\,\mathrm{OPT}_{LP}\) and satisfies every terminal-pair requirement.

notation.meaning: Optimum value of the element-connectivity relaxation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factor-two consequence under the standard terminal element-connectivity model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In the terminal element-connectivity design problem, two paths are element-disjoint when they share neither an edge nor a nonterminal vertex. Under the standard set-pair or bi-set relaxation whose residual requirement function admits skew-supermodular uncrossing, iterative rounding selects a variable of value at least \(\tfrac12\) at every nonzero residual extreme point. Consequently it returns a subgraph \(F\) satisfying all prescribed terminal-pair element connectivities and
\[c(F)\le2\,\mathrm{OPT}_{LP}\le2\,\mathrm{OPT}.\]
The bound presupposes the element-connectivity-specific relaxation, rather than the ordinary edge-cut relaxation alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With the appropriate set-pair or bi-set relaxation, the half-variable iterative-rounding framework extends to a factor-two guarantee for terminal element connectivity.
knowledge_statements.title: Element-Connectivity Consequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The precise terminal convention, applicable set-pair or bi-set relaxation, half-variable theorem, and factor-two guarantee are source-dependent and currently unsupported.

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-to-Element Transfer Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete obstruction to transferring edge-connectivity guarantees directly to element connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every integer \(k\ge 2\), let \(G_k\) be the undirected multigraph on \(\{s,v,t\}\) having \(k\) parallel edges between \(s\) and \(v\) and \(k\) parallel edges between \(v\) and \(t\). Then \(\lambda_{G_k}(s,t)=k\) while \(\kappa_{\mathrm{el},G_k}(s,t)=1\). Consequently, arbitrarily large local edge connectivity does not imply element connectivity greater than one, and ordinary edge-cut constraints alone do not certify element connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every k at least two, the three-vertex multigraph with k parallel edges on each side of one nonterminal middle vertex has edge connectivity k but element connectivity one. Thus edge-cut guarantees do not transfer directly to element connectivity.
assumptions_latex: \(G_k\) is an undirected multigraph in which parallel edges are permitted.
Element-disjoint paths may share neither edges nor nonterminal vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_{G_k}(s,t)=k\) and \(\kappa_{\mathrm{el},G_k}(s,t)=1\), so edge connectivity does not provide a comparable element-connectivity guarantee.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given edges \(su,sv\in E\) with \(u\ne v\), splitting off the pair at \(s\) forms the multigraph
\[G'=G-su-sv+uv,\]
where a new parallel edge is allowed. The pair is admissible relative to \(V\setminus\{s\}\) if
\[\lambda_{G'}(a,b)=\lambda_G(a,b)\qquad\text{for all distinct }a,b\in V\setminus\{s\}.\]
A complete splitting-off at \(s\) is a sequence of such operations that removes every edge incident to \(s\); it is admissible when every operation in the sequence is admissible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Undirected splitting-off replaces two edges incident to a vertex by an edge joining their other endpoints; admissibility means preserving all local edge connectivities away from that vertex.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Splitting-Off
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the orientation-compatible local splitting operation at a vertex of a directed multigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph and let \(s\in V\). For arcs \(us\in A\) and \(sv\in A\), a directed splitting-off at \(s\) deletes one copy of each of \(us\) and \(sv\) and adds one copy of \(uv\); a loop is permitted when \(u=v\). The pair \((us,sv)\) is admissible for a prescribed terminal set \(T\subseteq V\setminus\{s\}\) when the resulting digraph \(D'\) satisfies \(\lambda_{D'}(x,y)=\lambda_D(x,y)\) for every ordered pair \((x,y)\in T\times T\), where \(\lambda_D(x,y)\) is the maximum number of arc-disjoint directed \(x\)-to-\(y\) paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split an incoming–outgoing arc pair through a vertex into one directed shortcut; the pair is admissible when all prescribed terminal connectivities remain unchanged.

\(s\notin T\).

knowledge_statements.title: Orientation-Sensitive Splitting Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that an orientation-compatible split need not preserve every ordered terminal connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) have vertices \(\{x,y,z,s\}\) and exactly the arcs \(xs,sy,sz\), and take terminals \(T=\{x,y,z\}\). Initially \(\lambda_D(x,y)=1\) and \(\lambda_D(x,z)=1\). Splitting the directed pair \((xs,sz)\) produces the arc \(xz\) while deleting \(xs\) and \(sz\). In the resulting digraph \(D'\), one has \(\lambda_{D'}(x,z)=1\) but \(\lambda_{D'}(x,y)=0\). Thus matching an incoming arc with an outgoing arc is necessary for a directed split but is not sufficient for admissibility relative to all ordered terminal pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even a direction-compatible split can destroy another ordered terminal connection, so admissibility requires global cut or connectivity checks.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_{D'}(x,y)<\lambda_D(x,y)\), although the split pairs one arc entering \(s\) with one leaving \(s\).

knowledge_statements.title: Orientation-Based Connectivity Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut formulation for selecting minimum-cost arcs subject to directed connectivity requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\) be a finite multiset of candidate arcs on a finite vertex set \(V\), let \(c_a\ge 0\) be the cost of arc \(a\in A\), and let \(r:2^V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) prescribe entering-cut requirements. The orientation-based design problem has the integer cut representation
\[\min\left\{\sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a: \sum_{a\in\delta^-(S)}x_a\ge r(S)\ \text{for every }\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V,\quad x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{A}\right\}.\]
For a root \(q\in V\) and demands \(k_v\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) for \(v\in V\setminus\{q\}\), choosing \(r(S)=\max\{k_v:v\in S\}\) when \(q\notin S\), and \(r(S)=0\) otherwise, enforces the corresponding root-to-vertex arc connectivities by the directed cut form of Menger's theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed connectivity design selects arc copies at minimum cost while every entering cut meets its prescribed requirement; the rooted specialization enforces the stated root-to-vertex connectivities.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) and \(A\) are finite.
Selected arcs have nonnegative integral multiplicities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible designs are exactly the vectors \(x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{A}\) satisfying all prescribed directed entering-cut inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Tree Packings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nash-Williams–Tutte characterization of edge-disjoint spanning-tree packings in multigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected multigraph and let \(k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\). Then \(G\) contains \(k\) pairwise edge-disjoint spanning trees if and only if, for every partition \(\mathcal P\) of \(V\) into nonempty parts, the number \(e_G(\mathcal P)\) of edges having endpoints in distinct parts satisfies
\[e_G(\mathcal P)\ge k\bigl(|\mathcal P|-1\bigr).\]
Consequently, a displayed collection of \(k\) edge-disjoint spanning trees is a constructive certificate that every such partition inequality holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multigraph packs k edge-disjoint spanning trees exactly when every vertex partition has at least k times one fewer crossing edges than parts.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected multigraph.
\(k\) is a positive integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) has \(k\) edge-disjoint spanning trees if and only if \(e_G(\mathcal P)\ge k(|\mathcal P|-1)\) for every partition \(\mathcal P\).

notation.meaning: Number of edges joining distinct parts of partition P.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Nash-Williams–Tutte statement is standard, precise, and appropriately classified as a theorem, but no authoritative theorem or page locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Branching Packings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines arc-disjoint packing of directed forests with prescribed root sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a finite digraph \(D=(V,A)\), a branching is an arc set \(B\subseteq A\) such that every vertex has indegree at most one in \((V,B)\) and the underlying undirected graph of \((V,B)\) is acyclic. Its root set is \(R(B)=\{v\in V:\rho_B(v)=0\}\). A branching packing of size \(k\) is a family \((B_1,\ldots,B_k)\) of branchings satisfying \(B_i\cap B_j=\varnothing\) whenever \(i\ne j\). It is spanning when every \(B_i\) spans \(V\), and it respects prescribed roots \((R_1,\ldots,R_k)\) when \(R(B_i)=R_i\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branching packing is a family of arc-disjoint directed forests, optionally spanning and having specified root sets.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a finite directed multigraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((B_1,\ldots,B_k)\) is a branching packing exactly when each \(B_i\) is a branching and their arc sets are pairwise disjoint.

notation.meaning: Indegree of v in the subgraph induced by arc set B.
Set of indegree-zero roots of branching B.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No definition source is cited. Moreover, defining every branching as \((V,B)\) makes the later distinction that a branching is spanning potentially vacuous; the intended convention must be sourced and clarified.

children.title: Arborescence Packings

knowledge_statements.title: Arborescence Packings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edmonds' cut characterization for packing spanning out-arborescences with a common root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed multigraph, let \(r\in V\), and let \(k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\). There exist \(k\) pairwise arc-disjoint spanning out-arborescences rooted at \(r\) if and only if
\[|\delta_D^-(X)|\ge k\quad\text{for every nonempty }X\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}.\]
Each arborescence has indegree zero at \(r\), indegree one at every other vertex, and contains a directed path from \(r\) to every vertex. Hence the packing supplies \(k\) arc-disjoint root-to-vertex routes for every \(v\ne r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A digraph packs k arc-disjoint spanning out-arborescences rooted at r exactly when every nonempty set excluding r has at least k entering arcs.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a finite directed multigraph.
\(k\) is a positive integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rooted arborescence packing exists if and only if \(|\delta_D^-(X)|\ge k\) for every nonempty \(X\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}\).

notation.meaning: Arcs entering X from its complement in D.
Common root of all packed out-arborescences.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The common-root arborescence-packing theorem is standard and correctly stated, but an authoritative theorem-level locator is required.

children.title: Cactus Connectivity Certificates
children.top_down_role: Cactus representations of cut and connectivity structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Cactus Connectivity Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cactus representation of all global minimum cuts of an undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite connected undirected multigraph. A cactus minimum-cut certificate consists of a cactus \(C\) and a map \(\phi:V\to V(C)\) such that every global minimum cut of \(G\) is the inverse image under \(\phi\) of a component separation obtained either by deleting one bridge of \(C\) or by deleting two edges on one cycle of \(C\). Conversely, every designated bridge or same-cycle edge pair induces a global minimum cut of \(G\). Thus the global minimum cuts are represented by a cactus of size linear in \(|V|\), together with the vertex map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All global minimum cuts of an undirected graph can be encoded by designated bridge or same-cycle edge deletions in a linear-size cactus.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, connected, and undirected.
Parallel edges are allowed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The global minimum cuts of \(G\) admit an exact cactus representation of size \(O(|V|)\).

notation.meaning: Cactus graph representing the global minimum cuts.
Map from original vertices to cactus vertices.

children.title: Sparse Subgraph Certificates
children.top_down_role: Sparse subgraphs preserving designated connectivity information.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Subgraph Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nagamochi–Ibaraki-style certificate preserving every undirected cut up to threshold k.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected multigraph and let \(k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\). There exists a spanning subgraph \(H=(V,F)\) with \(|F|\le k(|V|-1)\) such that, for every \(S\subseteq V\),
\[|\delta_H(S)|\ge \min\{k,|\delta_G(S)|\}.\]
Because \(H\) is a subgraph of \(G\), this is equivalent to \(|\delta_H(S)|=|\delta_G(S)|\) whenever \(|\delta_G(S)|<k\), while every larger cut retains at least \(k\) edges. Therefore \(H\) certifies all cuts and all pairwise edge connectivities below threshold \(k\) using at most \(k(|V|-1)\) edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgraph with at most k(n−1) edges preserves every cut smaller than k exactly and leaves at least k edges in every larger cut.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected multigraph.
\(k\) is a positive integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a spanning \(H\subseteq G\) with \(|E(H)|\le k(|V|-1)\) and \(|\delta_H(S)|\ge\min\{k,|\delta_G(S)|\}\) for all \(S\subseteq V\).

notation.meaning: Edges of G with exactly one endpoint in S.

children.title: Certificate Compression Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on compressing connectivity structure into cactus or sparse representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Compression Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact preservation of every cut cannot generally be achieved by deleting edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(n\ge2\), let \(G=K_n\), and suppose a spanning subgraph \(H\subseteq G\) satisfies \(|\delta_H(S)|=|\delta_G(S)|\) for every \(S\subseteq V\). For any edge \(uv\in E(G)\), the singleton cut \(S=\{u\}\) and the two-vertex cut \(S=\{u,v\}\), together with the singleton cut \(\{v\}\), determine whether \(uv\) is present through
\[2\mathbf 1_{uv\in E(H)}=d_H(u)+d_H(v)-|\delta_H(\{u,v\})|.\]
Cut equality therefore forces every edge of \(G\) into \(H\), so \(|E(H)|=\binom n2\). Linear-size compression requires thresholding, approximation, or a non-subgraph representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgraph preserving every cut exactly may need every original edge; complete graphs therefore forbid linear-size exact subgraph certificates.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is required to be a spanning subgraph of \(G\).
Every cut cardinality must be preserved exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(G=K_n\), exact preservation of all cuts implies \(H=G\) and \(|E(H)|=\binom n2\).

notation.meaning: Degree of vertex v in H.
Indicator that edge uv is retained in H.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Survivable Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines minimum-cost directed network design under ordered-pair survivability requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a finite directed multigraph \(D=(V,A)\), nonnegative arc costs \(c_a\), and ordered-pair requirements \(r_{uv}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\), directed survivable design seeks a minimum-cost selected arc multiset \(F\) such that \(\lambda_{(V,F)}(u,v)\ge r_{uv}\) for every ordered pair \((u,v)\in V\times V\). If \(x_a\) denotes the selected multiplicity of arc \(a\), define
\[r(S)=\max\{r_{uv}:u\in V\setminus S,\ v\in S\}.\]
Then feasibility is equivalent to \(x(\delta^-(S))\ge r(S)\) for every nonempty proper set \(S\subset V\), by the directed arc form of the max-flow min-cut theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed survivable design buys arcs so that every ordered vertex pair has its required number of arc-disjoint directed paths; equivalently, every entering cut meets its induced requirement.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is finite and arc costs are nonnegative.
Survivability is measured by arc-disjoint directed paths.
The requirements \(r_{uv}\) are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is equivalent to satisfying \(x(\delta^-(S))\ge r(S)\) for every nonempty proper \(S\subset V\).

notation.meaning: Required directed connectivity from u to v.
Largest ordered-pair requirement entering S across its cut.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacitated Survivable Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines survivable network design when selected facilities contribute integral cut capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph in which each edge \(e\in E\) has cost \(c_e\ge 0\), capacity \(u_e\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\), and selection variable \(y_e\in\{0,1\}\). Given pair requirements \(r_{ij}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\), capacitated survivable design minimizes \(\sum_{e\in E}c_ey_e\) subject to
\[\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}u_ey_e\ge r(S)\quad\text{for every }\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V,\]
where \(r(S)=\max\{r_{ij}:i\in S,\ j\notin S\}\). By max-flow min-cut, these inequalities are equivalent to requiring selected capacity at least \(r_{ij}\) between every pair \((i,j)\). Parallel facility copies may be modeled by separate edge variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacitated survivable design selects minimum-cost indivisible facilities so every cut carries enough installed integral capacity for all separated pair requirements.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
Capacities and requirements are nonnegative integers.
Facilities are selected indivisibly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A selection \(y\) is feasible exactly when every cut has installed capacity at least its largest separated pair requirement.

notation.meaning: Integral capacity installed when edge facility e is selected.
Binary selection variable for edge facility e.
Largest pair requirement separated by cut S.

children.title: Crossing Requirement Families
children.top_down_role: Requirement systems with materially crossing cut structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Crossing Requirement Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the closure and supermodularity conditions used to uncross cut requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Two sets \(X,Y\subseteq V\) cross when each of \(X\cap Y\), \(X\setminus Y\), \(Y\setminus X\), and \(V\setminus(X\cup Y)\) is nonempty. A family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^V\) is crossing when \(X,Y\in\mathcal F\) crossing implies \(X\cap Y\in\mathcal F\) and \(X\cup Y\in\mathcal F\). A requirement function \(f:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\) is crossing supermodular when every crossing \(X,Y\in\mathcal F\) satisfies
\[f(X)+f(Y)\le f(X\cap Y)+f(X\cup Y).\]
These predicates ensure that replacing two crossing tight requirements by their intersection and union remains within the requirement domain and does not decrease their combined right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A crossing requirement family is closed under intersection and union of crossing sets, with requirements satisfying the corresponding supermodular inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
\(f\) is defined on every member of \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For crossing \(X,Y\in\mathcal F\), both \(X\cap Y,X\cup Y\in\mathcal F\) and \(f(X)+f(Y)\le f(X\cap Y)+f(X\cup Y)\).

notation.meaning: Family of vertex subsets carrying cut requirements.

children.title: Nonproper Requirement Families
children.top_down_role: Requirement systems lying outside standard properness conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonproper Requirement Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Properness is interpreted for symmetric set-requirement functions in undirected survivable network design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite and let \(r:2^V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) satisfy \(r(\varnothing)=r(V)=0\) and \(r(S)=r(V\setminus S)\). The requirement family is nonproper if there exist disjoint sets \(A,B\subseteq V\) such that \[r(A\cup B)>\max\{r(A),r(B)\}.\] For example, on \(V=\{1,2,3\}\), the symmetric function determined by \(r(\{1,2\})=r(\{3\})=1\) and value zero on every other set is nonproper, since \(r(\{1,2\})>\max\{r(\{1\}),r(\{2\})\}=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric requirement family is nonproper when joining two disjoint sets can create a requirement larger than both original requirements.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
\(r:2^V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) is symmetric and vanishes on \(\varnothing,V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\) is nonproper exactly when the displayed disjoint-union inequality is violated.

notation.meaning: required capacity across the cut of S

children.title: Uncrossing Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where conventional uncrossing organization ceases to apply.

knowledge_statements.title: Uncrossing Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete cut-covering instance shows that crossing tight sets need not admit tight uncrossings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{1,2,3,4\}\), \(A=\{1,2\}\), and \(B=\{2,3\}\). Define a symmetric requirement by \(r(A)=r(V\setminus A)=r(B)=r(V\setminus B)=1\) and \(r(S)=0\) otherwise. Assign edge values \(x_{12}=x_{23}=1/5\), \(x_{24}=x_{13}=2/5\), and zero elsewhere. Then \(x(\delta(A))=x(\delta(B))=1\), so both crossing constraints are tight. However, each cut belonging to \(A\cap B,A\cup B,A\setminus B,B\setminus A\) has requirement zero and strictly positive cut value. Thus neither standard uncrossed pair consists of tight constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two crossing cut constraints can be tight while neither their intersection–union pair nor their difference pair is tight.
assumptions_latex: Cut constraints have the form \(x(\delta(S))\ge r(S)\).
All unspecified edge variables are zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tight-set uncrossing is not guaranteed for arbitrary symmetric requirement functions.

notation.meaning: edges with exactly one endpoint in S
sum of edge values across the cut of S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The numerical cut values support the stated counterexample and the counterexample kind fits the container. children.title: Degree-Constrained Design
children.top_down_role: Survivable design under local degree restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Constrained Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degree bounds are imposed on the selected undirected survivable-network subgraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), edge costs \(c_e\ge0\), cut requirements \(r:2^V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), and degree bounds \(\ell_v,b_v\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), a degree-constrained survivable design is a vector \(y\in\{0,1\}^E\) minimizing \[\sum_{e\in E}c_ey_e\] subject to \[\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}y_e\ge r(S)\quad(\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V),\qquad \ell_v\le\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}y_e\le b_v\quad(v\in V).\] Infinite or omitted bounds remove the corresponding degree restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select a minimum-cost survivable subgraph while enforcing lower and upper bounds on each vertex’s selected incident edges.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
\(c_e\ge0\) and \(r(S),\ell_v,b_v\) are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible design satisfies every connectivity cut requirement and every prescribed vertex-degree interval.

notation.meaning: indicator that edge e is selected

children.title: Order-Constrained Design
children.top_down_role: Survivable design under ordering or precedence restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Order-Constrained Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order constraints are interpreted as precedence closure among selectable network elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph and let \(\preceq\) be a partial order on \(E\). An order-constrained network design is an incidence vector \(y\in\{0,1\}^E\) satisfying the underlying connectivity requirements and \[e\preceq f\ \Longrightarrow\ y_f\le y_e\qquad(e,f\in E).\] Hence the selected set \(Y=\{e\in E:y_e=1\}\) is an order ideal: selecting an element forces selection of every predecessor. A minimum-cost version minimizes \(\sum_{e":[0,1]}c_ey_e\) over these vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An order-constrained design is a feasible network whose selected elements form a downward-closed set under a specified precedence order.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite.
\(\preceq\) is a partial order on \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected edge set is downward closed under \(\preceq\).

notation.meaning: e is a prerequisite of f

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The order-ideal formulation is internally correct for the declared precedence interpretation and the definition kind fits the leaf. However, no source establishes that this is the intended meaning of order-constrained network design in this taxonomy, where other meanings of order constraints are possible.

children.title: Joint Constraint Interactions
children.top_down_role: Feasibility and approximation effects arising when multiple constraint types coexist.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Constraint Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degree upper bounds can conflict with predecessor closure even when each constraint family is separately feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let selectable edges \(e,f\) share a vertex \(v\), impose \(e\preceq f\), and set the upper-degree bound \(b_v=1\). The order inequality \(y_f\le y_e\) and degree inequality \(y_e+y_f\le1\) imply \(y_f=0\). Consequently, any connectivity requirement forcing \(f\) makes the joint system infeasible, although the order constraints alone admit \(y_e=y_f=1\) and the degree constraint alone admits \(y_f=1,y_e=0\). Thus separate feasibility of degree and order restrictions does not imply joint feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Precedence can force an additional incident edge, violating a degree bound and making two separately feasible constraint systems jointly infeasible.
assumptions_latex: Edges \(e\) and \(f\) are both incident to \(v\).
The precedence relation contains \(e\preceq f\).
The design requires \(y_f=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The joint constraints imply both \(y_e=1\) and \(y_e+y_f=2>b_v\), so the instance is infeasible.

notation.meaning: upper bound on selected edges incident to v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary two-edge construction correctly demonstrates separate versus joint feasibility and failure_boundary is an appropriate role. Its interpretation depends on the unsourced precedence semantics of the sibling record, and no inspectable source supports this particular interaction boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Regime Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Increasing installed capacities monotonically interpolates between restrictive and effectively uncapacitated fixed-charge models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z(u)\) be the optimal value of a capacitated fixed-charge instance with nonnegative costs and arc-capacity vector \(u\). If \(u'\ge u\) componentwise, every solution feasible under \(u\) is feasible under \(u'\), hence \[Z(u')\le Z(u).\] Let \(D=\sum_{k\in K}d_k\). If flows may be chosen without positive-cost cycles and \(u_a\ge D\) for every arc, then each aggregate capacity inequality is redundant whenever \(y_a=1\). In that regime the capacitated formulation has the same optimum as its uncapacitated fixed-charge counterpart.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Larger capacities cannot increase optimal cost; capacities at least total demand make shared-capacity constraints redundant for cycle-free routing.
assumptions_latex: All demands and routing costs are nonnegative.
Comparable instances differ only in their capacity vectors.
An optimal flow can be chosen without positive-cost circulations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u'\ge u\) implies \(Z(u')\le Z(u)\), with equality to the uncapacitated optimum when every \(u_a\ge D\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each arc \(a\in A\), let each module type \(m\in M_a\) provide capacity \(q_{am}>0\) at cost \(f_{am}\). Modular capacity expansion chooses integers \(z_{am}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) and commodity flows \(x_a^k\ge 0\), minimizes \[\sum_{a\in A}\sum_{m\in M_a}f_{am}z_{am}+\sum_{a\in A}\sum_{k\in K}c_a^k x_a^k,\] satisfies every commodity balance equation, and enforces \[\sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\le\sum_{m\in M_a}q_{am}z_{am}\qquad(a\in A).\] Upper bounds on \(z_{am}\) may restrict module availability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Install integer numbers of capacity modules on arcs and route all commodities within the resulting aggregate capacities at minimum cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Modular Capacity Expansion

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(G=(V,A)\) and commodities \(k\in K\), introduce \(y_a\in\{0,1\}\) and \(x_a^k\ge 0\). The arc-activation representation consists of commodity balance equations together with valid linking bounds \[x_a^k\le M_a^k y_a\qquad(a\in A,\ k\in K),\] or, with shared capacity, \[\sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\le u_a y_a\qquad(a\in A).\] Here \(M_a^k\) is any valid upper bound on commodity \(k\)'s use of arc \(a\). Therefore \(y_a=0\) forces all associated arc flows to zero, while \(y_a=1\) permits routing within the stated bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary arc variables activate routing: a closed arc carries no commodity flow, while an open arc carries flow within valid bounds.

children.title: Path-Activation Models
children.top_down_role: Design formulations whose activation decisions are attached to routing paths.

knowledge_statements.title: Path-Activation Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path-flow representation with binary arc installation and shared capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A path-activation model uses variables \(z_{kp}\ge 0\) and \(y_a\in\{0,1\}\) satisfying \[\sum_{p\in P_k}z_{kp}=d_k\quad(k\in K),\qquad \sum_{k\in K}\sum_{p\in P_k}\delta_{ap}z_{kp}\le u_a y_a\quad(a\in A).\] With fixed installation costs \(f_a\ge0\) and path-routing costs \(c_{kp}\), a standard objective is \[\min\left\{\sum_{a\in A}f_a y_a+\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{p\in P_k}c_{kp}z_{kp}\right\}.\] Consequently, positive flow on a path is possible only when every capacity-constrained arc used by that path is activated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Commodity demand is assigned to admissible paths, total path flow on each arc is limited by capacity available only when the arc is activated, and the objective may combine arc installation costs with path-routing costs.
assumptions_latex: A directed graph \(G=(V,A)\), a finite commodity set \(K\), demands \(d_k\ge0\), and admissible path sets \(P_k\) are given.
Each arc \(a\in A\) has installed capacity \(u_a y_a\), where \(u_a\ge0\) and \(y_a\in\{0,1\}\).
Fixed costs \(f_a\ge0\), path costs \(c_{kp}\in\mathbb R\), and arc-path incidences \(\delta_{ap}\in\{0,1\}\) are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed constraints define the path-activation feasible set, and the displayed objective defines a fixed-charge path-flow model.

notation.meaning: nonnegative flow assigned to path p of commodity k
indicator that arc a belongs to path p
fixed installation cost of arc a

children.title: Arc-to-Path Formulation Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Relative compactness, strength, and decomposition behavior of the two representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Arc-to-Path Formulation Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of design choices and optimal values after removable circulations are accounted for.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For path flows, define \[x_a^k=\sum_{p\in P_k}\delta_{ap}z_{kp}.\] This map preserves flow conservation, shared-capacity feasibility, and the design vector \(y\). Conversely, every nonnegative feasible commodity arc flow decomposes into source-to-sink path flows and a nonnegative circulation. Removing the circulation preserves demand satisfaction and design feasibility. If all admissible simple source-to-sink paths are included, arc costs satisfy \(c_a^k\ge0\), and path costs are additive, \[c_{kp}=\sum_{a\in A}c_a^k\delta_{ap},\] then circulation removal cannot increase cost, and the arc-flow and path-flow integer models have equal optimal values. Their formulation sizes and computational behavior may nevertheless differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Path flows aggregate to feasible arc flows. A feasible arc flow may also contain circulation; after that circulation is removed, all-simple-path models with nonnegative additive arc costs yield the same feasible designs and optimal value.
assumptions_latex: A finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\), commodities \(K\) with specified sources, sinks, and demands, and the same binary design variables and shared arc capacities are used in both formulations.
For every commodity \(k\), the set \(P_k\) contains all admissible simple source-to-sink paths.
Arc-routing costs satisfy \(c_a^k\ge0\), and path costs are defined additively by \(c_{kp}=\sum_{a\in A}c_a^k\delta_{ap}\).
The fixed design-cost term is identical in both formulations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under these assumptions, the two formulations admit the same design vectors and have equal optimal values, although an arc-flow vector containing circulation need not equal the aggregation of the retained path flows.

notation.meaning: arc flow of commodity k on arc a
path flow of commodity k on path p
indicator that arc a belongs to path p

children.title: Aggregated Design Models
children.top_down_role: Design formulations combining commodity or capacity information into shared structures.

assumptions_latex: Commodities \(K\) share each arc \(a\), whose installed capacity is \(u_a y_a\).
Commodity arc flows are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The aggregated coupling is \(\sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\le u_a y_a\) for every arc.

notation.meaning: flow of commodity k on arc a
capacity installed by activating arc a

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregation across commodities in the design-capacity linking constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An aggregated design model couples all commodities to one arc-design variable through \[\sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\le u_a y_a\qquad(a\in A),\] together with commodity-specific flow-conservation constraints and \(y_a\in\{0,1\}\). The single inequality for arc \(a\) records only total use of its installed capacity; it does not separately bound each commodity by a commodity-indexed design copy. Fixed charges may therefore be represented by \(\sum_{a\in A}f_a y_a\) without duplicating installation decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An aggregated model links the sum of all commodity flows on each arc to one shared binary installation decision and its capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Aggregated Design Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and its kind fits the model leaf, but no evidence supports that this is the intended aggregated-design convention.

children.title: Disaggregated Design Models
children.top_down_role: Design formulations retaining commodity-specific or module-specific structures.

assumptions_latex: A common binary installation decision \(y_a\) exists for each arc.
Valid commodity-specific bounds \(M_a^k\ge0\) are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Commodity-indexed activation constraints imply the corresponding individual flow bounds and retain a common physical design decision.

notation.meaning: valid upper bound for commodity k on arc a

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Commodity-wise disaggregation of activation links, alongside shared capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A disaggregated design model retains the common decision \(y_a\in\{0,1\}\) but imposes commodity-indexed links \[0\le x_a^k\le M_a^k y_a\qquad(a\in A,\ k\in K),\] in addition to flow conservation and, when capacity is shared, \(\sum_k x_a^k\le u_a y_a\). Each inequality independently forbids commodity \(k\) from using an uninstalled arc. The constants \(M_a^k\) must be valid for the underlying routing model; demand-based bounds such as \(M_a^k=d_k\) are valid when commodity flow cannot circulate or split beyond its demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A disaggregated model adds one activation link per arc and commodity, while preserving the common installation variable and any shared-capacity constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Disaggregated Design Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation is plausible, but the meaning of disaggregation and the validity of commodity bounds such as \(M_a^k=d_k\) depend on routing assumptions requiring a direct source.

children.title: Aggregation Projection Relationships
children.top_down_role: Strength and size relationships induced by aggregation or disaggregation.

assumptions_latex: The disaggregated model includes shared capacity and valid commodity-specific activation bounds.
The aggregated model uses the same flow and design variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every disaggregated feasible point projects to an aggregated feasible point; equality requires the extra links to be redundant for the aggregated feasible region.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set inclusion induced by dropping commodity-indexed activation links.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) contain the shared-capacity constraints and the valid links \(x_a^k\le M_a^k y_a\), and let \(A\) be obtained by deleting those commodity-indexed links while retaining all common constraints. For the projection \(\pi\) onto the common \((x,y)\)-coordinates, \[\pi(D)\subseteq A.\] Hence, under minimization with the same objective, the disaggregated linear relaxation gives a lower bound at least as large as the aggregated relaxation. Equality holds exactly when every deleted link is valid for \(A\), so that \(A\subseteq\pi(D)\) also holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dropping commodity-specific activation links yields the aggregated relaxation, so the disaggregated projection is contained in it and can provide a stronger minimization bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation Projection Relationships

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set-inclusion argument is correct for models differing only by deletion of the stated links, but a source is needed to establish that these are the taxonomy's intended aggregation pair.

children.title: Extended-Formulation Models
children.top_down_role: Fixed-charge formulations using auxiliary spaces to expose stronger structure.

assumptions_latex: A base flow-design feasible set is described in variables \((x,y)\).
Auxiliary variables \(w\) and linear constraints are introduced without changing intended feasible designs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An extended formulation represents the base set when its projection onto \((x,y)\) equals that set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear extended formulations for fixed-charge routing-design feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a flow-design set \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\{0,1\}^m\), an extended-formulation model is a linear or mixed-integer set \[Q=\{(x,y,w):B x+C y+D w\le b,\ y\in\{0,1\}^m\}\] such that \[P=\{(x,y):\exists w\text{ with }(x,y,w)\in Q\}.\] The auxiliary variables may encode paths, capacity modules, commodity-design products, or other composite states. The formulation is exact only when projection neither loses feasible base points nor introduces infeasible ones.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended model adds auxiliary variables and constraints but is exact only when projecting them out recovers precisely the original flow-design feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Formulation Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a standard extended-formulation definition and the content kind fits, but the record has no source for either the definition or its stated network-design encodings.

children.title: Composite-Variable Models
children.top_down_role: Fixed-charge formulations using variables that combine design and routing information.

assumptions_latex: Binary design variables \(y_a\) and bounded continuous variables \(x_a^k\) are given.
A composite variable is intended to encode a conjunction or product of base decisions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed linear constraints give an exact binary-continuous product representation for \(w_a^k=x_a^k y_a\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linearization of a bounded flow-design product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(0\le x_a^k\le M_a^k\) and \(y_a\in\{0,1\}\). The composite relation \(w_a^k=x_a^k y_a\) is represented exactly by \[0\le w_a^k\le M_a^k y_a,\qquad w_a^k\le x_a^k,\qquad w_a^k\ge x_a^k-M_a^k(1-y_a).\] If \(y_a=0\), these inequalities force \(w_a^k=0\); if \(y_a=1\), they force \(w_a^k=x_a^k\). Such variables can express flow carried specifically by installed components while keeping the model linear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite variable can encode the product of bounded flow and a binary design decision through an exact four-inequality linearization.
knowledge_statements.title: Composite-Variable Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary-continuous product linearization is correct for \(0\le x_a^k\le M_a^k\), but no source supports its placement as the intended composite-variable model family.

children.title: Extended-Space Projection Relations
children.top_down_role: Projection relationships between auxiliary-space and composite-variable representations.

assumptions_latex: An extended set \(Q\) and a base set \(P\) use common coordinates \((x,y)\).
Projection eliminates only auxiliary coordinates \(w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactness is equivalent to the two projection inclusions \(P\subseteq\pi_{x,y}(Q)\) and \(\pi_{x,y}(Q)\subseteq P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness and relaxation strength under elimination of auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+m+r}\), define \[\pi_{x,y}(Q)=\{(x,y):\exists w\text{ such that }(x,y,w)\in Q\}.\] The extended model is exact for \(P\) precisely when \(\pi_{x,y}(Q)=P\). If only \(P\subseteq\pi_{x,y}(Q)\) holds, the projection is a relaxation; if only \(\pi_{x,y}(Q)\subseteq P\) holds, it is a restriction. For minimization with a base-variable objective, projection equality preserves the optimum, while strict containment can weaken or invalidate the bound according to its direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating auxiliary variables yields the base model exactly when both projection inclusions hold; one-sided inclusion instead gives a relaxation or restriction.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Space Projection Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection claims are standard and correct, but this relational leaf is better classified as a property than a representation, and no source is supplied.

children.title: Flow-Cover Inequalities
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral strengthening derived from flow-cover structures.

assumptions_latex: \(X=\{(x,y):\sum_{i\in N}x_i\le b,\ 0\le x_i\le u_i y_i,\ y_i\in\{0,1\}\}\), with \(b,u_i>0\).
A set \(C\subseteq N\) satisfies \(\sum_{i\in C}u_i=b+\lambda\) for some \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed flow-cover inequality is valid for \(X\).

notation.meaning: flow upper bound for item i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical single-node capacitated flow-cover inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the capacitated fixed-charge set \(X\), let \(C\) be a flow cover and put \(\lambda=\sum_{i\in C}u_i-b>0\). Then \[\sum_{i\in C}x_i+\sum_{i\in N\setminus C}(u_i-\lambda)^+y_i\le b+\sum_{i\in C}(u_i-\lambda)^+(1-y_i),\] where \((t)^+=\max\{t,0\}\), is valid for every \((x,y)\in X\). It strengthens the continuous relaxation by combining the total-flow constraint with the binary upper-bound links; additional hypotheses are needed for facetness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When selected upper bounds exceed available flow by a positive amount, a flow-cover inequality couples actual flow with activated and inactive fixed-charge variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Cover Inequalities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed inequality is not valid for the stated set. An activated unused variable outside \(C\) contributes the positive term \((u_i-\lambda)^+y_i\) even when its flow is zero, which can violate the inequality. A source cannot cure the stated formula without substantive replacement.

children.title: Residual-Capacity Inequalities
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral strengthening based on capacity remaining after selected design commitments.

assumptions_latex: A cut or facility set has required routed amount \(D>0\) and installable capacities \(u_i y_i\).
A subset \(C\) has capacity below demand: \(\sum_{i\in C}u_i<D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible design satisfies the displayed residual-capacity inequality.

notation.meaning: residual demand after all capacity in C is used

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic residual-demand inequality for an insufficient installed-capacity subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let feasibility require \(\sum_{i\in N}u_i y_i\ge D\), with \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\), and let \(C\subseteq N\) satisfy \(u(C)=\sum_{i\in C}u_i<D\). Define the residual demand \(r_C=D-u(C)>0\). Since capacity contributed by \(C\) is at most \(u(C)\), every feasible design obeys \[\sum_{i\in N\setminus C}u_i y_i\ge r_C.\] Coefficient truncation, sequential lifting, or interaction with continuous routed-flow variables can produce stronger residual-capacity inequalities, but those variants require separately stated conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a subset cannot meet demand even when fully installed, capacity selected outside it must cover the positive residual demand.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Capacity Inequalities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed residual-demand inequality is valid for the stated covering model, but evidence is needed to identify it as the intended residual-capacity inequality family in this network-design context.

children.title: Cover-to-Residual Dominance Relations
children.top_down_role: Strength and overlap relationships between the two inequality families.

assumptions_latex: Two valid inequalities are compared over the same relaxation \(R\).
Both inequalities use the same variable space after any required lifting or projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A residual-capacity inequality dominates a flow-cover inequality exactly when its feasible halfspace cuts no less of \(R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Halfspace-inclusion criterion; family-specific coefficient tests remain unresolved.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_F\) and \(H_R\) denote the halfspaces defined by a flow-cover inequality and a residual-capacity inequality, respectively. Relative to a common relaxation \(R\), the residual inequality dominates the cover inequality if and only if \[R\cap H_R\subseteq R\cap H_F.\] Dominance is strict when the inclusion is strict. Thus no unconditional family-wide dominance follows merely from the names of the inequalities: it must be established after matching their underlying cover, residual amount, lifting convention, and variable space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dominance means every relaxed point satisfying the residual inequality also satisfies the cover inequality; strict dominance requires strict containment after matching formulations.
knowledge_statements.title: Cover-to-Residual Dominance Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The halfspace-inclusion condition correctly defines dominance, but it does not establish a substantive cover-to-residual dominance relation or coefficient criterion for the named families.

children.title: Cutset Inequalities
children.top_down_role: Fixed-charge inequalities indexed by network cutsets.

knowledge_statements.title: Cutset Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed capacity cut separating commodity sources from their sinks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(S\subset V\), define \[K(S)=\{k\in K:s_k\in S,\ t_k\notin S\},\qquad D(S)=\sum_{k\in K(S)}d_k.\] Every feasible capacitated routing-design solution satisfies the directed cutset inequality \[\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}u_a y_a\ge D(S).\] If every arc has the same capacity \(U>0\), the rounded inequality \[\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}y_a\ge\left\lceil\frac{D(S)}{U}\right\rceil\] is also valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every vertex subset, installed capacity on arcs leaving it must cover the total demand of commodities whose sources are inside and sinks are outside; uniform capacities give the corresponding rounded installation-count inequality.
assumptions_latex: A directed graph \(G=(V,A)\) and a finite commodity set \(K\) are given.
Each commodity \(k\in K\) has source \(s_k\in V\), sink \(t_k\in V\), and demand \(d_k\ge0\).
Arc \(a\in A\) has capacity \(u_a y_a\), where \(u_a\ge0\) and \(y_a\in\{0,1\}\), and all routed commodity flow shares this capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible routing-design solution satisfies the stated directed cutset inequality and, under uniform positive capacities, its rounded form.

notation.meaning: set of arcs directed from S to its complement
commodities whose sources lie in S and sinks lie outside S
total demand of commodities in K(S)

children.title: Partition Inequalities
children.top_down_role: Fixed-charge inequalities indexed by vertex partitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Partition Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valid capacity inequalities induced by terminal-separating vertex partitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected network, let \(\mathcal P=\{V_1,\ldots,V_p\}\) partition \(V\), and let \(E(\mathcal P)\) contain edges whose endpoints lie in different blocks. Commodity \(k\) has terminals \(s_k,t_k\), demand \(d_k\ge0\), and feasible splittable flow; installed capacity on edge \(e\) is \(u_e y_e\). If \(K(\mathcal P)=\{k:s_k\text{ and }t_k\text{ lie in different blocks}\}\), every feasible routing-design solution satisfies
\[
\sum_{e\in E(\mathcal P)}u_e y_e\ge \sum_{k\in K(\mathcal P)}d_k.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Across every vertex partition, installed interblock capacity must cover the total demand whose terminals occupy different blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(d_k\ge0\) and \(u_e y_e\ge0\).
Flows obey conservation and shared edge-capacity constraints.
Each commodity is splittably routed between its stated terminals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{e\in E(\mathcal P)}u_e y_e\ge\sum_{k\in K(\mathcal P)}d_k\).

children.title: Metric Inequalities
children.top_down_role: Fixed-charge inequalities derived from metric representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path-metric lower bounds for splittable multicommodity capacity design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected network with installed capacities \(u_e y_e\). Assign lengths \(\ell_e\ge0\), and let \(\operatorname{dist}_{\ell}(s,t)\) be shortest-path distance. If \(\operatorname{dist}_{\ell}(s_k,t_k)\ge1\) for every commodity \(k\) of demand \(d_k\), then every feasible splittable multicommodity routing satisfies
\[
\sum_{e\in E}\ell_e u_e y_e\ge\sum_k d_k.
\]
More generally, without normalization, the right-hand side is \(\sum_k d_k\operatorname{dist}_{\ell}(s_k,t_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any nonnegative edge metric prices installed capacity at least as highly as the metric-weighted terminal demands of a feasible routing.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_e\ge0\) for every edge.
Flows satisfy conservation and shared capacity constraints.
Commodity demands are nonnegative and splittable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_e\ell_eu_ey_e\ge\sum_kd_k\operatorname{dist}_{\ell}(s_k,t_k)\).

notation.meaning: Nonnegative edge length or capacity multiplier.
Shortest-path distance induced by the edge lengths.
