children.title: Lifted Inequality Families
children.top_down_role: Strengthened valid inequalities obtained through coefficient lifting.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifted Inequality Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential lifting of valid inequalities over binary design variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^m\times\{0,1\}^n\), and suppose \(a^Tx+b^Ty\le\beta\) is valid on the face \(X_0=X\cap\{y_j=0:j\in J\}\). For an ordering \((j_1,\ldots,j_r)\) of \(J\), define recursively
\[
\alpha_{j_t}=\beta-\max\left\{a^Tx+b^Ty+\sum_{q<t}\alpha_{j_q}y_{j_q}:(x,y)\in X,\ y_{j_t}=1,\ y_{j_q}=0\ (q>t)\right\}.
\]
Whenever each maximum is finite, \(a^Tx+b^Ty+\sum_{j\in J}\alpha_jy_j\le\beta\) is valid for \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential lifting extends a face-valid inequality to omitted binary design variables by assigning each the largest coefficient preserving validity at that lifting step.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^m\times\{0,1\}^n\).
The base inequality is valid on \(X_0\).
Every lifting optimization has a finite maximum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a^Tx+b^Ty+\sum_{j\in J}\alpha_jy_j\le\beta\) is valid for \(X\).

notation.meaning: Face on which the variables to be lifted are fixed to zero.
Indices of binary variables introduced by lifting.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential up-lifting formula is plausible under the stated ordering convention, and property is a reasonable kind for the valid-inequality family. No source is supplied, however, and coefficient conventions differ depending on whether the original coefficients of fixed variables are retained; an authoritative lifting reference is required.

children.title: Mixed Inequality Families
children.top_down_role: Valid inequalities coupling multiple variable or constraint structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Inequality Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-capacity inequalities combining cut demand and binary installations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a cut with required routed load \(D>0\), continuous edge loads \(z_i\), binary installations \(y_i\), and constraints \(\sum_{i\in I}z_i\ge D\) and \(0\le z_i\le u_i y_i\). For any \(C\subseteq I\) satisfying \(u(C)=\sum_{i\in C}u_i<D\), set \(r_C=D-u(C)\). Every feasible point satisfies the residual-capacity inequality
\[
\sum_{i\in I\setminus C}\min\{u_i,r_C\}y_i\ge r_C.
\]
Together with the load and variable-bound constraints, these inequalities form a mixed continuous-binary cut family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After crediting an insufficient subset of cut capacities, the remaining installed edges must provide at least the residual cut demand.
assumptions_latex: \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\) and \(0\le z_i\le u_i y_i\).
\(C\subseteq I\) satisfies \(u(C)<D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i\in I\setminus C}\min\{u_i,r_C\}y_i\ge r_C\).

notation.meaning: Continuous load routed through cut edge i.
Demand remaining after all capacity in C is credited.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-capacity inequality follows from the stated load and variable-bound system and is mathematically valid. No source supports its identification or placement as a mixed network-design inequality family, so authoritative polyhedral evidence is required.

children.title: Lifting Strength Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on dominance and formulation improvement achieved through lifting.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifting Strength Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp coefficient boundary and ordering limitation for sequential lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g(x,y)\le\beta\) be valid on \(X\cap\{y_j=0\}\), where \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\), and define
\[
\alpha_j^*=\beta-\sup\{g(x,y):(x,y)\in X,\ y_j=1\}.
\]
If the supremum is finite, then \(g(x,y)+\alpha_jy_j\le\beta\) is valid for \(X\) exactly when \(\alpha_j\le\alpha_j^*\). Thus any coefficient exceeding \(\alpha_j^*\) destroys validity. With several lifted variables, sequential coefficients may depend on their order, so locally maximal coefficients need not define a unique or globally strongest lifted inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted coefficient cannot exceed its residual-slack supremum; with multiple binary variables, lifting order can change the resulting valid inequality.
assumptions_latex: The base inequality is valid when \(y_j=0\).
The displayed supremum is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x,y)+\alpha_jy_j\le\beta\text{ is valid on }X\iff\alpha_j\le\alpha_j^*\).

notation.meaning: Left side of the inequality before lifting variable j.
Largest valid lifting coefficient for the stated face.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The single-variable coefficient boundary is correct when the stated supremum is finite, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. The broader claim about order dependence and absence of a unique globally strongest lift needs an authoritative lifting source.

children.title: Design Master Problems
children.top_down_role: Master formulations governing network-design decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Design Master Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Benders master representation for discrete capacity-installation decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\min\{c^Ty+q^Tx:Ay\ge b,\ Wx\ge h-Ty,\ x\ge0,\ y\in Y\}\), where \(Y\) contains the discrete design restrictions. With \(Q(y)=\inf\{q^Tx:Wx\ge h-Ty,\ x\ge0\}\), the Benders master is
\[
\min_{y,\theta}\{c^Ty+\theta:Ay\ge b,\ y\in Y,\ \theta\ge\pi^T(h-Ty)\ (\pi\in\mathcal P),\ r^T(h-Ty)\le0\ (r\in\mathcal R)\},
\]
where \(\mathcal P\) and \(\mathcal R\) are respectively the relevant dual extreme points and rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The design master retains discrete installation variables and represents routing recourse through feasibility and optimality cuts generated by flow subproblems.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) contains the intended discrete design decisions.
The flow subproblem is a linear program.
Linear-programming duality applies whenever the subproblem is feasible and bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_y\{c^Ty+Q(y):Ay\ge b,\ y\in Y\}\) has the displayed Benders master representation.

notation.meaning: Optimal routing cost for fixed design y.
Master variable representing routing recourse cost.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed master has the standard Benders form, but exact equivalence requires explicit assumptions excluding unbounded recourse and a precise definition of the dual extreme-point and ray sets. No Benders source is supplied, so the representation and sign convention cannot be validated as written.

children.title: Flow Subproblems
children.top_down_role: Routing subproblems induced by fixed design decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow Subproblems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous multicommodity routing recourse under a fixed design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a fixed design \(\bar y\), let commodity \(k\) have node-balance vector \(b^k\), and let \(B\) be the node-arc incidence matrix. The routing subproblem is
\[
Q(\bar y)=\min\left\{\sum_{k}\sum_{e}q_e^kx_e^k:Bx^k=b^k\ (k\in K),\ \sum_kx_e^k\le u_e\bar y_e\ (e\in E),\ x^k\ge0\right\}.
\]
It is a linear program whose finite optimum supplies the recourse value and whose dual solution or infeasibility ray supplies a Benders cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing installation decisions leaves a linear multicommodity-flow problem; its optimum, dual multiplier, or infeasibility ray informs the design master.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar y\) is fixed and satisfies the master design restrictions.
Flows are directed, nonnegative, and splittable.
Capacities and routing costs are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(\bar y)\) is the displayed linear multicommodity-flow recourse problem.

notation.meaning: Flow of commodity k on arc e.
Capacity available under the fixed design.

source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models
source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Multicommodity Flow Problems p. 17

source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models
source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.3 Multicommodity Flow Problems p. 17

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-design multicommodity-flow LP is a suitable representation and is supported provisionally by the cited flow section. That source does not establish the added claim that dual solutions or infeasibility rays generate Benders cuts; a decomposition-specific source is required for the complete record.

children.title: Master–Subproblem Coupling
children.top_down_role: Information exchanged between design decisions and flow evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Master–Subproblem Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual cuts coupling fixed-design routing recourse to the master.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(Q(y)=\min\{q^Tx:Wx\ge h-Ty,\ x\ge0\}\), the dual is
\[
Q(y)=\max\{\pi^T(h-Ty):W^T\pi\le q,\ \pi\ge0\}
\]
whenever the primal is feasible and has a finite optimum. Hence every dual-feasible \(\pi\) gives the master lower bound \(\theta\ge\pi^T(h-Ty)\). If a dual ray \(r\ge0\) satisfies \(W^Tr\le0\), primal feasibility requires \(r^T(h-Ty)\le0\). Iteratively adding violated bounds couples the master design to the routing subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual points generate recourse-cost lower bounds, while dual rays exclude designs that cannot support feasible routing.
assumptions_latex: The subproblem has the displayed inequality form.
Linear-programming strong duality applies to feasible bounded instances.
Master variable \(\theta\) represents the routing recourse value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta\ge\pi^T(h-Ty)\) for dual points, and \(r^T(h-Ty)\le0\) for dual rays.

notation.meaning: Dual-feasible point generating an optimality cut.
Dual recession ray generating a feasibility cut.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The primal-dual signs and the point and ray cuts are correct for the displayed canonical form, and duality fits the terminal container. Because no source is supplied, the Benders coupling claim and its sign convention require authoritative confirmation.

children.title: Feasibility Cut Families
children.top_down_role: Benders cuts excluding design decisions that cannot support required flows.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Cut Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-ray certificates excluding routing-infeasible designs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed \(\bar y\), consider \(Wx\ge h-T\bar y\), \(x\ge0\). A vector \(r\) satisfying \(r\ge0\), \(W^Tr\le0\), and \(r^T(h-T\bar y)>0\) certifies that no feasible \(x\) exists. The associated Benders feasibility cut is
\[
r^T(h-Ty)\le0.
\]
It is valid for every design admitting feasible routing and is violated by \(\bar y\). The family consists of such cuts generated by recession rays, with extreme rays sufficient for an exact finite polyhedral representation when the ray cone is polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual recession ray proves routing infeasibility and yields a valid inequality excluding the current design.
assumptions_latex: The routing feasibility system is linear.
\(r\ge0\) and \(W^Tr\le0\).
The current design satisfies \(r^T(h-T\bar y)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r^T(h-Ty)\le0\) is valid and excludes \(\bar y\).

notation.meaning: Dual recession ray and infeasibility certificate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ray conditions give a valid Farkas infeasibility certificate and the resulting cut excludes the current design. Certificate is the correct content kind, but the entire claim, including extreme-ray sufficiency, lacks a cited source.

children.title: Optimality Cut Families
children.top_down_role: Benders cuts representing flow-cost or recourse information.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimality Cut Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-point certificates supporting the routing value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q(y)=\min\{q^Tx:Wx\ge h-Ty,\ x\ge0\}\), and let \(\pi\ge0\) satisfy \(W^T\pi\le q\). Weak duality gives
\[
Q(y)\ge\pi^T(h-Ty),
\]
so \(\theta\ge\pi^T(h-Ty)\) is a valid Benders optimality cut. If \(\pi\) is dual-optimal at a feasible design \(\bar y\), the cut is tight there: \(Q(\bar y)=\pi^T(h-T\bar y)\). Under polyhedral recourse, all relevant dual extreme-point cuts represent \(Q\) exactly on designs with feasible bounded recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each dual-feasible point supports the routing value function; a dual optimum produces a cut tight at the design that generated it.
assumptions_latex: The routing subproblem is feasible and bounded at \(\bar y\).
\(\pi\ge0\) and \(W^T\pi\le q\).
Linear-programming strong duality holds at \(\bar y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta\ge\pi^T(h-Ty)\), with equality at \(\bar y\) when \(\pi\) is dual-optimal there.

notation.meaning: Dual-feasible point defining a supporting affine function.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dual-point cut and tightness statement are correct under feasible bounded recourse and strong duality. Certificate fits the cut-family container, but no source supports the Benders interpretation or the exact extreme-point representation.

children.title: Pareto Cut Families
children.top_down_role: Nondominated Benders cuts selected for stronger master refinement.

knowledge_statements.title: Pareto Cut Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nondominated Benders cuts relative to the feasible master-design set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_M\) be the feasible master-design set. For dual-feasible points \(\pi^1,\pi^2\), define \(L_i(y)=(\pi^i)^T(h-Ty)\). The optimality cut \(\theta\ge L_1(y)\) dominates \(\theta\ge L_2(y)\) on \(Y_M\) if \(L_1(y)\ge L_2(y)\) for every \(y\in Y_M\), with strict inequality for at least one \(y\in Y_M\). A cut is Pareto-optimal if no other valid Benders optimality cut dominates it. A Pareto cut family is any collection consisting solely of such nondominated supporting cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Pareto Benders cut is an optimality cut that no other valid cut uniformly strengthens over the feasible master set.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_M\) is the feasible master-design set.
Both compared cuts are valid Benders optimality cuts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta\ge L_1(y)\) is Pareto-optimal iff no valid cut dominates it on \(Y_M\).

notation.meaning: Feasible design region of the Benders master.
Affine recourse lower bound generated by dual point i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dominance and nondominance definitions are internally consistent, and definition is the correct content kind. An authoritative Pareto-optimal Benders-cut source is required; the standard definition and its domain cannot be accepted without one.

children.title: Commodity Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Subproblem organization by commodity-specific routing structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Commodity Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient structural condition for direct fixed-design routing decomposition by commodity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a fixed design \(\bar y\), let the routing variables be \(x=(x^k)_{k\in K}\). If the feasible region factors as \(X(\bar y)=\prod_{k\in K}X_k(\bar y)\) and the objective is additive, then
\[
Q(\bar y)=\min_{x\in X(\bar y)}\sum_{k\in K}(q^k)^Tx^k=\sum_{k\in K}\min_{x^k\in X_k(\bar y)}(q^k)^Tx^k.
\]
Thus the routing problem can be solved independently by commodity. Shared constraints such as \(\sum_{k\in K}x_e^k\le u_e\bar y_e\) generally destroy this direct Cartesian-product structure unless they are redundant or replaced by fixed commodity capacity allocations. Dualizing such shared constraints instead produces commodity-separable Lagrangian subproblems, whose combined value is a bound unless conditions ensuring exact dual recovery hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An additive fixed-design routing problem decomposes directly by commodity when its feasible set is a Cartesian product. Shared capacities generally prevent direct separation unless redundant or allocated; dualizing them yields separable Lagrangian subproblems but is not automatically exact.
assumptions_latex: The design \(\bar y\) is fixed.
The feasible region satisfies \(X(\bar y)=\prod_{k\in K}X_k(\bar y)\).
The objective is additive across commodities, and every commodity subproblem has a finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X(\bar y)=\prod_{k\in K}X_k(\bar y)\Rightarrow Q(\bar y)=\sum_{k\in K}Q_k(\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: Feasible routing set for commodity k under the fixed design.
Independent optimal routing value for commodity k.

children.title: Period Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Subproblem organization by time period or planning stage.

knowledge_statements.title: Period Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Benders separation by time period for designs shared across a finite planning horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the fixed design vector be \(y\in Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^m\), and suppose that, after fixing \(y\), routing variables and constraints are separable over periods \(t\in T\). If period \(t\) has recourse value \(Q_t(y)\), then the design problem admits the representation \[\min_{y\in Y}\left\{f^\top y+\sum_{t\in T}Q_t(y)\right\}.\] Each \(Q_t(y)\) is evaluated by an independent routing subproblem. A dual feasible solution for period \(t\) yields a Benders cut involving only \(y\) and a period epigraph variable \(\theta_t\); infeasible period subproblems analogously yield period-specific feasibility cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When periods interact only through fixed design decisions, fixing the design separates routing into one subproblem per period, each producing its own Benders cuts.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is finite.
All cross-period coupling variables are retained in the master problem.
Each fixed-design period subproblem is a linear program.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(y)=\sum_{t\in T}Q_t(y)\), with independently generated period cuts.

notation.meaning: optimal routing or recourse value in period t
master epigraph variable for period-t recourse

review_flags: Exact network-design Benders source and locator are required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and content kind fit period decomposition, but no inspectable source supports the separability hypotheses or period-specific Benders cuts.

children.title: Scenario Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Subproblem organization by uncertainty scenario.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Benders separation by uncertainty scenario with nonanticipative first-stage network design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite scenario set with probabilities \(p_s>0\), let \(y\in Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^m\) be a scenario-independent design, and let \(Q_s(y)\) be the optimal routing recourse in scenario \(s\). Under fixed recourse and relatively complete recourse, the stochastic design problem is \[\min_{y\in Y}\left\{f^\top y+\sum_{s\in S}p_sQ_s(y)\right\}.\] Fixing \(y\) produces independent scenario linear programs. Their dual solutions generate scenario-indexed optimality cuts; if relatively complete recourse is absent, dual rays generate scenario-indexed feasibility cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonanticipative design shared by all scenarios permits independent scenario routing subproblems whose dual solutions or rays generate Benders cuts.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite and \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s=1\).
The first-stage design is nonanticipative.
Each fixed-design scenario subproblem is a linear program.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(y)=\sum_{s\in S}p_sQ_s(y)\), and scenario subproblems can be separated independently.
review_flags: A stochastic Benders source supporting the stated hypotheses is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scenario-decomposition representation is mathematically plausible, but the fixed-recourse, recourse-feasibility, and scenario-cut claims lack a cited source and locator.

children.title: Hybrid Decomposition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Decomposition structures combining multiple separability axes.

knowledge_statements.title: Hybrid Decomposition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested or joint decomposition across periods, scenarios, and commodities after fixing shared design variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a master design \(y\), partition the routing indices into blocks \(B\), where a block may combine a period, scenario, and commodity subset. Initialize the master with variables \(y\) and block epigraphs \(\theta_b\). At an incumbent or relaxation solution \(\bar y\), solve every block subproblem. Add a dual optimality cut for each finite block and a dual-ray feasibility cut for each infeasible block; aggregated cuts may instead sum compatible block cuts with their objective weights. Reoptimize the master and repeat until no violated block cut remains and the master gap satisfies the prescribed tolerance. Output the best feasible design and its routed solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hybrid decomposition partitions routing simultaneously or hierarchically by period, scenario, and commodity, then coordinates block cuts through a shared design master.
assumptions_latex: All coupling between blocks is represented by master variables.
Every fixed-master block is a linear program with an available dual solution or ray.
Aggregation combines only cuts valid for the same master domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Termination with no violated cuts gives a Benders-valid master bound; zero final gap certifies optimality.
review_flags: Hybrid disaggregation and cut-aggregation variants require a dedicated source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the hybrid-decomposition leaf, but no source supports the block construction, valid cut aggregation, or stated termination and optimality conditions.

children.title: Branching Integration
children.top_down_role: Embedding design-variable branching within a Benders-based search.

knowledge_statements.title: Branching Integration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Embedding Benders separation within branch-and-bound for binary fixed-charge design variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize branch-and-bound with a Benders master relaxation over design variables \(y\) and recourse bounds \(\theta\). At each node, solve the node master. If its solution \((\bar y,\bar\theta)\) violates a Benders feasibility or optimality cut obtained from the fixed-design routing subproblem, add the cut and reoptimize the node. Otherwise, prune by infeasibility or bound, accept an integral feasible \(\bar y\), or branch on a fractional design component \(\bar y_e\) into \(y_e=0\) and \(y_e=1\). Continue until every node is processed or the global bound gap meets tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch-and-bound handles design integrality while Benders subproblems separate routing cuts at search nodes before pruning, acceptance, or further branching.
assumptions_latex: Design variables are binary.
Every generated Benders cut is valid for all descendants to which it is applied.
Node bounds are computed from valid master relaxations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exhaustion of the tree with zero global gap certifies a globally optimal design.

notation.meaning: activation variable for design element e
master lower approximation of routing cost

review_flags: A branch-and-Benders-cut reference with node-processing details is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm matches branching integration, but its node-processing and global convergence claims require an authoritative branch-and-Benders-cut source.

children.title: Benders-Cut Generation
children.top_down_role: Generation of decomposition cuts during exact search.

knowledge_statements.title: Benders-Cut Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual generation of feasibility and optimality cuts from fixed-design multicommodity routing subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write the fixed-design routing subproblem as \(Q(y)=\min\{q^\top x:Wx\ge h-Ty,\ x\ge0\}\), with dual region \(D=\{\pi\ge0:W^\top\pi\le q\}\). At a master point \((\bar y,\bar\theta)\), solve the subproblem. If it is feasible and has dual optimum \(\bar\pi\in D\), add \[\theta\ge\bar\pi^\top(h-Ty)\] when violated. If it is infeasible and \(\bar r\) is an extreme ray of \(\{r\ge0:W^\top r\le0\}\) satisfying \(\bar r^\top(h-T\bar y)>0\), add \[\bar r^\top(h-Ty)\le0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve the fixed-design routing dual: an optimal dual point yields an optimality cut, while a certifying dual ray yields a feasibility cut.
assumptions_latex: The routing subproblem is a linear program.
The master contains \(y\) and a recourse epigraph variable \(\theta\).
Strong duality or the alternative theorem applies to the subproblem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each displayed inequality is valid for every feasible master design.
review_flags: The supplied sources do not locate general Benders cut generation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed dual-point and dual-ray cuts are consistent with the stated primal sign convention, but no cited source and locator support this nontrivial Benders-generation result.

children.title: Search-Tree Cut Management
children.top_down_role: Placement, reuse, and validity scope of cuts across search-tree nodes.

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Tree Cut Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity-based classification and retention of Benders cuts throughout a branch-and-bound tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every generated inequality \(a^\top y+b\theta\ge d\), assign the cut globally only if it is valid over the root master domain; otherwise assign it locally to the node whose branching restrictions establish validity. A global cut may be inherited by every descendant. A local cut may be inherited only while all restrictions used in its derivation remain active. Cuts may be deleted from the active relaxation for efficiency, but deletion does not alter the certified incumbent or node bounds already established; any cut needed to validate a stored bound must remain recoverable or its bound must be recomputed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cuts valid at the root are globally reusable; cuts relying on branch restrictions remain local, and deleting active cuts must not invalidate stored bounds.
assumptions_latex: Every cut carries its validity domain.
Branching restrictions are explicitly recorded at each node.
Stored bounds are derived only from valid active or recoverable inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Managed node relaxations remain valid lower-bounding relaxations of their corresponding subproblems.
review_flags: Cut aging, deletion, and locality rules require an authoritative implementation reference.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits search-tree cut management, but locality, inheritance, deletion, recoverability, and stored-bound rules lack an authoritative source.

children.title: Network-Design Branching
children.top_down_role: Branching structures tailored to network-design decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Network-Design Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branching rules that preserve the pricing structure of path-based network-design formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a fractional restricted-master solution, first choose a fractional installation variable \(y_e\) and create children \(y_e=0\) and \(y_e=1\). If all installation variables are integral but path columns remain fractionally combined, select a branching disjunction expressible as additive restrictions in each pricing problem, such as requiring versus forbidding use of an arc by a designated commodity. In each child, impose the disjunction in both the restricted master and its pricing oracle. Continue separation and pricing before selecting the next branch; prune a node only by valid infeasibility or bound tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prefer branching on installation variables; when path mixtures remain fractional, use routing disjunctions that can be enforced consistently by the pricing oracle.
assumptions_latex: The master uses installation variables and generated routing columns.
Each branching disjunction can be represented in the pricing oracle.
The two children partition all integer solutions of the parent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every integer solution belongs to a child, and column generation remains valid at each child.

notation.meaning: installation variable for network element e

review_flags: The precise branch-cut-price routing disjunction requires a network-design reference.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A source is required because the proposed require-versus-forbid arc disjunction is not generically a valid pricing-compatible partition without a precise routing-integrality and path-column formulation.

children.title: Network-Design Cut Separation
children.top_down_role: Separation of valid inequalities during exact network-design search.

knowledge_statements.title: Network-Design Cut Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of capacity-linking and connectivity inequalities in a fractional network-design relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a fractional design-flow solution \((\bar y,\bar x)\), test each explicit linking row and add every violated inequality of the form \(\sum_k\bar x_e^k\le u_e\bar y_e\). For connectivity separation, assign arc capacity \(u_e\bar y_e\); for each required origin-destination pair \((s_k,t_k)\), compute a minimum \(s_k\)-\(t_k\) cut \(\delta^+(S)\). If \(\sum_{e\in\delta^+(S)}u_e\bar y_e<d_k\), add \[\sum_{e\in\delta^+(S)}u_ey_e\ge d_k.\] Repeat separation after reoptimization until no inequality in the selected families is violated beyond tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Check explicit flow–activation links and use minimum cuts to find capacity designs unable to carry a commodity’s required demand.
assumptions_latex: Arc capacities are \(u_ey_e\) with \(u_e\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Network-Design Column Pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced-cost generation of commodity paths for a restricted network-design master problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_k\) be the feasible paths for commodity \(k\), and let \(\lambda_p^k\) denote a path-flow column. After solving the restricted master, obtain dual prices \(\alpha_k\) for demand constraints and \(\mu_e\) for shared-capacity rows. For each commodity \(k\), assign arc reduced length \(c_e^k-\mu_e\) under the master’s sign convention and find a minimum-length feasible \(s_k\)-\(t_k\) path \(p\). Its reduced cost is \[\bar c_p^k=\sum_{e\in p}(c_e^k-\mu_e)-\alpha_k.\] Add any column with \(\bar c_p^k<0\); stop pricing when no commodity has such a path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual capacity prices modify arc costs; a shortest feasible commodity path with negative reduced cost is added as a new master column.
assumptions_latex: Routing is represented by commodity-path columns.
Path cost is additive over arcs.
The pricing restrictions include all branching decisions active at the node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every pricing optimum is nonnegative, the restricted-master solution is optimal for the current full LP relaxation.

notation.meaning: dual price of the shared-capacity row for element e
reduced cost of commodity-k path p

children.title: Integrated Search Coordination
children.top_down_role: Coordination of branching, separation, and pricing within one search tree.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrated Search Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Node-processing protocol coordinating branching, cut separation, and column pricing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At each search node, initialize the restricted master with inherited valid cuts and columns. Repeatedly solve it, separate violated network-design cuts, and price negative-reduced-cost columns; after either addition, reoptimize. Declare the node LP solved only when neither separator nor pricing oracle returns a violation beyond tolerance. Then prune by infeasibility or bound, update the incumbent from an integer feasible solution, or apply a pricing-compatible branching disjunction. Maintain a global incumbent upper bound and the minimum valid open-node lower bound. Stop when no node remains or their relative or absolute gap meets the prescribed tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every node, alternate cut separation and pricing to closure before pruning, accepting an incumbent, or applying a pricing-compatible branch.
assumptions_latex: Cut and pricing oracles are exact, or their declared tolerances are incorporated into certification.
All inherited objects are valid at the current node.
Branching decisions are enforced in both master and pricing problems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: With exact oracles and zero final gap, the returned incumbent is globally optimal.

notation.meaning: minimum valid lower bound over open nodes

review_flags: An authoritative branch-cut-price coordination reference is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The integrated protocol fits the leaf, but closure of separation and pricing, node-bound validity, and global optimality certification require an authoritative branch-cut-price reference.

knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Fixed-Charge Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower bounds obtained by dualizing capacity coupling between binary installations and multicommodity flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a minimization model with binary design \(y\in Y\), routing \(x\in X\), and coupling constraints \(Ax-By\le0\). For multipliers \(\lambda\ge0\), define \[L(\lambda)=\min_{x\in X,\,y\in Y}\left\{c^\top x+f^\top y+\lambda^\top(Ax-By)\right\}.\] The Lagrangian dual bound is \[L^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}L(\lambda).\] For every \(\lambda\ge0\), weak duality gives \(L(\lambda)\le z^*\), where \(z^*\) is the original optimum. If \(X\) separates by commodity and \(Y\) by installed element, evaluating \(L(\lambda)\) decomposes accordingly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing flow–installation capacity links yields a decomposable Lagrangian function whose supremum is a valid lower bound on the fixed-charge optimum.
assumptions_latex: The original problem is a minimization problem with finite optimum \(z^*\).
Coupling constraints have the form \(Ax-By\le0\).
Multipliers satisfy \(\lambda\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(\lambda)\le L^*\le z^*\) for every \(\lambda\ge0\).

notation.meaning: Lagrangian relaxation value at multiplier lambda
optimal value of the original fixed-charge model

review_flags: The supplied locators do not support Lagrangian relaxation of fixed-charge coupling.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality role and lower-bound direction are consistent with the stated minimization convention, but the Lagrangian fixed-charge decomposition claim has no cited evidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Activation–Flow Decoupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by omitting or weakening constraints that connect routed flow to installed capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an arc have activation \(y_e\in\{0,1\}\), flow \(x_e\ge0\), capacity \(u_e>0\), fixed cost \(f_e>0\), and intended link \(x_e\le u_ey_e\). If this link is omitted, the assignment \(y_e=0\) with any otherwise feasible \(0<x_e\le u_e\) is admitted, so positive flow avoids its fixed charge. If the link is replaced by \(x_e\le M_ey_e\) with \(M_e>u_e\), the LP relaxation admits \(y_e=x_e/M_e<x_e/u_e\), understating activation cost. Thus exact activation–flow coupling requires a valid tight upper bound, preferably \(M_e=u_e\) when \(u_e\) is the true capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a tight flow–activation link, positive flow can use a closed arc or pay only a fractional share of its fixed charge in the relaxation.
assumptions_latex: The intended semantics prohibit flow when \(y_e=0\).
The relaxation permits \(0\le y_e\le1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Omission destroys logical validity, while \(M_e>u_e\) strictly weakens the LP relaxation whenever \(0<x_e<u_e\).

notation.meaning: true installed capacity of arc e

review_flags: A fixed-charge formulation source explicitly documenting the linking constraint is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and big-M comparison are mathematically plausible, but no fixed-charge formulation source supports the intended linking semantics and tight-bound claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Capacity-Linking Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP-relaxation weakness of aggregate fixed-charge capacity linking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(a\in A\), the aggregate linking inequality \(\sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\le U_a y_a\) permits a total flow \(q_a\in(0,U_a)\) with \(y_a=q_a/U_a\) in the relaxation \(0\le y_a\le1\). Valid commoditywise inequalities \(x_a^k\le M_a^k y_a\) instead require \(y_a\ge\max_{k\in K}x_a^k/M_a^k\). They cut off an aggregate-feasible relaxed point whenever \(\max_{k\in K}x_a^k/M_a^k>\sum_{k\in K}x_a^k/U_a\). Moreover, they imply the aggregate inequality whenever \(\sum_{k\in K}M_a^k\le U_a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Aggregate linking can buy activation in proportion to total flow. Commoditywise bounds can exclude such fractional points, but they imply the aggregate capacity constraint only under an additional compatibility condition on their bounds.
assumptions_latex: A directed multicommodity network has arc set \(A\), commodity set \(K\), flows \(x_a^k\ge0\), activation variables \(y_a\), and capacities \(U_a>0\).
The integer model uses \(y_a\in\{0,1\}\), while its linear relaxation uses \(0\le y_a\le1\).
Each \(M_a^k\ge0\) is a valid upper bound for commodity \(k\)'s flow on arc \(a\) when that arc is active.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Commoditywise linking can be strictly stronger at particular relaxed flow vectors; implication of aggregate linking additionally follows when \(\sum_{k\in K}M_a^k\le U_a\).

notation.meaning: flow of commodity k on arc a
activation variable and installed capacity of arc a

children.title: Symmetric Design Orbits
children.top_down_role: Equivalent network designs created by interchangeable activation or capacity choices.

assumptions_latex: A finite group \(\Gamma\) acts on the design index set \(E\) by permutations.
The feasible set \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^E\) and objective \(f:F\to\mathbb R\) are invariant under this action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every orbit \(\Gamma y\) consists of feasible designs having the same objective value.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permutation symmetries of interchangeable design variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(y\in F\), define its design orbit by \(\Gamma y=\{\gamma y:\gamma\in\Gamma\}\), where \((\gamma y)_e=y_{\gamma^{-1}(e)}\). Invariance means \(\gamma y\in F\) and \(f(\gamma y)=f(y)\) for every \(y\in F\) and \(\gamma\in\Gamma\). Consequently, if \(y\) is optimal, every member of \(\Gamma y\) is optimal. The number of distinct symmetric copies is \(|\Gamma y|=|\Gamma|/|\operatorname{Stab}_\Gamma(y)|\), where \(\operatorname{Stab}_\Gamma(y)=\{\gamma\in\Gamma:\gamma y=y\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invariant model assigns identical feasibility and objective value to every design obtained by permuting interchangeable design indices.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Design Orbits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The orbit property and orbit–stabilizer formula are precise and property fits the leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied for the symmetry terminology or its design-model specialization.

children.title: Design Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Fixed-charge formulations with extensive alternative representations or bases.

assumptions_latex: A design optimization problem has feasible set \(F\) and objective \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Design degeneracy occurs exactly when an optimal fiber contains at least two distinct design vectors.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy of optimal installed designs, not simplex-basis degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S^*=\{z\in F:f(z)=\inf_{w\in F}f(w)\}\), and let \(\pi_y(z)\) denote the installed-design component of solution \(z\). The instance is design-degenerate when \(|\pi_y(S^*)|>1\); equivalently, there exist \(z^1,z^2\in S^*\) with \(\pi_y(z^1)\ne\pi_y(z^2)\). Routing degeneracy alone, where distinct optimal solutions share the same installed design, does not satisfy this definition. Symmetric optimal designs are one sufficient mechanism, but symmetry is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Design degeneracy means that at least two distinct installed designs attain the same optimal value; multiple routings on one design do not suffice.
knowledge_statements.title: Design Degeneracy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed definition is internally precise and distinguishes design multiplicity from routing or basis degeneracy, but “design degeneracy” in this exact sense requires a terminological source.

children.title: Symmetry-Breaking Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Scope and limitations of structural restrictions intended to remove equivalent designs.

assumptions_latex: A finite group \(\Gamma\) acts on a feasible design set \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^E\).
A total order \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\) of design indices is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lexicographic boundary retains exactly one representative from each design orbit.

notation.meaning: lexicographic order induced by the fixed index order

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lex-leader boundary; no claim of polynomial-size encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the symmetry-breaking region \(B=\{y\in F:y\succeq_{\mathrm{lex}}\gamma y\text{ for every }\gamma\in\Gamma\}\). For each orbit \(O=\Gamma y\), the finite set \(O\) has a unique lexicographically maximal vector, and this vector is the sole member of \(O\cap B\). Hence restricting the model to \(B\) preserves one representative of every feasible orbit and therefore preserves the optimal value whenever the objective is \(\Gamma\)-invariant. Omitting any required comparison may leave multiple representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lex-leader constraints select the unique lexicographically maximal design in every finite symmetry orbit while preserving the optimum of an invariant model.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Breaking Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact lex-leader region does select one representative from each finite orbit, and condition fits the boundary leaf, but no inspectable symmetry-breaking source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Undirected Steiner Tree

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An undirected Steiner tree is a minimum-cost connected subgraph spanning all terminals, with the zero-edge case allowed for a singleton terminal set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Undirected Steiner trees and full-component optimal substructure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the metric undirected Steiner tree problem and records structural properties of minimal solutions and optimal full components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$, terminals $R\subseteq V$, and nonnegative edge costs $c_e$, the Steiner tree problem seeks a minimum-cost set $F\subseteq E$ such that $(V,F)$ contains a path between every pair of terminals. By passing to the metric completion, one may assume without loss of generality that $G$ is complete and its costs satisfy the triangle inequality. Every minimal feasible solution is a tree whose leaves are terminals. A full component is a maximal subgraph having no terminal as a non-leaf. If an optimal Steiner tree decomposes into full components with vertex sets $V_1,\ldots,V_s$, each full component is optimal for the instance induced by its vertex set, and contracting such a component yields an optimal Steiner tree for the resulting contracted instance. If the vertices used by a Steiner tree are fixed as $V'\subseteq V$, an optimal such tree is a minimum spanning tree of the instance induced by $V'$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The undirected Steiner tree problem asks for a minimum-cost subgraph connecting all terminals. Under metric completion, a minimal solution is a tree with only terminals as leaves. Its full components have componentwise and contraction-based optimal substructure, and an optimum using a fixed vertex set is a minimum spanning tree on that set.

R\subseteq V
c_e\geq 0\quad\forall e\in E
\text{For the metric formulation, }G\text{ is complete and }c\text{ satisfies the triangle inequality}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\left\{\sum_{e\in F}c_e:F\subseteq E,\ (V,F)\text{ connects every pair of terminals in }R\right\}\text{ has the stated minimal-tree and full-component optimal-substructure properties.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Connector, Undirected Steiner Tree, Terminals, and Steiner Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational definitions for undirected Steiner-tree problems; the connector definition does not require the connector to be a subgraph of G.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be an undirected graph and \(T\subseteq V(G)\). A connector for \(T\) is a connected graph \(Y\) with \(T\subseteq V(Y)\). A Steiner tree for \(T\) in \(G\) is a tree \(S\) such that \(T\subseteq V(S)\subseteq V(G)\) and \(E(S)\subseteq E(G)\). The elements of \(T\) are called terminals, and the elements of \(V(S)\setminus T\) are called the Steiner points of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let G be an undirected graph and T a subset of its vertices. A connector for T is a connected graph containing T; it is not required here to be a subgraph of G. A Steiner tree for T in G is a tree whose vertices and edges lie in G and whose vertex set contains T. The vertices in T are terminals, and the remaining vertices of the tree are Steiner points.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is an undirected graph}
T\subseteq V(G)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Y\text{ is a connector for }T\iff Y\text{ is connected and }T\subseteq V(Y);\qquad S\text{ is a Steiner tree for }T\text{ in }G\iff S\text{ is a tree},\ T\subseteq V(S)\subseteq V(G),\ E(S)\subseteq E(G).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Steiner Forest via Binary Pairwise Connectivity Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the Steiner forest problem for designated vertex sets using binary requirements on unordered vertex pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given designated vertex sets \(S_1,\ldots,S_k\), define a requirement function on unordered vertex pairs by \[r(\{u,v\})=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }u,v\in S_i\text{ for some }i,\\0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\] The Steiner forest problem is to find a minimum-cost subgraph \(F\) containing a \(u\)-\(v\) path for every pair \(\{u,v\}\) satisfying \(r(\{u,v\})=1\). In general, the resulting subgraph is a forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign requirement 1 to an unordered pair of vertices when both vertices belong to at least one common designated set, and requirement 0 otherwise. The Steiner forest problem asks for a minimum-cost subgraph connecting every pair with requirement 1; in general, the resulting subgraph is a forest.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Single-Component Primal-Dual Growth Procedure for Steiner Forest
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-attempt procedure that grows one active component variable at a time and performs no reverse deletion; the extract asserts no approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $y\leftarrow0$ and $F\leftarrow\varnothing$. While some pair $s_i,t_i$ is disconnected in $(V,F)$, choose a component $C$ of $(V,F)$ and an index $i$ such that $|C\cap\{s_i,t_i\}|=1$. Increase $y_C$ until an edge $e'\in\delta(C)$ satisfies $\sum_{S\in\mathcal S_i:\,e'\in\delta(S)}y_S=c_{e'}$, and set $F\leftarrow F\cup\{e'\}$. Return $F$ once every terminal pair is connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with no selected edges and zero dual variables. Repeatedly choose a connected component separating a terminal pair, raise its dual variable until a boundary edge becomes tight, and add that edge. Return the edge set when all pairs are connected.

c_e\ge0\quad\forall e\in E

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform-Growth Primal-Dual Algorithm with Reverse Deletion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Steiner-forest procedure that grows all active-component dual variables uniformly and then prunes edges in reverse insertion order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $y\leftarrow0$, $F\leftarrow\varnothing$, and $\ell\leftarrow0$. While some terminal pair is disconnected in $(V,F)$, increment $\ell$ and let $\mathcal C$ be the components $C$ of $(V,F)$ for which $|C\cap\{s_i,t_i\}|=1$ for some $i$. Increase all $y_C$, $C\in\mathcal C$, uniformly until an edge $e_\ell\in\delta(C')$ for some $C'\in\mathcal C$ becomes tight, $c_{e_\ell}=\sum_{S:e_\ell\in\delta(S)}y_S$, and add $e_\ell$ to $F$. Set $F'\leftarrow F$ and examine $e_\ell,\ldots,e_1$ in reverse order, deleting $e_k$ whenever $F'\setminus\{e_k\}$ remains feasible. Return $F'$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly grow the dual variables of all active components until a boundary edge becomes tight, then add it. After all terminal pairs are connected, inspect added edges in reverse order and remove each edge whose deletion preserves feasibility.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is an undirected Steiner-forest instance}
c_e\ge0\quad\forall e\in E
\mathcal C=\{C:C\text{ is a component of }(V,F),\ |C\cap\{s_i,t_i\}|=1\text{ for some }i\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F'\subseteq E\text{ connects every terminal pair after the reverse-deletion phase}

children.title: Generalized Steiner Network
children.top_down_role: Steiner network problems with heterogeneous pairwise connectivity requirements.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with nonnegative edge costs \(c_e\).
Each unordered pair \(\{u,v\}\) has an integer connectivity requirement \(r_{uv}\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A generalized Steiner network is a minimum-cost subgraph satisfying every prescribed edge-connectivity requirement.

notation.meaning: required number of edge-disjoint paths between u and v
edge connectivity in the selected subgraph

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected survivable-network interpretation using edge-connectivity requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F\subseteq E\), let \(\lambda_F(u,v)\) be the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint \(u\)-\(v\) paths in \((V,F)\). The generalized Steiner network problem is \(\min\{\sum_{e\in F}c_e:F\subseteq E,\ \lambda_F(u,v)\ge r_{uv}\text{ for all distinct }u,v\in V\}\). Vertices with no positive incident requirement may nevertheless be used as Steiner vertices. Requirements exceeding one permit cycles and rule out an automatic forest representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose minimum-cost edges providing the required number of edge-disjoint paths for every vertex pair; zero-requirement vertices may serve as Steiner vertices.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Steiner Network

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula precisely defines an undirected edge-connectivity survivable-network variant, but “generalized Steiner network” has variant-dependent meanings and needs a source supporting this exact interpretation.

children.title: Forest-to-Network Generalization
children.top_down_role: Structural transition from pair connection to broader connectivity requirements.

assumptions_latex: The generalized Steiner network uses integer pair requirements \(r_{uv}\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Steiner forest is precisely the \(0\)-\(1\) requirement restriction; allowing requirements above one yields the generalized network model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Embedding of Steiner forest into edge-connectivity network design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a Steiner forest instance with required-pair set \(P\), set \(r_{uv}=1\) when \(\{u,v\}\in P\) and \(r_{uv}=0\) otherwise. Then \(\lambda_F(u,v)\ge r_{uv}\) holds exactly when every required pair is connected, so the feasible edge sets and costs coincide. Generalized Steiner network strictly extends this model by permitting \(r_{uv}\ge2\); such requirements demand multiple edge-disjoint paths and may force cycles, whereas a forest has edge connectivity at most one between distinct connected vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Steiner forest is the zero-one pair-requirement case of generalized Steiner network; higher requirements impose survivability and may require cycles.
knowledge_statements.title: Forest-to-Network Generalization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The embedding is correct under the preceding edge-connectivity interpretation, and property fits this generalization leaf, but neither that interpretation nor the claimed named generalization has a cited source.

assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph with nonnegative arc costs \(c_a\).
\(r\in V\) is a root and \(T\subseteq V\) is a terminal set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A directed Steiner tree is a minimum-cost arc set containing a directed root-to-terminal path for every terminal.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted, outward directed Steiner tree with arc costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The directed Steiner tree problem is \(\min\{\sum_{a\in F}c_a:F\subseteq A,\ (V,F)\text{ contains a directed }r\text{-}t\text{ path for every }t\in T\}\). Vertices outside \(\{r\}\cup T\) may be used as Steiner vertices. With nonnegative costs, an optimal feasible subgraph can be reduced to an out-arborescence rooted at \(r\) on the vertices reachable along the selected terminal paths, after deleting redundant incoming arcs and directed cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose minimum-cost arcs so the root reaches every terminal; nonterminals may be used, and an optimum can be reduced to an out-arborescence.
knowledge_statements.title: Directed Steiner Tree

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rooted outward formulation and arborescence qualification are mathematically coherent, and definition is appropriate, but no directed-Steiner source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Group Steiner Networks
children.top_down_role: Steiner networks governed by connectivity to designated vertex groups.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with nonnegative edge costs.
\(\mathcal G=\{G_1,\ldots,G_m\}\) is a family of nonempty vertex groups and \(r\in V\) is a root.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A rooted group Steiner network is a minimum-cost connected subgraph containing the root and at least one vertex from every group.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted group-Steiner interpretation; broader group-pair connectivity variants are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The rooted group Steiner network problem is \(\min\{\sum_{e\in F}c_e:F\subseteq E,\ (V(F),F)\text{ is connected},\ r\in V(F),\ V(F)\cap G_i\ne\varnothing\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m\}\). Feasibility requires selecting at least one representative from each group, but the representative is a decision variable. Groups may overlap, so one selected vertex may satisfy several group requirements. Under nonnegative edge costs, an optimal connected solution can be chosen as a tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Connect the root to at least one chosen representative of every vertex group at minimum edge cost; overlapping groups may share representatives.
knowledge_statements.title: Group Steiner Networks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record chooses a rooted group-Steiner-tree interpretation for the broader title without evidence. In addition, defining the vertex set as \(V(F)\) excludes valid zero-edge instances when the root represents every group. A source is needed before selecting and repairing the intended variant.

children.title: Node-Weighted Steiner Networks
children.top_down_role: Steiner networks whose selectable vertices carry costs.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with nonnegative vertex weights \(w_v\).
\(R\subseteq V\) is a nonempty terminal set whose weights follow the stated cost convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A node-weighted Steiner network is a minimum-weight connected vertex set containing all terminals.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Node-weighted connected-Steiner interpretation with explicit terminal-cost convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix whether terminal weights are charged or normalized to zero. The node-weighted Steiner network problem is \(\min\{\sum_{v\in S}w_v:S\subseteq V,\ R\subseteq S,\ G[S]\text{ is connected}\}\), with the selected edges taken from the induced subgraph \(G[S]\) at no additional cost. Vertices in \(S\setminus R\) are node-weighted Steiner vertices. If terminals are compulsory and their weights are charged, \(\sum_{v\in R}w_v\) is an instance-dependent constant; setting terminal weights to zero preserves the optimizing Steiner choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a minimum-weight connected vertex set containing all terminals, with terminal costs either charged explicitly or normalized away as a constant.
knowledge_statements.title: Node-Weighted Steiner Networks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula precisely defines a node-weighted connected-Steiner problem, but the broader “networks” title may also encompass pairwise or survivable requirements. No source fixes that scope or the terminal-weight convention.

children.title: Combined Variant Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Complexity and approximation effects when group requirements meet node-weighted costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined Variant Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary by specialization for the rooted group node-weighted Steiner family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible solution is a connected vertex set \(S\subseteq V\) satisfying \(r\in S\) and \(S\cap G_i\ne\varnothing\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), with cost \(w(S)=\sum_{v\in S}w(v)\). If \(w(v)=1\) for every selectable vertex \(v\), the model specializes to the node-cardinality form of group Steiner tree. If every group is a singleton, \(G_i=\{t_i\}\), it specializes to rooted node-weighted Steiner tree. Consequently, lower bounds for either of these restrictions also apply to the combined family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A connected solution must hit every group. Unit node costs give the node-cardinality group Steiner restriction, while singleton groups give rooted node-weighted Steiner tree; lower bounds for either restriction therefore apply to the combined family.
assumptions_latex: The input is an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with nonnegative node costs \(w:V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), a root \(r\in V\), and nonempty groups \(\mathcal{G}=\{G_1,\ldots,G_m\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The combined family contains node-cardinality group Steiner tree and rooted node-weighted Steiner tree as restrictions and inherits lower bounds established for those restrictions.

notation.meaning: connected vertex set selected by a feasible solution
family of groups that must be hit

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the two stated specializations follow by imposing unit node costs or singleton groups

children.title: Steiner Cut Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Steiner connectivity relaxations expressed through terminal-separating cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Steiner Cut Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted undirected edge-cut relaxation for Steiner tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(S\subseteq V\), let \(\delta(S)=\{uv\in E:|\{u,v\}\cap S|=1\}\). The rooted Steiner cut relaxation is
\[P_{\mathrm{cut}}=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{E}:\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}x_e\ge1\text{ for every }S\subseteq V\text{ with }r\notin S\text{ and }S\cap R\ne\varnothing\right\}.\]
Its optimization form minimizes \(\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e\) over \(P_{\mathrm{cut}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign nonnegative fractional values to edges and require value at least one across every cut separating the root from any required terminal.
assumptions_latex: The instance is an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with costs \(c_e\ge 0\), root \(r\), and required terminals \(R\subseteq V\) containing \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Steiner cut relaxation is the polyhedron defined by nonnegativity and all root-terminal cut inequalities.

notation.meaning: edges having exactly one endpoint in a vertex set

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Steiner-Network Cut Formulation and LP Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut-based integer formulation and continuous relaxation for pairwise connectivity requirements with optional finite edge capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each $S\subseteq V$, define $f(S)=\max\{r(u,v):u\in S,\ v\in V\setminus S\}$. The integer program minimizes $\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e$ subject to $\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}x_e\ge f(S)$ for every $S\subseteq V$, with $x_e\in\mathbb Z_+$ if $u_e=\infty$ and $x_e\in\{0,1,\ldots,u_e\}$ otherwise. Its LP relaxation replaces these domains by $x_e\ge0$ and $0\le x_e\le u_e$, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The requirement of a cut is the largest pairwise connectivity requirement it separates. The integer model minimizes edge cost while satisfying every cut requirement, and its LP relaxation permits real nonnegative edge variables while retaining finite capacity bounds.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)
c_e\text{ is the cost of edge }e
r(u,v)\in\mathbb Z_+
u_e\text{ is the capacity of edge }e
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}x_e\ge f(S)\ \forall S\subseteq V,\quad x_e\in\mathbb Z_+\text{ with the stated finite-capacity bounds; the relaxation replaces integrality by }0\le x_e\le u_e

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-to-Flow Strength Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection equivalence for the disaggregated rooted cut-flow pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_{\mathrm{mcf}}\) be the disaggregated multicommodity-flow polyhedron in variables \((x,f)\), where each terminal commodity has capacity \(x_e\) on edge \(e\), and let \(P_{\mathrm{cut}}\) contain all root-terminal cut inequalities. Then
\[\operatorname{proj}_x(P_{\mathrm{mcf}})=P_{\mathrm{cut}}.\]
Consequently, the two relaxations have the same optimal value for every edge-cost vector for which the corresponding minimization problems have finite optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With separate capacities for each terminal commodity, projecting out the flows gives exactly the rooted Steiner cut relaxation, so neither formulation is stronger in edge space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed Component LP for k-Restricted Steiner Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted component relaxation, relaxation direction, and fixed-k solvability for undirected Steiner trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\mathcal C^k=\{(t,R):t\in R\subseteq T,\ |R|\le k\}\), let \(c(C)\) be the minimum cost of a Steiner tree spanning \(R\). Fix \(r\in T\), and set \(\delta^+_{\mathcal C^k}(U)=\{(t,R)\in\mathcal C^k:t\in U,\ R\setminus U\ne\varnothing\}\). The directed component LP is
\[\min\sum_{C\in\mathcal C^k}c(C)x_C\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{C\in\delta^+_{\mathcal C^k}(U)}x_C\ge1\quad(r\in U\subset T),\qquad x_C\ge0.\]
Every \(k\)-restricted Steiner tree induces a feasible integral solution. For fixed \(k\), the component costs and \(O(k|T|^k)\) variables are polynomially manageable, and the cut constraints have an equivalent auxiliary-flow formulation, so the LP is polynomial-time solvable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed components are rooted terminal subsets of size at most k. Their LP weights must cover every proper terminal cut containing the chosen root. Every k-restricted Steiner tree yields an integral feasible solution, so the LP relaxes the k-restricted problem. For fixed k, it is polynomial-time solvable through a polynomial-size component set and an auxiliary-flow formulation of the cut constraints.

T\subseteq V,\quad r\in T
k\in\mathbb N
k\text{ is fixed for the polynomial-time solvability conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{DCLP}}\le\operatorname{OPT}_{k\text{-restricted Steiner}},\qquad \mathrm{DCLP}(k)\text{ is polynomial-time solvable for fixed }k.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gap induced by comparing compatible directed and undirected component feasible regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_{\mathrm{D}}\) and \(P_{\mathrm{U}}\) be compatible directed and undirected component polyhedra. Suppose the orientation-forgetting map \(Q\) satisfies \(Q(P_{\mathrm{D}})\subseteq P_{\mathrm{U}}\) and preserves the component-cost objective. For the corresponding minimization optima,
\[z_{\mathrm{D}}\ge z_{\mathrm{U}},\qquad \gamma_{\mathrm{orient}}=z_{\mathrm{D}}-z_{\mathrm{U}}\ge0.\]
The gap is zero exactly when an undirected optimum has a directed lift of the same cost. It is strictly positive exactly when every directed lift feasible for \(P_{\mathrm{D}}\) costs more than the undirected optimum. No strict gap follows from orientation alone without an instance witnessing this failure of equal-cost lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When forgetting orientations maps every directed feasible solution into the undirected relaxation, the directed optimum cannot be smaller. Equality requires an equal-cost directed lift of an undirected optimum.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(\mathcal{K}_k=\{K:K\text{ is a full component and }|R(K)|\le k\}\). Then
\[\mathcal{K}_2\subseteq\mathcal{K}_3\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathcal{K}_{|R|}.\]
For a component minimization relaxation whose constraints retain the same form while columns are added, let \(z_k\) denote the optimum restricted to \(\mathcal{K}_k\). Feasible-region inclusion gives
\[z_2\ge z_3\ge\cdots\ge z_{|R|}=z_*.\]
Thus smaller \(k\) yields a more restricted, potentially costlier relaxation, while \(k\ge|R|\) admits every full component and coincides with the unrestricted finite-instance formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Component Enumeration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustive generation of minimum-cost full-component columns spanning at most \(k\) terminals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \((G,c,R,k)\). Initialize \(\mathcal{L}\leftarrow\varnothing\). For each subset \(S\subseteq R\) with \(2\le|S|\le k\), invoke an exact Steiner subroutine constrained to return every minimum-cost full component whose terminal leaves are exactly \(S\), or to report that none exists. Insert each returned component \(K\) into \(\mathcal{L}\), retain its cost \(c_K\), and discard duplicate columns. For a directed master, additionally create every admissible sink orientation \(s\in S\). After all eligible subsets and orientations have been processed, output \(\mathcal{L}\). Under the stated subroutine contract, the output contains every minimum-cost \(k\)-restricted component column indexed by an eligible terminal leaf set, including all tied minimum-cost realizations returned by the subroutine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every terminal subset of size two through k, enumerate all minimum-cost full components for that exact leaf set, remove duplicate columns, and optionally create every sink orientation.
assumptions_latex: The graph and terminal set are finite, and a restriction parameter \(k\ge2\) is fixed.
An exact Steiner subroutine returns every minimum-cost full component for a prescribed terminal leaf set, or reports none.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure outputs the complete family of minimum-cost \(k\)-restricted component columns under the stated subroutine convention.

notation.meaning: terminal leaf set prescribed for a component

children.top_down_role: Implicit identification of improving component columns.

assumptions_latex: A restricted master LP has a dual-feasible vector \(y\).
For each candidate component \(K\), its master-column coefficients \(a_{iK}\) and cost \(c_K\) are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pricing either returns a negative-reduced-cost component to add to the master or certifies optimality over the full component family when none exists.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: reduced-cost optimality is the standard column-generation certificate
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced-cost pricing for a component-based master relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input the current dual-feasible vector \(y\) of the restricted master. For every admissible component \(K\), define
\[\bar c_K=c_K-\sum_i a_{iK}y_i.\]
Invoke a pricing oracle to compute \(K^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_K\bar c_K\). If \(\bar c_{K^*}<0\), add the column of \(K^*\) to the restricted master and reoptimize. Otherwise stop and return the current primal-dual pair. With exact master optimization and exact pricing, the stopping test \(\min_K\bar c_K\ge0\) certifies that the current solution is optimal for the LP containing all admissible component columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use the current dual solution to find a minimum-reduced-cost component. Add it when its reduced cost is negative; otherwise exact pricing certifies full-master LP optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Component Pricing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduced-cost stopping rule is standard and correctly conditioned on exact master optimization and pricing, but no inspectable source supports the algorithm or its full-master optimality certificate.

children.title: Enumeration–Pricing Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Scalability and formulation tradeoffs between explicit and implicit component access.

knowledge_statements.title: Enumeration–Pricing Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Column-count and oracle-call tradeoff for fixed-cardinality component families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The number of eligible undirected terminal subsets is
\[M_U(q,k)=\sum_{j=2}^{\min\{k,q\}}\binom{q}{j}.\]
If at most one column is retained per sink orientation, the directed column count is at most
\[M_D(q,k)=\sum_{j=2}^{\min\{k,q\}}j\binom{q}{j}.\]
For fixed \(k\), these quantities are respectively \(O(q^k)\) and \(O(kq^k)\). Explicit enumeration incurs the associated generation and storage costs before solving. Suppose exact column generation adds one previously absent negative-reduced-cost column per successful pricing call, and let \(N\) be the number of columns added in this way. Then \(N\) is at most the number of admissible columns, and termination after a final nonnegative-reduced-cost result uses \(N+1\) pricing calls. Total running time also includes pricing-oracle time and repeated restricted-master reoptimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fixed k, explicit enumeration considers polynomially many terminal subsets and their sink orientations. If pricing adds one new column per successful call, N added columns require N successful calls plus one final certification call.
assumptions_latex: There are \(q=|R|\) terminals and components are restricted to at most \(k\) terminals.
Each terminal subset contributes at most one undirected minimum-cost column, or at most one column per sink in the directed case.
Exact column generation adds one previously absent column per successful pricing call.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Explicit enumeration considers \(O(q^k)\) terminal subsets for fixed \(k\), whereas exact pricing stores only generated columns but incurs repeated oracle calls and master reoptimization.

notation.meaning: number of previously absent columns added by successful pricing calls

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Closure Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminal metric closure for undirected Steiner tree with nonnegative edge costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have costs \(c:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\) and terminals \(R\subseteq V\). Define the complete terminal graph \(K_R\) with length \(d_G(u,v)\) on edge \(uv\), where \(d_G\) is shortest-path distance in \(G\). Every tree \(T\) spanning \(R\) in \(K_R\) can be expanded by replacing each \(uv\in E(T)\) with a shortest \(u\)-\(v\) path in \(G\). The union is connected, spans \(R\), and has cost at most \(\sum_{uv\in E(T)}d_G(u,v)\); deleting cycles and nonterminal leaves preserves feasibility without increasing cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace terminal pairs by their shortest-path distances; any terminal tree in this metric expands and prunes to a no-more-expensive Steiner tree.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
\(c_e\ge 0\) for every \(e\in E\).

knowledge_statements.title: Spanning-Tree Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-spanning-tree construction in the terminal metric closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \((G,c,R)\). Compute all required terminal distances \(d_G(u,v)\) and corresponding shortest paths, form \(K_R\), and compute a minimum spanning tree \(T_R\) of \(K_R\). Replace every edge \(uv\in E(T_R)\) by its stored shortest path in \(G\), take the union \(H\), delete cycle edges, and repeatedly delete nonterminal leaves. Output the resulting tree \(S\). The stopping condition is that \(S\) is acyclic and every leaf belongs to \(R\); its cost satisfies \(c(S)\le d_G(T_R)\).

\(c_e\ge 0\) for every \(e\in E\).

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-to-Tree Approximation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factor-two interface between a terminal-closure MST and an optimal Steiner tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S^*\) be an optimal Steiner tree for terminals \(R\) in a finite undirected graph with nonnegative costs, and let \(T_R\) be a minimum spanning tree of the terminal metric closure. Doubling the edges of \(S^*\) gives an Eulerian terminal tour of cost \(2c(S^*)\). Shortcutting this tour in the shortest-path metric and deleting one tour edge yields a terminal spanning tree, so \(d_G(T_R)\le 2c(S^*)\). Consequently, expanding and pruning \(T_R\) produces a Steiner tree \(S\) satisfying \(c(S)\le 2c(S^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The terminal metric-closure MST expands to a Steiner tree costing at most twice optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
\(c_e\ge 0\) and all terminals are mutually reachable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c(S)\le d_G(T_R)\le 2\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{ST}}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Steiner-Forest Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut-based primal-dual schema for undirected Steiner forest with demand pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(G=(V,E)\), costs \(c_e\ge0\), and demand pairs \(D\), initialize \(F=\varnothing\) and \(y_S=0\) for every cut \(S\subset V\) separating a pair. While some pair is disconnected in \((V,F)\), uniformly raise dual variables of active components until an edge \(e\) becomes tight under \(\sum_{S:e\in\delta(S)}y_S=c_e\), then add \(e\) and merge its incident components. After all pairs are connected, scan chosen edges in reverse order and delete any edge whose removal preserves every demanded connection. Output the resulting forest \(F'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Grow duals on active components, add tight edges, and reverse-delete redundant edges to obtain a feasible Steiner forest.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
\(D\subseteq V\times V\) and \(c_e\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F'\) connects every \((s_i,t_i)\in D\) and is inclusion-minimal with that property.

notation.meaning: dual variable of a demand-separating cut
edges with exactly one endpoint in the cut set

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Component Gain Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy selection of full components by terminal-tree cost reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a tree on the current terminal metric and let \(K\) be a candidate full component whose leaves are terminals \(R(K)\). Define \(T/K\) by contracting \(R(K)\) to one vertex and let \(\operatorname{mst}(T/K)\) denote the cheapest tree obtainable after that contraction. Set \(\operatorname{gain}_T(K)=c(T)-c(\operatorname{mst}(T/K))-c(K)\). Repeatedly select a candidate maximizing positive gain, insert its realization, contract its terminal set, and replace \(T\) by the resulting minimum terminal tree. Stop when every candidate has nonpositive gain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly insert the full component whose cost is smaller than the terminal-tree saving it creates.
assumptions_latex: Candidate components are finite trees with terminal leaves and nonterminal internal vertices.
All edge costs are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gain}_T(K)>0\) implies \(c(K)+c(\operatorname{mst}(T/K))<c(T)\).

notation.meaning: net terminal-tree saving from selecting the component

review_flags: Exact Robins–Zelikovsky gain convention and update rule require a source
