With no cited Robins-Zelikovsky source, the exact mathematical version is unreliable.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Berman–Ramaiyer stack-based component algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-phase Steiner approximation method using conditional full-component gains, a stack, and a minimum spanning tree with modified weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) be the terminal set and \(k\ge 3\). Maintain a minimum spanning tree \(M(S)\) under modified edge weights. In the evaluation phase, examine full Steiner components in increasing order of terminal cardinality from \(3\) through \(k\). If \(T_j\) has positive conditional gain \(W(T_j\mid T_1,\ldots,T_{j-1})\), push it onto a stack. Insert each edge \(e_i\) of a spanning tree \(R_j\) on the terminals of \(T_j\), assigning
\[
w(e_i)=|e_i'|-W(T_j\mid T_1,\ldots,T_{j-1}),
\]
where \(e_i'\) is a longest edge in the cycle formed when \(e_i\) is inserted. In the construction phase, pop the components in reverse order. If \(R_j\) is intact, replace it by \(T_j\); otherwise replace its remaining edges by shortest edges reconnecting the corresponding pieces of \(M(S)\). When the stack is empty, output \(M(S)\). For \(k=3\), this algorithm coincides with Zelikovsky's original greedy algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The evaluation phase examines full Steiner components of three through k terminals, pushes components having positive conditional gain, and updates a modified-weight minimum spanning tree. The construction phase pops those components in reverse order, replacing intact terminal trees by the corresponding Steiner components and reconnecting disrupted trees with shortest edges. The final maintained tree is returned. For k equal to 3, the method is identical to the original greedy algorithm.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is a terminal set}
k\in\mathbb Z
k\ge 3
M(S)\text{ is a minimum spanning tree under the current modified weights}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{When the stack is empty, }M(S)\text{ is the output Steiner tree; for }k=3\text{ the method coincides with the original greedy algorithm.}

knowledge_statements.title: Loss-Contraction Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Component contraction after purchasing only its terminal-attachment loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a full component \(Kulleq G\) with terminal leaves \(R(K)\), define its loss \(L(K)\) as a minimum-cost subforest of \(K\) such that every connected component of \(L(K)\) contains a terminal. Purchase the edges of \(L(K)\), contract each component of \(L(K)\), and retain the remaining edges \(E(K)\setminus L(K)\) as the component core in the contracted instance. Subsequent terminal-tree or component-gain computations are performed after this contraction; at reconstruction, expand the contracted loss forest and prune cycles and nonterminal leaves.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Buy the cheapest part attaching every Steiner vertex to a terminal, contract it, and optimize over the remaining component core.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a finite full component with nonnegative edge costs.
Every leaf of \(K\) is a terminal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c(L(K))=\min\{c(F):F\subseteq E(K),\text{ every component of }F\text{ contains a vertex of }R(K)\}\).

notation.meaning: minimum loss forest of the full component

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Robins–Zelikovsky Loss-Contraction Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm for undirected Steiner tree using bounded-terminal optimum components, loss contraction, metric closure, and terminal minimum spanning trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an undirected graph $G$, nonnegative weights $c:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}_+$, terminals $T\subseteq V(G)$, and an integer $k\ge 2$, compute the metric closure $(\bar G,\bar c)$. Repeatedly choose $S\subseteq T$ with $|S|\le k$ and $K=(Y,L)$, where $Y$ is an optimum Steiner tree for $S$ and $L$ is a loss of $Y$, maximizing
\[
\frac{\operatorname{mst}(\bar c)-\operatorname{mst}(\bar c/K)}{\bar c(L)}
\]
among choices for which the ratio is at least $1$, and set $\bar c:=\bar c/K$. When no such choice exists, compute a minimum spanning tree in the subgraph of $(\bar G,\bar c)$ induced by $T$. Replace its edges by shortest paths in $(G,c')$, where $c'(e)=0$ when $e$ belongs to a selected loss and $c'(e)=c(e)$ otherwise, and return a minimal connected subgraph spanning $T$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute the metric closure and repeatedly contract a bounded-terminal optimum Steiner component whose MST saving per unit loss is maximal and at least one. Then connect the terminals by an MST, expand its edges into shortest paths while making selected loss edges free, and prune the result to a minimal connected subgraph spanning the terminals.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is an undirected graph}
c:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}_+
T\subseteq V(G)
k\in\mathbb{Z},\quad k\ge 2
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The returned minimal connected subgraph is a Steiner tree spanning }T.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Robins–Zelikovsky Approximation and Runtime Guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation and fixed-$k$ polynomial-time guarantee for the Robins–Zelikovsky loss-contraction algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each fixed integer $k\ge 2$, the Robins–Zelikovsky algorithm runs in polynomial time and has performance guarantee
\[
\rho_k\left(1+\frac{\ln 3}{2}\right).
\]
For sufficiently large $k$, this performance guarantee is less than $1.55$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each fixed component bound k, the Robins–Zelikovsky algorithm runs in polynomial time and has approximation guarantee rho-k times one plus half the natural logarithm of three. For sufficiently large k, the guarantee is below 1.55.
assumptions_latex: k\in\mathbb{Z},\quad k\ge 2
k\text{ is fixed for the polynomial-time assertion}
\rho_k\text{ is as defined in the associated restricted-Steiner-tree analysis}

knowledge_statements.title: Component-Size Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accuracy versus enumeration cost for bounded-terminal full components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an integer \(k\ge2\). A Steiner tree is \(k\)-restricted when every full component contains at most \(k\) terminals. In the metric closure of an undirected nonnegative-cost instance, there exists a \(k\)-restricted tree of cost at most \((1+1/\lfloor\log_2 k\rfloor)\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{ST}}\). For fixed \(k\), candidate full components can be generated by considering terminal subsets of size at most \(k\), giving \(|R|^{O(k)}\) subset-enumeration time apart from the exact subroutine used on each subset. Increasing \(k\) improves the structural factor but increases enumeration cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Larger full components improve the restricted-tree approximation while requiring exponentially more terminal-subset enumeration.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, metric, and undirected with nonnegative costs.
\(k\ge2\) is fixed during component enumeration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_k\le(1+1/\lfloor\log_2 k\rfloor)\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{ST}}\), with enumeration cost \(|R|^{O(k)}\).

notation.meaning: minimum cost of a k-restricted Steiner tree
maximum terminals in one full component

knowledge_statements.title: Iterative Randomized Component Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolve, sample, and contract scheme for a fractional full-component relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On the current terminal set \(R_i\), solve a component relaxation and obtain nonnegative values \(x_C^{(i)}\) for full components \(C\). Let \(M_i=\sum_Cx_C^{(i)}\), sample one component with probability \(x_C^{(i)}/M_i\), add its edges to the provisional solution, and contract all terminals of \(C\) into one terminal. Remove induced loops, update component costs and incidences, and resolve the relaxation. Repeat until one terminal remains; then expand contractions, take the union of sampled components, and prune cycles and nonterminal leaves.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly solve the component LP, sample proportionally to fractional weight, contract the sampled terminals, and finally prune the union.
assumptions_latex: Each relaxation solution has finite support and \(M_i>0\) whenever \(|R_i|>1\).
Every sampled component is realizable in the original graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|R_{i+1}|=|R_i|-|R_i(C)|+1\), so sampling only components with at least two current terminals terminates.

notation.meaning: fractional weight of component C at iteration i
total fractional component weight at iteration i
current terminals contained in sampled component C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Iterated randomized component-rounding guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the Steiner-tree approximation ratio and the corresponding directed-component integrality-gap upper bound.

For the Steiner tree problem, the iterated randomized rounding algorithm is a $1.694$-approximation algorithm. Moreover, if $\operatorname{OPT}$ is the integral optimum and $\operatorname{LP}_{\mathrm{DC}}$ is the optimum of the directed component relaxation, then
\[
\frac{\operatorname{OPT}}{\operatorname{LP}_{\mathrm{DC}}}\leq 1.694.
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected Time to Mark All Elements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Harmonic expected-iteration bound for a repeated marking process. The per-iteration probability condition is interpreted conditionally on the preceding history, as required for the bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varnothing\ne X\subseteq W\). Suppose that in every iteration, conditional on the preceding history, each as-yet-unmarked element of \(X\) is marked with probability at least \(1/M\). If \(\tau_X\) is the number of iterations until every element of \(X\) has been marked, then \(\mathbb E[\tau_X]\le M H(|X|)\), where \(H(i)=\sum_{j=1}^{i}1/j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If, at every iteration and conditional on the process history, each unmarked element has probability at least 1/M of being marked, then the expected time to mark the entire nonempty set is at most M times its harmonic number.
assumptions_latex: \varnothing\ne X\subseteq W
\Pr(e\text{ is marked in the current iteration}\mid\text{preceding history})\ge\frac1M\quad\text{for every currently unmarked }e\in X
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[\tau_X]\le M H(|X|),\qquad H(i)=\sum_{j=1}^{i}\frac1j

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Connectivity Invariant Under Successive Component Contractions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connectivity preservation after successive component contractions and valid bridge-set deletions in witness-tree analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((T,W)\) be a tree, let \(m\in\mathbb N\), and let \(C_i=(t_i,R_i)\in\mathcal C^k\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Set \(W_0=W\). For every \(i\), choose
\[B_i\in\mathcal B_{(T,W_{i-1})/C_1/\cdots/C_{i-1}}(R_i),\qquad W_i=W_{i-1}\setminus B_i.\]
Then all terminals lie in the same connected component of
\[\left(V(Y^*),\{e\in E(Y^*):W(e)\cap W_m\ne\varnothing\}\right)/C_1/\cdots/C_m.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a witness tree, successively contract chosen components and delete a valid bridge set at each step. After any finite sequence, the edges of the full Steiner tree represented by surviving witness edges still connect all terminals after the same contractions.

m\in\mathbb N
C_i=(t_i,R_i)\in\mathcal C^k\quad(i=1,\ldots,m)
B_i\in\mathcal B_{(T,W_{i-1})/C_1/\cdots/C_{i-1}}(R_i),\quad W_i=W_{i-1}\setminus B_i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{All terminals are connected in }\left(V(Y^*),\{e\in E(Y^*):W(e)\cap W_m\ne\varnothing\}\right)/C_1/\cdots/C_m.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Iterative Randomized Directed-Component Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Steiner-specific randomized rounding by repeatedly solving the directed component LP and contracting a sampled component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(\mathcal C'=\varnothing\). While \((G,c,T)/\mathcal C'\) has more than one terminal, compute an optimal directed-component-LP solution \(x\), choose a current component \(C\in\mathcal C^k\) with
\[\Pr[C]=\frac{x_C}{\sum_{C'\in\mathcal C^k}x_{C'}},\]
and add \(C\) to \(\mathcal C'\), thereby contracting its terminal set in the next instance. For every selected \(C=(t,R)\), let \(Y_C\) be an optimal Steiner tree spanning \(R\) in \((G,c)\). Return an inclusion-minimal connected subgraph containing \(T\) of \(\bigcup_{C\in\mathcal C'}Y_C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly solve the directed component LP on the instance contracted by the previously selected components, sample a component proportionally to its LP value, and contract it. Once only one terminal remains, realize every selected component by an optimal Steiner tree and return a minimal connected subgraph of their union spanning the original terminals.

T\subseteq V
k\ge2

knowledge_statements.title: Terminal-Subset Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dreyfus–Wagner subset dynamic program parameterized by terminal count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a root terminal \(r\), let \(Q=R\setminus\{r\}\), and precompute distances \(d(u,v)\). For \(t\in Q\), initialize \(D(\{t\},v)=d(t,v)\). knowledge_statements.title: Steiner Cut Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation for the standard rooted undirected Steiner cut relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every terminal \(t\in R\setminus\{r\}\), compute a minimum \(r\)-\(t\) cut using capacities \(x_e\). Let \(S_t\subseteq V\) be its side containing \(t\), so \(r\notin S_t\). If \(x(\delta(S_t))<1\), output the violated valid inequality \[x(\delta(S_t))\ge 1.\] If no terminal produces a cut of capacity below \(1\), stop and declare the candidate feasible for the rooted Steiner cut system.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Convert the decomposition into a nice tree decomposition. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A metric quasi-bipartite representation consists of all terminal-terminal edges with costs \(d(u,v)\), selected terminal-Steiner edges with costs \(c_{us}\), and no Steiner-Steiner edges. Compatibility with Steiner shortcuts requires \[d(u,v)\le c_{us}+c_{sv}\] whenever \(u,v\in R\) and \(s\in S\) is adjacent to both. Feasible trees span \(R\) and may use vertices of \(S\). This formulation avoids interpreting a complete metric closure as quasi-bipartite, because such a closure would generally add edges between distinct Steiner vertices.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct a directed acyclic graph with root \(r\), one vertex \(s_F\) for each \(F\in\mathcal{F}\), and one terminal \(t_u\) for each \(u\in U\). Add an arc \((r,s_F)\) of cost \(1\), and add a zero-cost arc \((s_F,t_u)\) exactly when \(u\in F\). Any directed subgraph reaching every terminal from \(r\) selects a collection \(\mathcal{C}=\{F:(r,s_F)\text{ is chosen}\}\) that covers \(U\). Conversely, every cover yields such a directed Steiner solution of the same cost. Hence the two optimum values are equal even for depth-two acyclic instances.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Form a star with center \(r\), one leaf \(v_F\) for each \(F\in\mathcal{F}\), and unit cost on every edge \(rv_F\). For each element \(u\in U\), define the group \[G_u=\{v_F:F\in\mathcal{F},\ u\in F\}.\] A subtree containing \(r\) is determined by its selected leaves. It intersects every group \(G_u\) exactly when the corresponding sets cover every element of \(U\), and its edge cost equals the number of selected sets. Thus the optimum Group Steiner value equals the optimum Set Cover value, already when the host tree has depth one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Group Steiner Tree on a star exactly encodes Set Cover: leaves represent sets, element groups contain the leaves whose sets cover that element.
knowledge_statements.title: Group-Steiner Boundaries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shared Set Cover barrier across directed and group-Steiner generalizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every Set Cover instance \(I\), let \(D(I)\) be its depth-two directed-Steiner construction and \(H(I)\) its star group-Steiner construction. Both satisfy \[\operatorname{OPT}(D(I))=\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\operatorname{OPT}(H(I)).\] Moreover, any feasible solution of cost \(C\) for either constructed instance maps in polynomial time to a cover of cost at most \(C\). Therefore an \(\alpha\)-approximation for Directed Steiner Tree even on \(D(I)\), or for Group Steiner Tree even on \(H(I)\), would give an \(\alpha\)-approximation for Set Cover. Structural restrictions excluding these embedded constructions are consequently necessary to evade this shared barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed Steiner and Group Steiner both contain cost-preserving Set Cover encodings, so approximation guarantees for those restricted families transfer directly to Set Cover.

knowledge_statements.title: Prize-Collecting Steiner Forest
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected edge-cost formulation with optional pairwise connectivity demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), nonnegative edge costs \(c_e\), and demand pairs \((s_i,t_i)\) with nonnegative penalties \(\pi_i\), the prize-collecting Steiner forest problem is
\[\min_{F\subseteq E}\left\{\sum_{e\in F}c_e+\sum_{i:\,s_i\not\leftrightarrow_F t_i}\pi_i\right\}.\]
Here \(s_i\leftrightarrow_F t_i\) means that the endpoints lie in the same connected component of \((V,F)\). Because cycles of nonnegative cost may be deleted, an optimal solution may be chosen as a forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a minimum-cost forest while paying the stated penalty for every demand pair whose endpoints remain disconnected.

\(c_e\ge 0\) for every \(e\in E\), and \(\pi_i\ge 0\) for every demand pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^*\in\arg\min_{F\subseteq E}\bigl(c(F)+\sum_{i:s_i\not\leftrightarrow_F t_i}\pi_i\bigr)\) may be chosen acyclic.

knowledge_statements.title: Tree–Forest Transfer Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of direct reductions between rooted prize-collecting trees and pair-demand forests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rooted prize-collecting Steiner tree instance is exactly representable as a prize-collecting Steiner forest instance by replacing each optional vertex \(v\) with the demand pair \((r,v)\) carrying penalty \(\pi_v\). The converse fails for reductions that force all served pairs into one connected tree. For vertices \(a,b,c,d\), let \(c_{ab}=c_{cd}=1\), let every edge between \(\{a,b\}\) and \(\{c,d\}\) cost \(M\), and give pairs \((a,b)\) and \((c,d)\) penalties exceeding \(M+2\). The optimal forest costs \(2\), whereas any connected subgraph serving both pairs costs at least \(M+2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rooted vertex prizes reduce directly to root-terminal pairs, but arbitrary pair demands may require separate components and cannot generally be merged without unbounded cost.
assumptions_latex: All omitted edges have cost at least \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ratio between the cheapest single connected solution serving both pairs and the optimal forest is at least \((M+2)/2\), which is unbounded as \(M\to\infty\).

notation.meaning: The distinguished root in the tree instance.
The cost separating the two useful regions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduction and separating example are coherent and the failure-boundary kind fits, but the asserted transfer boundary lacks cited support.

knowledge_statements.title: Quota Steiner Tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted vertex-prize quota formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), root \(r\in V\), nonnegative edge costs \(c_e\), nonnegative vertex prizes \(p_v\), and quota \(Q\ge 0\), a quota Steiner tree is a connected acyclic subgraph \(T=(V_T,E_T)\) satisfying \(r\in V_T\) and
\[\sum_{v\in V_T}p_v\ge Q.\]
The optimization problem minimizes \(c(T)=\sum_{e\in E_T}c_e\) over all such trees. The instance is feasible exactly when the component of \(r\) in \(G\) contains vertices of total prize at least \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find the cheapest tree containing the root and vertices whose total collected prize reaches the prescribed quota.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^*\in\arg\min\{c(T):T\text{ is a tree},\ r\in V_T,\ \sum_{v\in V_T}p_v\ge Q\}\).

notation.meaning: Prize collected by including vertex v.

children.title: k-MST Connectivity

knowledge_statements.title: k-MST Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted minimum-cost tree spanning at least a prescribed number of vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), nonnegative edge costs \(c_e\), root \(r\in V\), and integer \(1\le k\le |V|\), the rooted \(k\)-MST problem is
\[\operatorname{OPT}_k=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E_T}c_e:T=(V_T,E_T)\text{ is a tree},\ r\in V_T,\ |V_T|\ge k\right\}.\]
In the unrooted variant the condition \(r\in V_T\) is omitted. With nonnegative costs, a feasible connected subgraph may be reduced to a spanning tree without increasing cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find the cheapest rooted tree containing at least k vertices; omit the root condition for the unrooted variant.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected.
\(c_e\ge0\) and \(1\le k\le |V|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_k\) equals the minimum cost of a connected subgraph containing \(r\) and at least \(k\) vertices.

notation.meaning: Optimal cost for cardinality threshold k.
Vertices contained in the selected tree.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rooted and unrooted definitions are coherent, but a specific source is needed to substantiate the selected at-least-k convention and variant terminology.

children.title: Budgeted Connectivity
children.top_down_role: Connectivity selection under an explicit resource budget.

knowledge_statements.title: Budgeted Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted prize maximization subject to an edge-cost budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), root \(r\in V\), nonnegative edge costs \(c_e\), nonnegative vertex rewards \(p_v\), and budget \(B\ge0\), budgeted connectivity selects a tree \(T=(V_T,E_T)\) solving
\[\max\left\{\sum_{v\in V_T}p_v:T\text{ is a tree},\ r\in V_T,\ \sum_{e\in E_T}c_e\le B\right\}.\]
When \(p_v=1\) for every vertex, the objective is the number of vertices connected to the root within budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximize the reward of vertices connected to the root by a tree whose edge cost does not exceed the budget.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a feasible rooted tree attaining the maximum collected reward under \(c(T)\le B\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation is mathematically well-defined, but “budgeted connectivity” denotes multiple models; an authoritative locator is needed for this rooted prize-maximization version.

children.title: Cardinality–Budget Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Navigation across target-size guarantees, budget limits, plus bicriteria regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality–Budget Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact inverse relation between cardinality thresholds and feasible cost budgets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a rooted graph instance with unit vertex rewards. Let \(C(k)\) be the minimum cost of a rooted connected subgraph containing at least \(k\) vertices, and let \(K(B)\) be the maximum number of vertices in a rooted connected subgraph of cost at most \(B\). Then
\[K(B)=\max\{k\in\{1,\ldots,|V|\}:C(k)\le B\},\]
with the maximum defined as \(0\) when the set is empty. Equivalently,
\[C(k)=\inf\{B\ge0:K(B)\ge k\}.\]
Thus \(C\) is nondecreasing and \(K\) is its generalized integer inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum cost for k connected vertices and maximum cardinality under budget are generalized inverses of one another.
assumptions_latex: The same finite rooted graph and nonnegative edge costs define both value functions.
Vertex rewards are unit rewards.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K(B)=\max\{k:C(k)\le B\}\) and \(C(k)=\inf\{B:K(B)\ge k\}\).

notation.meaning: Minimum cost for connecting at least k vertices.
Maximum connected cardinality achievable within budget B.

children.title: Active-Component Growth
children.top_down_role: Dual-growth structure for components that remain eligible for connection.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Component Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-driven dual growth for rooted prize-collecting Steiner tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize the forest with singleton components and dual variables \(y_S=0\); the root component is inactive and every other eligible component is active. During a growth phase, increase \(y_S\) at common rate \(1\) for every active component \(S\). Stop at the first event at which either an edge constraint
\[\sum_{S:e\in\delta(S)}y_S\le c_e\]
becomes tight or a relevant penalty constraint
\[\sum_{S\subseteq U}y_S\le\sum_{v\in U}\pi_v\]
becomes tight. A tight edge joining distinct components is added and its components are merged; a tight penalty event is handled by deactivation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Grow all active component duals uniformly until an edge or penalty constraint becomes tight, then merge components or deactivate one.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected with root \(r\).
Edge costs \(c_e\) and vertex penalties \(\pi_v\) are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each growth interval ends at the earliest positive time preserving all edge and penalty dual inequalities.

notation.meaning: Dual variable associated with component or vertex set S.
Edges having exactly one endpoint in S.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, but the active-set eligibility, penalty constraints, and merge/deactivation rules depend on the exact Goemans–Williamson formulation and cannot be validated without a source.

children.title: Penalty-Triggered Deactivation
children.top_down_role: Component retirement governed by exhausted penalty potential.

knowledge_statements.title: Penalty-Triggered Deactivation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-tightness rule for stopping the growth of an optional component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be an active component not containing the root. Deactivation is permitted when a penalty-set inequality becomes tight for a set \(U\) represented by \(C\):
\[\sum_{S\subseteq U}y_S=\pi(U),\qquad \pi(U)=\sum_{v\in U}\pi_v.\]
After the event, the represented component is marked inactive and its dual variables receive no further growth unless the chosen algorithm explicitly specifies reactivation after a merge. Deactivation records that the available penalty budget supporting continued isolated growth has been exhausted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deactivate a nonroot component only when its associated penalty inequality is tight, so further dual growth would violate feasibility.
assumptions_latex: The current dual vector satisfies every edge and penalty inequality.
\(C\) is active and does not contain the root.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tightness implies that any positive isolated increase assigned within \(U\) would violate \(\sum_{S\subseteq U}y_S\le\pi(U)\).

notation.meaning: Total penalty of vertices in U.
Dual mass assigned to set S.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is plausible, but the meaning of a set represented by a component and the permitted post-merge behavior are formulation-specific and require authoritative support.

children.title: Growth–Deactivation Coupling
children.top_down_role: Interaction between component merging, penalty exhaustion, plus activity status.

knowledge_statements.title: Growth–Deactivation Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility coupling between continuous dual growth and discrete component states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At every time \(t\), dual growth rates must satisfy
\[\dot y_S(t)=\begin{cases}1,&S\text{ is active at }t,\\0,&S\text{ is inactive at }t.\end{cases}\]
Growth continues only while all edge and penalty inequalities remain feasible. When an edge inequality first becomes tight, the corresponding components are merged and the active status of the new component is recomputed. When a penalty inequality first becomes tight, its represented nonroot component is deactivated. Consequently, state changes occur exactly at dual-feasibility boundary events, and no inactive component consumes additional penalty slack.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform growth and component activity are coupled: tight edges cause merges, tight penalties cause deactivation, and inactive components stop growing.
assumptions_latex: The dual vector is feasible immediately before each event.
Events are processed at their earliest tightness time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For all event times, the updated active-set rule preserves dual feasibility and assigns zero subsequent growth rate to deactivated components.

notation.meaning: Instantaneous growth rate of the dual variable for S.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle matches the leaf, but its rate rule, event processing, and claimed feasibility invariant depend on an unstated precise primal-dual algorithm.

children.title: Premature-Deactivation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where early retirement obstructs useful connectivity.

knowledge_statements.title: Premature-Deactivation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded loss caused by deactivation before penalty tightness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a rooted instance with vertices \(\{r,v\}\), one edge \(rv\) of cost \(c>0\), and penalty \(\pi_v>c\). If a growth algorithm permanently deactivates the component \(\{v\}\) at some dual value \(\tau<c\), before either the edge constraint or penalty constraint is tight, it may return only the root and pay \(\pi_v\). The optimum buys \(rv\) and costs \(c\). Hence premature irreversible deactivation can have approximation ratio
\[\frac{\pi_v}{c},\]
which is unbounded as \(\pi_v/c\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Permanently deactivating a component before tightness can reject a cheap connection and produce an unbounded approximation ratio.
assumptions_latex: \(0\le\tau<c<\pi_v\).
A deactivated component is never reactivated or connected during pruning.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned-to-optimal cost ratio can equal \(\pi_v/c\) and is therefore unbounded.

notation.meaning: Cost of the sole root-terminal edge.

knowledge_statements.title: Pruning Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse-delete pruning on a growth-phase forest with protected vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a forest \(H=(V_H,E_H)\) produced by a growth phase and a protected vertex set \(P\subseteq V_H\). Repeatedly choose a leaf \(v\notin P\), delete \(v\) and its incident edge, and continue until every remaining leaf belongs to \(P\). Output the remaining forest \(H'\). Equivalently, within each component containing protected vertices, \(H'\) is the unique minimal subtree spanning those protected vertices; components containing no protected vertex are deleted. The procedure preserves connectivity among vertices of \(P\) that were connected in \(H\) and never increases edge cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly remove unprotected leaves from the growth forest, leaving the minimal subtrees needed to connect protected vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite forest.
Edge costs are nonnegative and \(P\subseteq V_H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For protected vertices \(u,v\), \(u\leftrightarrow_H v\) implies \(u\leftrightarrow_{H'}v\), and \(c(H')\le c(H)\).

notation.meaning: Vertices whose inherited connectivity must be retained.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic reverse-delete procedure is coherent, but the plural family container and its PCST context require a source establishing the relevant protected-set marking and pruning variant.

knowledge_statements.title: Rooted Prize-Collecting Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Root-mandatory prize-collecting connected-subgraph formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), a distinguished root \(r\in V\), nonnegative edge costs \(c_e\), and nonnegative vertex penalties \(\pi_v\), the rooted prize-collecting Steiner tree problem is
\[\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E_T}c_e+\sum_{v\notin V_T}\pi_v:T=(V_T,E_T)\text{ is a tree and }r\in V_T\right\}.\]
The root is mandatory and its penalty is irrelevant. Equivalent rooted variants may specify mandatory terminals by assigning them infinite penalties or by requiring their membership explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a tree containing the designated root, paying edge costs for selected connections and penalties for excluded optional vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected.
\(c_e\ge0\) and \(\pi_v\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal solution minimizes \(c(T)+\pi(V\setminus V_T)\) over all trees containing \(r\).

notation.meaning: Penalty paid when vertex v is omitted.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rooted prize-collecting objective is precise and fits the definition leaf, but no authoritative locator supports this exact rooted convention or the claimed mandatory-terminal equivalences.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rooted Prize-Collecting TSP and Steiner Tree Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint definition of two rooted optional-service models and the stated root-enumeration reduction for prize-collecting TSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be undirected, with $c_e\ge0$ and $\pi_v\ge0$. Rooted prize-collecting TSP minimizes $c(H)+\sum_{v\notin V(H)}\pi_v$ over tours $H$ containing a prescribed root $r$. Rooted prize-collecting Steiner tree minimizes the analogous objective over trees containing $r$. For prize-collecting TSP, an unrooted solution can be obtained by running the rooted algorithm once for every $r\in V$ and taking the best result.

The unrooted TSP variant can be handled by trying every vertex as the root.

children.title: Unrooted Prize-Collecting Variants
children.top_down_role: Optional-service connectivity without a designated root.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an undirected graph with edge costs \(c_e\ge 0\).
\(K\subseteq \binom{V}{2}\) is a set of demand pairs with penalties \(\pi_k\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{UPCF}}=\min_{F\subseteq E}\left\{\sum_{e\in F}c_e+\sum_{\{s,t\}\in K:\,s\not\leftrightarrow_F t}\pi_{\{s,t\}}\right\}.\)

notation.meaning: Connectivity using only edges in F

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the unrooted prize-collecting Steiner-forest objective for penalized demand pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An unrooted prize-collecting connection solution is any edge set \(F\subseteq E\); no vertex is required to belong to every selected component. A pair \(k=\{s,t\}\in K\) is served exactly when \(s\leftrightarrow_F t\). Its objective value is
\[
C(F)=\sum_{e\in F}c_e+\sum_{k=\{s,t\}\in K:\,s\not\leftrightarrow_F t}\pi_k.
\]
The unrooted prize-collecting problem is to find \(F\subseteq E\) minimizing \(C(F)\). Isolated vertices and the empty edge set are permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose edges to connect selected demand pairs, paying edge costs plus penalties for disconnected pairs; no common root or mandatory component is imposed.
knowledge_statements.title: Unrooted Prize-Collecting Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unrooted prize-collecting Steiner-forest formulation is precise and locally appropriate, but no inspectable source or locator supports this specialized definition.

children.title: Rooted–Unrooted Reductions
children.top_down_role: Structural transfers between rooted plus unrooted formulations.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) has nonnegative edge costs and pair penalties \(\pi_{st}\).
A rooted instance requires every served terminal to connect to a designated root \(r\).

notation.meaning: Auxiliary graph containing a new root
A cost exceeding every feasible original objective value

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the solution-correspondence criterion that a rooted–unrooted gadget must satisfy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A rooted–unrooted reduction is cost preserving when it constructs an auxiliary instance \(G'\) and maps solutions in both directions so that served demands correspond and objective values agree. Mandatory root incidence may be enforced by a zero-cost attachment to a chosen terminal, while an edge of cost \(M\), with \(M\) larger than every admissible original objective, forbids unintended attachments. The reduction is approximation preserving only if
\[
C_G(\Phi(F'))\le C_{G'}(F')\quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{OPT}(G')\le \operatorname{OPT}(G).
\]
These inequalities must be checked for the particular prize-collecting variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid rooted–unrooted gadget must preserve served demands, feasible-solution costs, and the optimum inequalities needed to transfer an approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Rooted–Unrooted Reductions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduction is variant-dependent: the construction, solution map Phi, admissible objective bound M, and correspondence of served demands are not formally specified. A source for the exact rooted–unrooted reduction and its approximation preservation is required.

Penalty for excluding the prize vertex

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-vertex instance isolates the effect of requiring a prescribed root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{r,v\}\), let the only edge \(rv\) have cost \(M>1\), and assign exclusion penalty \(1\) to \(v\). In the rooted problem, a selected tree must contain \(r\); it either buys \(rv\) or excludes \(v\), so its optimum is \(1\). In the unrooted problem, the singleton tree \(\{v\}\) serves \(v\) at zero edge cost, so its optimum is \(0\). Thus forgetting the root can change feasibility and optimum discontinuously; no multiplicative comparison follows without an anchoring condition or an explicit root gadget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Requiring a root can change a zero-cost unrooted optimum into a positive rooted optimum, so simply forgetting the root is not approximation preserving.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\) is a family of feasible network designs.
Each \(F\in\mathcal F\) has installation cost \(c(F)\) and unserved penalty \(p(F)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(\lambda)=\min_{F\in\mathcal F}\{c(F)+\lambda p(F)\}\) is concave and nondecreasing in \(\lambda\), while an optimal \(p(F_\lambda)\) may be chosen nonincreasingly.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric penalty scaling underlying Lagrangian-multiplier-preserving network algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every multiplier \(\lambda\ge0\), the penalty-scaled problem is
\[
L(\lambda)=\min_{F\in\mathcal F}\bigl(c(F)+\lambda p(F)\bigr).
\]
Because \(L\) is the pointwise minimum of affine functions of \(\lambda\), it is concave; nonnegativity of \(p(F)\) makes it nondecreasing. If \(0\le\lambda_1<\lambda_2\) and \(F_i\) is optimal at \(\lambda_i\), the optimality inequalities imply \(p(F_2)\le p(F_1)\). Hence increasing the penalty scale weakly decreases the amount of rejected demand, subject to tie-consistent selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying rejection penalties by a parameter yields a concave value function, and larger multipliers weakly reduce rejected demand among consistently chosen optima.
knowledge_statements.title: Penalty-Scaling Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parametric property is standard, but the assumptions must explicitly require p(F) to be nonnegative and finite where needed. The statement also contains derivational proof text and lacks a supporting source with locator.

assumptions_latex: Each feasible design \(F\) serves weight \(w(F)\) and has cost \(c(F)\).
The quota requirement is \(w(F)\ge Q\).
A solver is available for objectives \(c(F)+\lambda(W-w(F))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w(F^-)<Q\le w(F^+)\) and \(\theta w(F^-)+(1-\theta)w(F^+)=Q\) for \(\theta=(w(F^+)-Q)/(w(F^+)-w(F^-))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian search brackets a quota; integral feasibility still requires a variant-specific rounding argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \(W=\sum_i w_i\) and solve the penalized objective \(c(F)+\lambda(W-w(F))\) for varying \(\lambda\ge0\). Binary or parametric search stops with solutions \(F^-\) and \(F^+\) satisfying \(w(F^-)<Q\le w(F^+)\), unless an exact-quota solution is found. Define
\[
\theta=\frac{w(F^+)-Q}{w(F^+)-w(F^-)}.
\]
Then the randomized choice of \(F^-\) with probability \(\theta\) and \(F^+\) otherwise serves expected weight \(Q\). Producing one integral quota-feasible design requires an additional alteration or rounding guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search the penalty multiplier for solutions bracketing the quota, then combine them fractionally; an extra rounding argument is needed for deterministic feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Quota-Conversion Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The expected-weight identity is correct for a genuine bracket, but the stated oracle assumptions do not ensure that binary or parametric search returns such a bracket. Tie handling, attainable weights, search precision, and the LMP guarantee require a variant-specific source.

assumptions_latex: The attainable pairs \((p(F),c(F))\) are discrete.
A conversion accesses designs only by minimizing \(c(F)+\lambda p(F)\) for \(\lambda\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((1,100)\notin\arg\min_{(p,c)\in S}(c+\lambda p)\) for every \(\lambda\ge0\), where \(S=\{(2,0),(1,100),(0,101)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An unsupported Pareto point shows why multiplier search alone need not recover a quota optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider feasible designs whose penalty-cost pairs are
\[
S=\{(2,0),(1,100),(0,101)\}.
\]
The middle design is optimal for the quota requiring penalty at most \(1\). It is never optimal for a scaled objective \(c+\lambda p\): beating \((2,0)\) requires \(100+\lambda\le2\lambda\), hence \(\lambda\ge100\), but then \((0,101)\) costs \(101<100+\lambda\). Thus scalar penalty scaling exposes only supported Pareto points. Without convexification, randomization, or an alteration theorem, a Lagrangian conversion need not preserve the integral quota optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplier optimization can skip an integral quota optimum when that solution is an unsupported Pareto point, necessitating rounding or alteration beyond scalar search.

A realizable network instance or an authoritative abstract conversion result is also needed.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an undirected graph with edge lengths \(\ell_e\ge0\).
Commodity \(i\) has terminals \((s_i,t_i)\) and demand \(d_i\ge0\).
Cable type \(j\) has capacity \(u_j>0\) and per-length cost \(a_j\ge0\).

notation.meaning: Number of type-j cables installed on edge e
Total routed load on edge e

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the standard discrete-capacity multicommodity buy-at-bulk formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A buy-at-bulk design chooses nonnegative integers \(x_{ej}\) and routes every commodity from \(s_i\) to \(t_i\). If \(f_e\) is the aggregate routed demand on edge \(e\), feasibility requires
\[
f_e\le\sum_j u_jx_{ej}\qquad(e\in E).
\]
The installation objective is
\[
\min\sum_{e\in E}\ell_e\sum_j a_jx_{ej}.
\]
Economies of scale are represented by cable types whose unit-capacity prices \(a_j/u_j\) weakly decrease as capacities increase. Splittable or unsplittable routing must be specified as part of the instance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Buy-at-Bulk Network Design Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected multicommodity network-design model with economies-of-scale capacity costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with edge lengths $\ell_e\ge 0$, source-sink pairs $(s_i,t_i)$ with demands $d_i$, and a capacity-cost function $f$ satisfying $f(0)=0$, monotonicity, and nonincreasing cost per unit of capacity, choose a path $P_i$ from $s_i$ to $t_i$ for each $i$ and capacities $c_e$ sufficient to carry all routed demands, minimizing $\sum_{e\in E}f(c_e)\ell_e$. The economies-of-scale assumption implies that $f$ is subadditive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose one path for every demand pair and enough capacity on each edge to carry all demands routed through it, minimizing length-weighted capacity cost. The capacity cost is nondecreasing and has nonincreasing cost per unit, which implies subadditivity.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is undirected}
\ell_e\ge 0\quad(e\in E)
s_i,t_i\in V\quad(i=1,\ldots,k)
f\text{ is nondecreasing}
f(u)/u\text{ is nonincreasing for }u>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{(P_i),(c_e)}\sum_{e\in E}f(c_e)\ell_e\quad\text{subject to}\quad c_e\ge\sum_{i:e\in P_i}d_i,\qquad f(u_1+u_2)\le f(u_1)+f(u_2).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In single-source rent-or-buy, every client demand is routed to one root \(r\). For aggregate edge load \(f_e\), one may rent capacity at unit price until expenditure reaches the cost of buying unlimited capacity. Under the normalization in which both the rental rate and buy price are incorporated into \(\ell_e\) and \(M\), the objective is
\[

\]
The problem is to choose routes minimizing \(C(f)\). The function \(x\mapsto\min\{x,M\}\) is nondecreasing and concave.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable concave installation costs model economies of scale in aggregate edge load.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A concave-cost network installation instance asks for a feasible routing of the prescribed commodities and charges each edge according to its aggregate load. If \(f_e\) is that load, the total cost is
\[
C(f)=\sum_{e\in E}\ell_e g_e(f_e).
\]
The conditions that \(g_e\) is nondecreasing, concave, and vanishes at zero express nonnegative installation cost and economies of scale. The optimization problem is to minimize \(C(f)\) over all feasible routings; integrality or unsplittability requirements are additional model choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Route the commodities while paying a nondecreasing concave cost for aggregate load on each edge, thereby modeling economies of scale.

assumptions_latex: \((V,d)) is a finite metric with \(n=|V|\ge2\).
The network objective is nonnegative and linear in the pairwise distances used by a fixed routing or design.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(u,v)\le d_T(u,v)\) and \(\mathbb E[d_T(u,v)]\le C\log n\,d(u,v)\) imply an expected \(O(\log n)\) transfer from tree metrics.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-metric probabilistic tree embedding and its linear-cost approximation transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every finite metric \((V,d)\) with \(n\ge2\), there is a distribution over tree metrics \(d_T\) on \(V\) such that, for all \(u,v\in V\),
\[
d(u,v)\le d_T(u,v),\qquad \mathbb E[d_T(u,v)]\le C\log n\,d(u,v),
\]
where \(C\) is universal. Consequently, if a routing-design cost is a nonnegative linear combination of terminal-pair distances and a solution can be transferred from the sampled tree without additional loss, its expected cost increases by at most \(C\log n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite metric admits a dominating random tree metric with expected logarithmic stretch, giving logarithmic approximation transfer for compatible linear-distance objectives.

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a terminal set with nonnegative marginal bounds \(b_i\).

notation.meaning: Marginal traffic bound at terminal i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the symmetric hose uncertainty set using terminal marginal bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given terminal bounds \(b_i\ge0\), the symmetric hose-demand uncertainty set is
\[
\mathcal D(b)=\left\{D:\ D_{ij}=D_{ji}\ge0,\ D_{ii}=0,\ \sum_{j\ne i}D_{ij}\le b_i\text{ for every }i\right\}.
\]
A robust network design must support every matrix \(D\in\mathcal D(b)\), although the realized matrix is not known when capacities are installed. The model specifies only endpoint marginals, not individual pair demands; directed hose models replace the single marginal bound by separate ingress and egress bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hose model permits every nonnegative traffic matrix whose total traffic incident to each terminal does not exceed that terminal's prescribed marginal bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Hose-Demand Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The symmetric hose uncertainty set is precise and fits the definition leaf, but it has no cited robust-network-design source or inspectable locator.

assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a tree spanning terminals with hose bounds \(b_i\ge0\).
Each terminal pair is routed on its unique path in \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u_e^{\min}=\min\left\{\sum_{i\in S_e}b_i,\sum_{i\notin S_e}b_i\right\}\) is the exact robust capacity required on edge \(e\).

notation.meaning: One component of the tree after deleting edge e

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact edge-capacity formula for unique-path routing of symmetric hose demands on a tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Deleting an edge \(e\) of \(T\) partitions the terminals into \(S_e\) and \(V\setminus S_e\). Under unique-path routing, the load on \(e\) is precisely the traffic crossing this cut. Over the symmetric hose set, its maximum is
\[
\max_{D\in\mathcal D(b)}\sum_{i\in S_e,\,j\notin S_e}D_{ij}
=
\min\left\{\sum_{i\in S_e}b_i,\sum_{j\notin S_e}b_j\right\}.
\]
Therefore a tree design supports every admissible hose matrix exactly when each edge capacity is at least this cut value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For hose traffic routed on a tree, an edge needs capacity equal to the smaller total terminal bound on either side of its induced cut.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Routing Designs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cut-capacity formula is standard for fractional symmetric hose traffic on a tree, but S_e must explicitly denote terminals on one side of the cut and the demand convention must be sourced. The statement also includes derivational proof text.

knowledge_statements.title: Oblivious Routing Templates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractional oblivious routing on a fixed capacitated graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,u)\) be a graph with \(u_e>0\). An oblivious routing template is a family \(R=(f^{st})_{s\ne t}\), where each \(f^{st}\) is a nonnegative unit \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow chosen independently of the demand matrix. For a nonnegative demand matrix \(D=(d_{st})\), its edge load and congestion are \[L_e(R,D)=\sum_{s\ne t}d_{st}f^{st}_e,\qquad \operatorname{cong}(R,D)=\max_{e\in E}\frac{L_e(R,D)}{u_e}.\] Its competitive ratio on an uncertainty set \(\mathcal D\) is \(\sup_{D\in\mathcal D}\operatorname{cong}(R,D)/\operatorname{opt}(D)\), with ratio zero when both terms vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oblivious template fixes one unit flow per terminal pair before demands are known; demands scale and superpose these flows, and performance is measured against demand-adaptive optimal congestion.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,u)\) is finite and \(u_e>0\).
Demands and routing flows are nonnegative and splittable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) determines a demand-independent linear routing operator and its worst-case competitive ratio on \(\mathcal D\).

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Tree Packings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractional packing of terminal cut trees into a capacitated host graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,u)\). A cut-tree packing consists of capacitated trees \(T_i=(V,E_i,c^i)\), nonnegative weights \(\lambda_i\), and embeddings that map every tree edge \(a\in E_i\) to a unit flow \(g^{i,a}\) between its endpoints in \(G\). Its load on host edge \(e\) is \[\ell_e=\sum_i\lambda_i\sum_{a\in E_i}c^i_a g^{i,a}_e.\] The collection is feasible when \(\ell_e\le u_e\) for all \(e\), and normalized when \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\). Each tree edge represents the vertex cut formed by deleting that edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut-tree packing is a weighted collection of capacitated terminal trees whose tree edges are embedded in the host without exceeding host capacities.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) and every \(T_i\) are finite.
Every embedding flow \(g^{i,a}\) is nonnegative and has value one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is exactly the componentwise condition \(\ell\le u\).

notation.meaning: host-graph embedding of tree edge a

knowledge_statements.title: Routing–Packing Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of embedded tree mixtures into fractional oblivious routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each packed tree \(T_i\), route a terminal pair \((s,t)\) along its unique tree path and embed every traversed tree edge through \(g^{i,a}\). Mixing these routes with probabilities \(\lambda_i\) defines \[f^{st}_e=\sum_i\lambda_i\sum_{a\in P_{T_i}(s,t)}g^{i,a}_e.\] Thus a normalized cut-tree packing induces an oblivious routing template. Conversely, any routing explicitly expressed as such a convex combination is represented by that tree packing. If the packing load is at most \(\beta u\), then routing any demand whose load on every packed tree edge is at most its tree capacity produces host congestion at most \(\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Embedding unique paths from a distribution of terminal trees yields an oblivious routing template; bounded embedding load transfers tree-feasible demands to bounded host congestion.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed convex combination represents the induced oblivious unit flows, with congestion bounded by the packing load factor \(\beta\).

knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Representation Losses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative losses incurred by cut approximation and tree embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every admissible demand \(D\) is routable in a capacitated tree \(T\) with congestion at most \(ho\operatorname{opt}_G(D)\), and the embedding of \(T\) into \(G\) has load factor at most \(eta\). Routing \(D\) on the unique paths of \(T\) and then through the embedding has congestion at most \[\beta\rho\operatorname{opt}_G(D).\] Hence approximation loss in the tree representation and congestion loss in the embedding multiply. Neither factor can generally be omitted unless the corresponding comparison is lossless.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have finite installed capacities \(u\), and let \(D^0\ne 0\) be a nonnegative demand matrix. If an uncertainty set \(\mathcal D\) contains \(\lambda D^0\) for every \(\lambda\ge 0\), then no fixed finite-capacity design can route every demand in \(\mathcal D\). For any terminal cut \(S\) separating the endpoints of a positive entry of \(D^0\), required traffic across \(\delta(S)\) grows linearly with \(\lambda\), whereas \(u(\delta(S))\) is finite. Therefore robust finite design requires bounded demand across every finite-capacity separating cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed finite network cannot protect against an uncertainty set containing an unbounded ray of positive demand across some terminal cut.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Axis Formulation Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path versus arc choice and aggregate versus disaggregate choice affect formulations independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fractional multicommodity routing, replacing commodity-specific arc flows by complete commodity-specific path flows preserves the projected design-load region. By contrast, replacing commodity-specific conservation with only summed conservation generally enlarges that region. Therefore representation strength cannot be inferred from variable count alone: path expansion may be an exact extension, while commodity aggregation may be a genuine relaxation. Combining the two axes yields exact projection only when both the arc–path conversion is complete and the aggregation retains every constraint needed to preserve terminal pairings and commodity-dependent side conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arc-to-path reformulation may be exact, while commodity aggregation may weaken the model; the two representation choices must be assessed separately.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be directed, with capacity variables \(u_e\ge 0\), source \(s\), sink \(t\), and required flow value \(d\ge 0\). The extended flow system consists of conservation, \(0\le x_e\le u_e\), and flow value \(d\). Its projection onto the capacity variables is exactly the cut system \[\sum_{e=(v,w)\in E:\,v\in S,\,w\notin S}u_e\ge d\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V\text{ with }s\in S\text{ and }t\notin S.\] Thus the complete cut and flow formulations have equal single-commodity strength. Per-commodity cuts alone do not provide the analogous characterization for shared-capacity multicommodity flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For one commodity, all source-sink cut inequalities exactly project the flow formulation; separate commodity cuts are insufficient under shared multicommodity capacities.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strength comparison through projection onto common original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\) be a compact relaxation and \(Q=\{(x,z)\in\mathbb R^{n+m}:Cx+Dz\le h\}\) an extended relaxation for the same integer-feasible set. The extended formulation is at least as strong as the compact formulation when \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\subseteq P\), equally strong when equality holds, and strictly stronger when the inclusion is proper. These comparisons concern feasible-region containment in the common \(x\)-space, not the number of variables or inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact and an extended relaxation are compared after projection: containment means stronger, equality means equally strong, and proper containment means strictly stronger.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact relationship between an extended formulation and its projected compact description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a polyhedron \(Q=\{(x,z):Cx+Dz\le h\}\), its represented set in the original variable space is \[\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists z\in\mathbb R^m,\ Cx+Dz\le h\}.\] The system defining \(Q\) is an exact extended formulation of a polyhedron \(P\) precisely when \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=P\). Every inequality valid for \(P\) is then valid for the projected points of \(Q\); eliminating \(z\) recovers a possibly much larger valid description in \(x\)-space. Inclusion instead of equality represents a strengthening or relaxation according to its direction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic comparison principle for compact, cut, and extended routing-design relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) be linear relaxations of one routing-design model, and let \(P(F_i)\) denote projection onto their common design variables. Say that \(F_1\) is at least as strong as \(F_2\) when \(P(F_1)\subseteq P(F_2)\). Their sizes \(s(F_i)\), measured by encoded variables and inequalities, do not determine this inclusion: a compact system can project to a weaker region than an exponentially indexed cut system, while a polynomial-size extended formulation can project to a region defined by exponentially many inequalities. Thus size and projected strength are separate comparison coordinates.

A component-based relaxation assigns each \(C\in\mathcal C\) a variable \(z_C\ge 0\), imposes linear covering, balance, or partition constraints ensuring the required connectivity, and links edge use by inequalities such as \(\sum_{C\in\mathcal C}a_{eC}z_C\le y_e\) or the model-appropriate reverse inequality. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be the terminal set and let \(\mathcal H\subseteq 2^R\) contain terminal subsets represented by realizable connected components. A hypergraphic relaxation assigns \(z_H\ge 0\) to every \(H\in\mathcal H\) and imposes a linear hypergraph-connectivity system, for example partition inequalities requiring selected hyperedges to cross every nontrivial partition sufficiently often. When underlying design variables are retained, additional linear constraints map each hyperedge to a realizing component or its edge-incidence vector. Replacing integral hyperedge selection by nonnegative continuous variables yields the hypergraphic relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hypergraphic relaxation fractionally selects realizable terminal hyperedges and enforces connectivity through partition or equivalent hypergraph constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection-based dominance criterion; no unconditional hierarchy is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_E\), \(P_C\), and \(P_H\) be edge, component, and hypergraphic relaxation polyhedra, and project each onto the same design-variable space. For two representations \(A\) and \(B\), \(A\) dominates \(B\) precisely when \(\operatorname{proj}(P_A)\subseteq\operatorname{proj}(P_B)\). A claimed chain such as \(\operatorname{proj}(P_H)\subseteq\operatorname{proj}(P_C)\subseteq\operatorname{proj}(P_E)\) therefore requires explicit decomposition or lifting maps establishing both inclusions. Without fixed component families, hyperedge realizations, and linking constraints, no universal edge-component-hypergraphic dominance order follows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dominance means nesting after projection to common design variables; a hierarchy requires explicit model-specific lifting or decomposition maps.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-flow comparison of disaggregated and aggregate activation-linking inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite commodity set \(K\), compare disaggregated linking \(x_e^k\le y_e\) for every \(k\in K\) with aggregate linking \(\sum_{k\in K}x_e^k\le |K|y_e\). Summing the disaggregated inequalities proves that every point satisfying them satisfies the aggregate inequality. The converse fails: with \(|K|\ge2\), \(y_e=1/2\), one commodity value \(x_e^{k_0}=1\), and all other values zero, the aggregate inequality is feasible while \(x_e^{k_0}\le y_e\) is violated. Hence disaggregated linking gives an at-least-as-strong, potentially strictly stronger, relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Commodity-wise linking implies aggregate linking and can be strictly stronger, even though it uses more inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Activation-Linking Strength Comparisons

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cut-Separable Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of fixed-terminal cut lower bounds in a finite undirected graph by one minimum-cut computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, let \(s,t\in V\) be distinct terminals, let \(c\in\mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}^{E}\) be the capacity vector supplied by a candidate point, and let \(d\in\mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}\). For \(S\subseteq V\), let \(\delta(S)=\{uv\in E:|\{u,v\}\cap S|=1\}\). Compute an \(s\)-\(t\) minimum cut \(S^*\), where \(s\in S^*\) and \(t\notin S^*\). If \(\sum_{e\in\delta(S^*)}c_e<d\), return the violated inequality \(\sum_{e\in\delta(S^*)}c_e\ge d\); otherwise certify that every inequality \(\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}c_e\ge d\) with \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\) is satisfied. This gives polynomial-time exact separation for the family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite undirected graph, separate fixed-terminal cut lower bounds by computing a minimum s–t cut and returning its inequality exactly when its capacity is below the required value.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with distinct terminals \(s,t\in V\).
The input capacities \(c\in\mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}^{E}\) and requirement \(d\in\mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}\) have polynomial encoding length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut supplies a most violated member of the fixed-terminal cut family, yielding polynomial-time exact separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Shortest-Path-Priced Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path-column pricing with additive rational arc reduced costs on a finite directed graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(s,t\in V\), let \(\bar c\in\mathbb{Q}^{A}\) be arc reduced costs, and let \(\tau\in\mathbb{Q}\). Assume that no negative-cost directed cycle is both reachable from \(s\) and able to reach \(t\). For every directed \(s\)-\(t\) path \(P\), define \(\bar c(P)=\sum_{a\in P}\bar c_a\). Compute a shortest \(s\)-\(t\) path \(P^*\). If such a path exists and \(\bar c(P^*)<\tau\), return \(P^*\) as an improving column; otherwise certify that no admissible path column has reduced cost below \(\tau\). The pricing problem is therefore polynomially solvable by an applicable shortest-path algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When path-column reduced cost is additive over the arcs of a finite directed graph and no relevant negative-cost cycle exists, pricing reduces to a polynomial-time shortest-path computation.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph with vertices \(s,t\in V\).
The reduced costs \(\bar c\in\mathbb{Q}^{A}\) and threshold \(\tau\in\mathbb{Q}\) have polynomial encoding length.
No negative-cost directed cycle is both reachable from \(s\) and able to reach \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Minimum reduced-cost path pricing reduces to a polynomial-time shortest-path computation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pricing is optimization of reduced cost over the admissible component family; tractability depends on that component optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic column-generation oracle for connected routing components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given dual multipliers from the restricted master problem, compute for each admissible component \(C\in\mathcal C\) its reduced cost \(\bar c_C=c_C-a_C^{\mathsf T}\pi\). Solve \(C^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{C\in\mathcal C}\bar c_C\). If \(\bar c_{C^*}<\tau\), return \(C^*\) as an improving column; otherwise certify that no component in \(\mathcal C\) crosses the threshold \(\tau\). This is a pricing algorithm only when the component minimization oracle is exact; its complexity is inherited from the prescribed component family and cost structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Component pricing minimizes reduced cost over admissible connected components; its tractability is exactly that of the underlying component optimization problem.

children.title: Hard-Separation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Formulation families lacking efficient separation access.

assumptions_latex: The inequality family has a polynomially evaluable encoding.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: NP-hardness of the separation problem excludes a polynomial-time exact separation oracle unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

notation.meaning: polyhedron described by the inequality family

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity boundary for exact separation of implicitly indexed inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rational point \(x\), the exact separation task for a polyhedron \(P\) must either certify \(x\in P\) or return an inequality valid for \(P\) that \(x\) violates. A regime is hard-separation when this task is NP-hard under polynomial-time reductions for the specified family of instances. Consequently, a polynomial-time exact separation oracle for that family would imply a polynomial-time algorithm for the reducing NP-hard problem. Unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), no such oracle exists; this statement does not rule out restricted, approximate, or heuristic separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If exact separation for a family is NP-hard, no polynomial-time exact separator exists unless P equals NP.
knowledge_statements.title: Hard-Separation Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate, but no concrete inequality family or hardness reduction is identified. The generic conditional implication is valid, yet the claimed regime cannot be populated as mathematical knowledge without family-specific evidence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity boundary for exact pricing over implicit column families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact pricing over an implicit family \(\mathcal C\) asks for a column \(C^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{C\in\mathcal C}\bar c_C\), or equivalently decides whether some column has reduced cost below a specified rational threshold. A regime is hard-pricing when this decision or optimization problem is NP-hard for the prescribed columns and dual-induced costs. Hence a polynomial-time exact pricing oracle would solve the reducing NP-hard problem in polynomial time. Unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), such an oracle cannot exist, although restricted families, approximation, and heuristic pricing may remain tractable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If finding a minimum reduced-cost admissible column is NP-hard, exact polynomial-time pricing is impossible unless P equals NP.

children.title: Joint-Oracle Limitations
children.top_down_role: Settings where separation access fails to resolve pricing difficulty or conversely.

assumptions_latex: An algorithm requires both exact separation for one constraint family and exact pricing for one column family.
Oracle calls and all intervening computations must run in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial-time joint oracle access requires both constituent tasks to be polynomially solvable; hardness of either exact task blocks the interface unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary tractability condition for algorithms combining exact separation and pricing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an exact method whose iterations call both \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{sep}}\), which separates an implicit inequality family, and \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{price}}\), which minimizes reduced cost over an implicit column family. A polynomial-time implementation of this joint interface requires polynomial-time implementations of both oracles and polynomially many calls. If either constituent task is NP-hard on the admitted instances, then a polynomial-time exact joint oracle would solve that hard task by invoking the corresponding interface component. Therefore, unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), tractability of one oracle cannot compensate for NP-hardness of the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time exact joint interface needs both separation and pricing to be tractable; hardness of either oracle blocks it.
knowledge_statements.title: Joint-Oracle Limitations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement fits Joint-Oracle Limitations, but the claimed reduction from a polynomial-time joint interface to each constituent oracle depends on how that interface exposes and invokes its components. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(S\subset V\) satisfying \(S\cap R\ne\varnothing\) and \(R\setminus S\ne\varnothing\), unit terminal connectivity requires \[x(\delta(S))\ge 1.\] Therefore, a set \(S\) satisfying \(x(\delta(S))<1\) is a cut certificate of infeasibility. Given \(S\), verification consists of checking that terminals lie on both sides and summing the rational capacities \(x_e\) over \(\delta(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every cut separating required terminals must have capacity at least one; a terminal-separating cut of capacity below one is a directly checkable infeasibility certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every partition \(\mathcal P=\{P_1,\ldots,P_q\}\) of \(V\) into \(q\ge 2\) nonempty parts, a connected spanning design satisfies \[x(\delta(\mathcal P))\ge q-1.\] Indeed, after contracting each part, connectivity requires enough crossing edges to connect the \(q\) contracted vertices. Hence the displayed strict reverse inequality supplies a finite certificate; verification requires only checking the partition and summing \(x_e\) over edges joining distinct parts.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every cut inequality is the partition inequality for a partition with two parts. The converse fails. Let \(G=C_3\) and set \(x_e=\tfrac12\) on all three edges. Every nontrivial cut contains two edges, so \(x(\delta(S))=1\) and all cut inequalities hold. For the partition \(\mathcal P\) into three singleton sets, however, \(x(\delta(\mathcal P))=\tfrac32<2=|\mathcal P|-1\). Thus a multi-part partition certificate can reject a point accepted by every cut certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two-part partition inequalities are cuts, while a half-valued triangle satisfies every cut inequality but violates the three-part partition inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A metric dual certificate is a vector \(\ell\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{E}\) satisfying \[\sum_k d_k\operatorname{dist}_{\ell}(s_k,t_k)\ge1.\] Its certified value is \[U(\ell)=\sum_{e\in E}u_e\ell_e.\] Every feasible certificate satisfies \(\lambda^*\le U(\ell)\). The dual program minimizes \(U(\ell)\) over normalized nonnegative lengths, and its optimum equals \(\lambda^*\) by linear-programming strong duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized nonnegative edge metric certifies an upper bound on concurrent throughput by its capacity-weighted total length, and the best such certificate equals the concurrent-flow optimum.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fewer than five points, every finite semimetric lies in the cut cone, whereas for \(|V|\ge5\) the inclusion \[\operatorname{CUT}(V)\subsetneq\operatorname{MET}(V)\] is strict. Hence an unrestricted metric dual can select \(d\in\operatorname{MET}(V)\setminus\operatorname{CUT}(V)\). Such a certificate remains valid as a metric certificate, but no coefficients \(\alpha_S\ge0\) satisfy \(d=\sum_S\alpha_S\delta_S\); exact conversion to a cut-packing certificate therefore fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: From five vertices onward, the metric cone strictly exceeds the cut cone, so some valid metric duals cannot be represented by weighted cuts.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonrepresentable Dual Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, and the strict cut-cone versus metric-cone boundary from five points is a specialized claim requiring an exact metric-geometry source. The record also must qualify that an outside-cut-cone semimetric becomes a valid dual certificate only when it satisfies the relevant normalization, possibly after admissible scaling.

children.title: Lagrangian Relaxation Bounds
children.top_down_role: Bounds obtained through penalized coupling constraints.

assumptions_latex: The primal value is \(z^*=\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in X,\ Ax\ge b\}\), where \(X\ne\varnothing\) and \(z^*\) is finite.
The inequalities \(Ax\ge b\) are dualized with multipliers \(\mu\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every finite value \(L(\mu)\) is a lower-bound certificate for \(z^*\), and \(z_{LD}=\sup_{\mu\ge0}L(\mu)\le z^*\).

notation.meaning: Lagrangian relaxation value at a multiplier.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-bound certificates for a minimization model obtained by dualizing coupling inequalities.

source_refs.locator: 0.6 Lagrangian Relaxation p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(\mu\ge0\), define \[L(\mu)=\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(c^{\mathsf T}x+\mu^{\mathsf T}(b-Ax)\bigr).\] Every finite value \(L(\mu)\) satisfies \(L(\mu)\le z^*\) and is a lower-bound certificate. The optimized Lagrangian bound is \[z_{LD}=\sup_{\mu\ge0}L(\mu)\le z^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite Lagrangian relaxation value obtained from a nonnegative multiplier is a lower-bound certificate, and optimizing over all such multipliers gives the Lagrangian-dual bound.

children.title: Benders Decomposition Bounds
children.top_down_role: Master–subproblem bounds supported by generated feasibility or optimality cuts.

assumptions_latex: The recourse function is \(Q(y)=\min\{q^{\mathsf T}x:Wx\ge h-Ty,\ x\ge0\}\).
The recourse linear program is feasible and bounded for every master point under consideration.
The master minimizes \(c^{\mathsf T}y+\theta\) over \(y\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any finite collection of dual-feasible Benders cuts yields a valid master lower bound; the complete cut family represents \(Q(y)\) exactly.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every dual-feasible vector \(\pi\ge0\) satisfying \(W^{\mathsf T}\pi\le q\), weak duality gives \[Q(y)\ge\pi^{\mathsf T}(h-Ty).\] Hence \(\theta\ge\pi^{\mathsf T}(h-Ty)\) is a valid Benders optimality cut. Minimizing \(c^{\mathsf T}y+\theta\) over \(y\in Y\) and any finite subset of such cuts gives a lower bound on the original minimization problem. Under feasible bounded linear recourse, including all dual extreme-point cuts yields \(\theta=Q(y)\) at optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual-feasible recourse solutions generate Benders cuts; any cut subset gives a lower bound, while all required cuts recover linear recourse exactly.
