children.title: Component-Based Bounds
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds derived from full-component connectivity structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Component-Based Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic cut-covering component relaxation for network design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the component bound by
\[
L_{\mathcal C}:=\min\left\{\sum_{C\in\mathcal C}c_Cz_C:\sum_{C\in\mathcal C}a_C(S)z_C\ge r(S)\ \text{for every }S\subset V,\ z_C\ge0\right\}.
\]
If every feasible integral design can be partitioned into members of \(\mathcal C\), with total component cost equal to its edge cost and component cut incidences satisfying the displayed inequalities, then its incidence vector induces a feasible integral \(z\). Consequently, \(L_{\mathcal C}\le\operatorname{OPT}\), so the relaxation optimum is a valid lower-bound certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut-covering LP over connected components lower-bounds the optimal design whenever every feasible integral design admits a cost-preserving decomposition into those components.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an undirected network with nonnegative edge costs.
\(r:2^V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) specifies residual cut requirements.
\(\mathcal C\) is a prescribed family of connected edge components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_{\mathcal C}\le \operatorname{OPT}\).

notation.meaning: Cost and cut-incidence count of component C

children.title: Hypergraphic Bounds
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds derived from hyperedge-based connectivity representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Hypergraphic Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract full-component hypergraphic relaxation over terminal subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_H\subseteq\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{\mathcal H}\) be a hypergraphic relaxation whose valid inequalities enforce the required terminal connectivity, and define
\[
L_H:=\min\left\{\sum_{A\in\mathcal H}c_Ay_A:y\in P_H\right\}.
\]
Suppose every feasible integral network design admits a decomposition into full components such that each component induces some \(A\in\mathcal H\), the induced vector belongs to \(P_H\), and the sum of realization costs is no greater than the design cost. Then \(L_H\le\operatorname{OPT}\). Thus any feasible dual solution of this hypergraphic program certifies a lower bound on the integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid hypergraphic LP over terminal-spanning full components gives a lower bound when integral designs have cost-preserving feasible hyperedge decompositions.
assumptions_latex: \(T\subseteq V\) is the terminal set.
Each admissible full component connects a terminal subset and has minimum realization cost.
The hypergraphic constraints are valid for every feasible integral design.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_H\le \operatorname{OPT}\).

notation.meaning: Minimum cost of a full component spanning hyperedge A

children.title: Component–Hypergraphic Dominance
children.top_down_role: Equivalence, dominance, plus incomparability across the two bound families.

assumptions_latex: Both relaxations model the same minimization problem and use compatible component costs.
Every hypergraphic solution projects to a feasible component solution without increasing cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_C\le L_H\le\operatorname{OPT}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection-based dominance for minimization relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume that for every \(y\in P_H\), the vector \(z=\pi(y)\) lies in \(P_C\) and satisfies
\[
\sum_C c_Cz_C\le\sum_A c_Ay_A.
\]
Then minimizing over the two regions gives \(L_C\le L_H\). If both programs are valid relaxations of the same integral network-design problem, then also \(L_H\le\operatorname{OPT}\). Hence
\[
L_C\le L_H\le\operatorname{OPT},
\]
so the hypergraphic bound dominates the component bound. Equality holds whenever every optimal component solution has a cost-preserving lift into \(P_H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cost-nonincreasing projection from hypergraphic solutions to component solutions makes the hypergraphic lower bound at least as strong as the component bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Component–Hypergraphic Dominance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection argument and dominance direction are correct under the stated hypotheses, but no source identifies the exact component and hypergraphic formulations for which the projection and lifting assumptions hold.

children.title: Component-Enumeration Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits imposed by large or implicit component families.

assumptions_latex: Components are indexed by subsets of an \(n\)-element terminal set.
The maximum permitted component rank is \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\mathcal H_k|=O(n^k)\) for fixed \(k\), whereas unrestricted enumeration may require \(2^n-1\) indices.

notation.meaning: Hyperedges of rank at most k

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Index-count boundary for subset-indexed component relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For rank at most \(k\), the number of possible terminal subsets is
\[
|\mathcal H_k|=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\binom ni=O(n^k)
\]
when \(k\) is fixed. If \(k\) is part of the input, this count need not be polynomial; unrestricted subset indexing gives
\[
|\mathcal H_n|=2^n-1.
\]
Therefore explicit enumeration is polynomially bounded only under a fixed-rank restriction, unless additional structure supplies a polynomial-size representation or a polynomial-time pricing or separation oracle. Multiple realizations of one terminal subset can increase the index count further.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-rank terminal components have polynomially many subset indices, while unrestricted component enumeration is exponential unless an implicit oracle or compact representation is available.
knowledge_statements.title: Component-Enumeration Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The subset counts and fixed-rank asymptotic bound are correct, and complexity_bound fits the enumeration-boundary leaf. A cited locator is still required, particularly for the claims about representations, oracles, and multiple realizations.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the residual instance \(I_0\) and an empty integral decision set \(F\). At iteration \(t\), compute an extreme optimal solution \(x^{(t)}\in P_t\). Delete every variable with \(x^{(t)}_e=0\). If some variable satisfies \(x^{(t)}_e\ge\alpha\), fix it to one, add \(e\) to \(F\), and update demands and capacities to obtain \(I_{t+1}\). Otherwise apply only a relaxation step whose validity is established for the problem class. Stop when no residual requirement remains and output \(F\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent path sampling from fractional unit-flow decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each commodity \(i\), let \(\mathcal P_i\) be its admissible paths and let \(f_{iP}\ge0\) satisfy \(\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_i}f_{iP}=1\). Independently sample one path \(P_i\) with \(\Pr[P_i=P]=f_{iP}\), and route the entire commodity on \(P_i\). For each edge \(e\), set \(X_e:=|\{i:e\in P_i\}|\). Then
\[
\mathbb E[X_e]=\sum_i\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_i:e\in P}f_{iP}.
\]
Accept the sample if the prescribed congestion bounds hold; otherwise resample or invoke a separately justified alteration or repair procedure.

children.title: Component-Based Rounding
children.top_down_role: Rounding schemes driven by fractional connectivity components.

assumptions_latex: A fractional solution is expressed as nonnegative weights on admissible connected components.
The selected component can be installed integrally and residualized.
A problem-specific selection rule guarantees progress.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is the union of all installed components after residual requirements vanish.

notation.meaning: Residual component family at iteration t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic rounding template for component-indexed relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(F=\varnothing\) and the original residual instance. At iteration \(t\), solve the component relaxation and obtain \(z^{(t)}\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{\mathcal C_t}\). Choose a component \(C_t\) satisfying the problem-specific rounding predicate, install all edges of \(C_t\), set \(F\leftarrow F\cup C_t\), reduce the requirements already supplied by \(C_t\), and delete or contract only objects certified safe by the residual model. Feasibility and an approximation ratio follow only from corresponding residual-validity and charging invariants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve a component LP, install a component meeting a valid rounding rule, residualize safely, and repeat until all connectivity requirements are supplied.

children.title: Connectivity Contraction
children.top_down_role: Instance reduction through contraction of selected connectivity structures.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq V\) induces connectivity already installed at no additional residual cost.
Residual demands and capacities are constant on contraction fibers.
Cuts are transferred through the quotient map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility in the quotient lifts to residual feasibility in the original graph.

notation.meaning: Quotient map contracting K to one vertex

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient quotient condition for safe contraction of installed connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Contraction of \(K\) is safe if there exists a quotient requirement \(\bar r\) such that, for every \(\bar S\subseteq V/K\),
\[
\bar r(\bar S)=r'(q^{-1}(\bar S)),
\]
and every quotient edge solution \(\bar F\) satisfies
\[
|\bar F\cap\delta(\bar S)|\ge\bar r(\bar S)
\]
if and only if its lift, together with the already installed edges inside \(K\), satisfies all residual cuts represented by unions of contraction fibers. Demands separated inside \(K\) must already be met, and capacities or costs of parallel quotient edges must preserve their original contributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contract an installed connected set only when quotient cuts exactly represent residual cuts and all demands internal to the contracted set are already satisfied.
knowledge_statements.title: Connectivity Contraction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quotient condition covers cuts that are unions of contraction fibers, but full residual feasibility can involve cuts splitting the contracted set. A model-specific source must establish that installed internal connectivity and the transferred requirements cover every omitted cut class.

children.title: Rounding–Contraction Coupling
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between component selection plus subsequent contraction.

assumptions_latex: Each rounded component is feasible for the current residual relaxation.
Each contraction satisfies the quotient-lifting condition.
Residual requirements subtract exactly the connectivity supplied by installed edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lifted final solution is feasible, and valid per-iteration charges add to a global cost bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariant coupling component installation with safe quotient contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At iteration \(t\), install \(C_t\), update the residual requirement by precisely its certified contribution, and contract only vertex sets whose quotient solutions lift feasibly. Maintain the invariant that every feasible solution of \(I_{t+1}\), lifted and united with \(C_0,\ldots,C_t\), is feasible for \(I_0\). If additionally constants \(\rho\ge1\) satisfy
\[
c(C_t)\le\rho\bigl(L_t-L_{t+1}\bigr)
\]
for every iteration, with \(L_m=0\) at termination, then
\[
c\left(\bigcup_{t<m}C_t\right)\le\rho L_0.
\]
Thus feasibility lifting and telescoping cost charging jointly certify the rounding-contraction scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Safe contractions preserve liftable feasibility; if each installed component is charged to the drop in the residual bound, costs telescope to a global guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Rounding–Contraction Coupling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The feasibility-lifting invariant and telescoping calculation are correct when the stated per-iteration conditions hold. Sources are needed for the residual update, safe-contraction invariant, and bound-drop charging inequality in an actual network-design model.

children.top_down_role: Regimes where contraction disrupts residual feasibility or approximation control.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a graph with distinct terminals \(s\) and \(t\) and the requirement that they be connected. Suppose no edge has yet been installed. If an algorithm contracts \(s\) and \(t\) so that \(q(s)=q(t)\), the quotient instance regards the terminal pair as colocated; hence the empty quotient edge set appears feasible. Its lift is empty and does not connect \(s\) to \(t\) in the original graph. Therefore identifying vertices across an unmet terminal-separating cut is unsafe unless installed connectivity or an equivalent certificate already joins every pair identified by the contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contracting an unconnected demanded terminal pair makes the quotient falsely accept an empty solution, so contraction requires a certificate of internal connectivity.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the primal-dual pair
\[
\min\{c^Tx:Ax\ge b,\ x\ge0\},\qquad \max\{b^Ty:A^Ty\le c,\ y\ge0\},
\]
initialize \(y=0\) and an empty primal set. Choose active indices \(U\), and increase their dual coordinates uniformly by the largest \(\varepsilon\ge0\) satisfying
\[
\sum_i A_{ij}(y_i+\varepsilon\mathbf1_{i\in U})\le c_j
\]
for every \(j\). Add a newly tight primal object \(j\) according to the algorithm's feasibility rule, update \(U\), and repeat until the provisional primal set covers all requirements.

children.title: Primal-Dual Pruning
children.top_down_role: Removal of redundant purchased structure after growth.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Pruning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse-delete pruning following primal-dual growth for a monotone covering problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let growth return a feasible set \(F=\{e_1,\ldots,e_m\}\), indexed by insertion time, and assume feasibility is monotone under adding primal objects. Initialize \(F'=F\). For \(j=m,m-1,\ldots,1\), test whether \(F'\setminus\{e_j\}\) remains feasible for every original requirement. If so, replace \(F'\) by \(F'\setminus\{e_j\}\); otherwise retain \(e_j\). Output \(F'\). The result is feasible and inclusion-minimal. A cost approximation requires an additional dual-charging argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a monotone covering problem, scan grown objects in reverse order and delete each dispensable one; the result is feasible and inclusion-minimal, while a cost ratio requires separate analysis.
assumptions_latex: Growth has produced a feasible provisional set of primal objects.
Feasibility is monotone under adding primal objects.
The objects have a recorded insertion order.
Feasibility can be tested after deleting one object.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reverse deletion returns an inclusion-minimal feasible subset of the provisional solution.

children.title: Growth–Pruning Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions linking growth output to valid pruning.

knowledge_statements.title: Growth–Pruning Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition for a minimization primal-dual approximation framework.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a covering problem with nonnegative costs and a dual lower bound. Growth and pruning are compatible with factor \(\alpha\ge 1\) if growth returns a dual-feasible vector \(y\) and a provisional integral set \(F\), pruning returns \(F'\subseteq F\), and
\[F'\text{ is primal feasible},\qquad c(F')\le c(F)\le \alpha b^{\mathsf T}y.\]
Weak duality then gives
\[c(F')\le \alpha b^{\mathsf T}y\le \alpha\operatorname{OPT}.\]
Thus compatibility requires pruning to preserve feasibility and the charging argument established during growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Growth and pruning are compatible when pruning preserves feasibility and cost, while the grown dual solution charges the provisional cost within factor alpha.
assumptions_latex: \(c\ge 0\) and \(\alpha\ge 1\).
\(y\) is feasible for a dual whose value lower-bounds \(\operatorname{OPT}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c(F')\le \alpha\operatorname{OPT}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition and weak-duality conclusion are mathematically coherent and the content kind fits the compatibility leaf, but no source identifies the covering formulation, dual, or growth-pruning framework supporting this certificate.

children.title: Overgrowth–Overpruning Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cost or feasibility losses caused by poorly balanced growth and pruning.

knowledge_statements.title: Overgrowth–Overpruning Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for growth charging and feasibility-preserving pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let growth produce a dual-feasible \(y\) and provisional solution \(F\), and let pruning produce \(F'\subseteq F\). If
\[c(F)\le \alpha\beta b^{\mathsf T}y\quad\text{and}\quad c(F')\le c(F),\]
then the surviving guarantee is at best the stated factor \(\alpha\beta\). If no finite \(\beta\) bounds the growth charge, no approximation factor follows from this certificate. If pruning makes \(F'\) infeasible, even the inequality \(c(F')\le c(F)\) supplies no approximation certificate. Hence bounded charging and preserved feasibility are separate necessary interfaces of this analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unbounded growth destroys the cost guarantee, whereas pruning past feasibility destroys the solution certificate; bounded overgrowth merely multiplies the approximation factor.
assumptions_latex: \(y\) is dual feasible and \(c\ge0\).
The analysis uses only weak duality and the displayed charging inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F'\text{ feasible}\Rightarrow c(F')\le\alpha\beta\operatorname{OPT}\); otherwise no such certificate follows.

notation.meaning: overgrowth multiplier beyond the nominal factor

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly separates loss of a bounded charging argument from loss of primal feasibility, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. An authoritative source is still required for the claimed abstract interface and its intended primal-dual setting.

children.title: Rounding with Congestion or Connectivity Repair

knowledge_statements.title: Rounding with Congestion or Connectivity Repair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic alteration template for rounded multicommodity routing or network design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a fractional design-routing pair \((x,f)\), a rounding distribution \(\mathcal D(x,f)\), a feasibility test, and a repair oracle \(R\). Sample an integral candidate \((X,P)\sim\mathcal D(x,f)\). While the test identifies a violated capacity constraint or connectivity requirement \(q\), replace
\[(X,P)\leftarrow R(X,P,q).\]
Stop and output \((X,P)\) when every required cut is connected and every edge load is at most the prescribed congestion factor times its installed capacity. Output failure if the oracle declares that no permitted repair exists or if a stipulated iteration budget is exhausted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Round the fractional solution, repeatedly identify congestion or connectivity violations, and invoke a repair oracle until the candidate is feasible or repair fails.
assumptions_latex: The feasibility test separates violated capacity and connectivity constraints.
Each accepted repair preserves integrality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns a certified feasible integral routing-design pair or an explicit failure outcome.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the appropriate content kind, but this is only a generic oracle template. No source or stated invariant establishes repair progress, termination, preservation of previously satisfied constraints, or an approximation guarantee.

children.title: Metric-Distortion Gaps
children.top_down_role: Relaxation losses attributable to embedding or metric representation distortion.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Distortion Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Least distortion of a finite metric into an \(L_1\) metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite metric space \((X,d)\), its \(L_1\)-distortion gap is
\[c_1(X,d)=\inf_f\inf\{D\ge1:\ d(x,y)\le \lVert f(x)-f(y)\rVert_1\le Dd(x,y)\ \text{for all }x,y\in X\},\]
where the first infimum ranges over maps into arbitrary finite-dimensional \(L_1\) spaces after an allowed positive rescaling. For a class \(\mathcal M\) of finite metrics, its worst metric-distortion gap is \(\sup_{(X,d)\in\mathcal M}c_1(X,d)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The metric-distortion gap is the smallest multiplicative expansion needed for a noncontracting embedding of the metric into an L1 space.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a finite metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c_1(X,d)\in[1,+\infty]\) quantifies the metric's least \(L_1\)-distortion.

notation.meaning: least distortion of the metric into an L1 space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalized noncontracting formulation is a coherent definition of least L1 distortion and fits the leaf, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the definition or its normalization convention.

children.title: Flow-Cut Gaps
children.top_down_role: Separation between routable flow value plus cut-based capacity bounds.

assumptions_latex: The graph and commodity set are finite.
At least one terminal pair has positive demand, and \(\lambda^*>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gap}_{FC}(I)=\phi^*/\lambda^*\ge 1\).

notation.meaning: edges crossing the cut defined by S

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concurrent multicommodity flow versus sparsest-cut ratio in finite undirected capacitated instances with positive concurrent-flow value.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Multicommodity Flow Problems p. 17
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with edge capacities \(c_e\ge 0\), and let \((s_i,t_i,d_i)\) be finitely many terminal-pair demands with \(d_i\ge 0\). Let \(\lambda^*>0\) be the maximum concurrent-flow value, so commodity \(i\) can route \(\lambda^*d_i\). Define
\[\phi^*=\min_{\substack{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\\ \sum_{i:\,|\{s_i,t_i\}\cap S|=1}d_i>0}}\frac{\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}c_e}{\sum_{i:\,|\{s_i,t_i\}\cap S|=1}d_i}.\]
The flow-cut gap of the instance \(I\) is
\[\operatorname{gap}_{FC}(I)=\frac{\phi^*}{\lambda^*}.\]
Every feasible concurrent flow obeys every cut-capacity constraint, hence \(\lambda^*\le\phi^*\) and \(\operatorname{gap}_{FC}(I)\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite undirected instance with positive maximum concurrent-flow value, the flow-cut gap is the sparsest cut's capacity-to-separated-demand ratio divided by the maximum common fraction of all demands that can be routed.

children.title: Distortion–Flow-Cut Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural links between metric embeddings plus flow-cut separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Distortion–Flow-Cut Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite undirected multicommodity flow-cut duality expressed through \(L_1\)-embeddability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(n\ge2\), let \(G_n\) be the supremum of the concurrent-flow/sparsest-cut gap over undirected instances on at most \(n\) vertices. Let \(D_n\) be the supremum of \(c_1(X,d)\) over metrics on at most \(n\) points. The metric formulation of multicommodity flow-cut duality gives
\[G_n=D_n,\]
when zero-demand pairs and degenerate pseudometric identifications are removed in the standard way. Consequently, an upper bound \(D\) for embedding every relevant dual metric into \(L_1\) yields flow-cut gap at most \(D\), while a metric requiring distortion \(D\) supplies a matching gap witness through separation duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case concurrent flow-cut gaps equal worst-case L1 distortions of the associated finite metrics under the standard dual formulations.
assumptions_latex: Instances are finite, undirected, and permit fractional splittable flow.
The sparsest-cut and metric programs use matching capacity-demand normalization.

notation.meaning: worst flow-cut gap on at most n vertices
worst L1 distortion of an at-most-n-point metric

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Duality is an appropriate content kind, but the exact finite-n equality depends on nontrivial separation duality, normalization, admissible demand pairs, and treatment of pseudometrics. No source is supplied for those choices, so the mathematical version cannot be validated reliably.

children.title: Low-Distortion Regimes
children.top_down_role: Graph or demand classes where metric loss remains controlled.

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Distortion Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tree metrics as an exact low-distortion regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \((X,d_T)\) is the shortest-path metric on a weighted tree with nonnegative edge lengths, then it embeds isometrically into an \(L_1\) space. Explicitly, choose a root and define one coordinate for each tree edge \(e\), weighted by its length, indicating which side of the cut induced by deleting \(e\) contains a vertex. Then
\[\lVert f(x)-f(y)\rVert_1=d_T(x,y)\quad\text{for all }x,y\in X.\]
Hence \(c_1(X,d_T)=1\), and any flow-cut formulation whose dual metrics are tree metrics has gap one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted tree metrics embed isometrically into L1, so corresponding flow-cut relaxations have no distortion-induced gap.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a finite tree with nonnegative edge lengths.
The flow-cut formulation satisfies the standard distortion correspondence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c_1(X,d_T)=1\), and the corresponding flow-cut gap equals \(1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tree-metric isometric embedding claim is standard and property fits the low-distortion leaf. The flow-cut consequence additionally depends on the unsourced distortion-flow-cut correspondence, and no authoritative locator is supplied for either claim.

children.title: Routing-Integrality Gaps
children.top_down_role: Separation between fractional routing plus integral routing structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Routing-Integrality Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost gap between integral path routing-design and its fractional relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a routing-design instance \(I\), let \(P_I\) be its fractional relaxation and let \(Z_I\subseteq P_I\) contain the admissible integral designs with each routed commodity assigned according to the integral routing convention. For nonnegative cost vector \(c\), define
\[\operatorname{gap}_{\mathrm{int}}(I)=\frac{\min\{c^{\mathsf T}z:z\in Z_I\}}{\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in P_I\}}.\]
The ratio is \(+\infty\) when the denominator is finite but no integral feasible solution exists. The gap of a class is the supremum of this ratio over its instances with positive fractional optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The routing-integrality gap is the ratio between the cheapest integral routing-design and the cheapest solution of its fractional relaxation.
assumptions_latex: Costs are nonnegative.
The fractional optimum is finite and positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gap}_{\mathrm{int}}(I)\ge1\) whenever \(Z_I\subseteq P_I\) and \(Z_I\ne\varnothing\).

children.title: Congestion Gaps
children.top_down_role: Capacity-violation losses required to realize discrete routing.

knowledge_statements.title: Congestion Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity augmentation required when converting fractional routing to integral paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an instance with capacities \(u_e>0\) and demands \(d_i\), assume a fractional routing of congestion at most one exists. Its integral congestion gap is
\[\rho(I)=\min_{(P_i)}\max_{e}\frac{\sum_{i:e\in P_i}d_i}{u_e},\]
where the minimum ranges over one admissible path \(P_i\) for every commodity; set \(\rho(I)=+\infty\) if no such path system exists. The congestion gap of an instance class is \(\sup_I\rho(I)\). Thus \(\rho(I)\) is the least uniform capacity multiplier making an integral unsplittable routing feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The congestion gap is the smallest uniform capacity enlargement needed to replace a feasible fractional routing by one path per commodity.
assumptions_latex: \(u_e>0\) for every usable edge.
A fractional routing with edge load at most \(u_e\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Capacities \(\rho(I)u_e\) admit an integral path routing, and no smaller uniform multiplier does.

notation.meaning: integral path chosen for commodity i

children.title: Integrality–Congestion Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Bicriteria regimes trading routing integrality against congestion.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality–Congestion Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bicriteria frontier relating integral cost and permitted congestion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a minimization instance \(I\) and congestion allowance \(\rho\ge1\), let \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}^{\rho}(I)\) be the minimum integral routing-design cost when edge \(e\) may carry load at most \(\rho u_e\). Define the class tradeoff function
\[G(\rho)=\sup_I\frac{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}^{\rho}(I)}{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{frac}}(I)}.\]
Then \(G\) is nonincreasing: if \(1\le\rho_1\le\rho_2\), every solution feasible under \(\rho_1\) is feasible under \(\rho_2\), so \(G(\rho_2)\le G(\rho_1)\). A bicriteria guarantee \((\alpha,\rho)\) is exactly the assertion \(G(\rho)\le\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing more congestion can only reduce the worst integral-cost gap; the resulting function records the complete bicriteria approximation frontier.
assumptions_latex: All instances use the same fractional relaxation and cost convention.
\(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{frac}}(I)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_1\le\rho_2\Rightarrow G(\rho_2)\le G(\rho_1)\), and \((\alpha,\rho)\iff G(\rho)\le\alpha\).

notation.meaning: worst integral-cost gap at congestion allowance rho
optimal integral cost with rho-capacity augmentation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The monotonicity of the optimum-value tradeoff is coherent and representation fits the leaf. However, calling the inequality exactly equivalent to a bicriteria guarantee is reliable only for an existential optimum guarantee, not necessarily an algorithmic approximation guarantee; no source fixes that interpretation.

children.title: Unsplittable-Routing Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Demand or topology regimes amplifying discrete-routing loss.

knowledge_statements.title: Unsplittable-Routing Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded congestion without a no-bottleneck restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each integer \(k\ge2\), take two vertices joined by \(k\) parallel edges, each of capacity \(1\), and one commodity of demand \(k\) between the vertices. A splittable routing is feasible with congestion \(1\) by sending one unit on every edge. An unsplittable routing must place all \(k\) units on one edge and therefore has congestion \(k\). Thus the fractional-to-unsplittable congestion gap is unbounded as \(k\to\infty\). The example violates the no-bottleneck condition because the commodity demand exceeds every edge capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A demand split across k unit parallel edges is fractionally feasible, but one-path routing incurs congestion k; no bounded gap exists without demand restrictions.
assumptions_latex: Parallel edges are permitted; equivalently, each may be replaced by an internally disjoint two-edge path.
Unsplittable routing assigns the entire commodity demand to one path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho(I_k)=k\), so \(\sup_k\rho(I_k)=+\infty\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parallel-edge construction correctly yields congestion k and counterexample is an appropriate role for this failure-boundary leaf. The common evidence contract nevertheless requires an inspectable source for this nontrivial boundary claim.

children.title: Connectivity-Cut Gaps
children.top_down_role: Losses caused by cut relaxations that underrepresent discrete connectivity.

knowledge_statements.title: Connectivity-Cut Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality gap of a cut relaxation for survivable connectivity design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) have nonnegative edge costs \(c_e\), and let \(r(S)\) be the required number of selected edges crossing each proper nonempty cut. Define
\[P_{\mathrm{cut}}=\{x\in[0,1]^E:x(\delta(S))\ge r(S)\text{ for every }\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\}.\]
If \(Z_{\mathrm{conn}}\subseteq\{0,1\}^E\) is the family of designs satisfying the intended connectivity requirements, the connectivity-cut gap is
\[\sup_{c\ge0}\frac{\min_{z\in Z_{\mathrm{conn}}}c^{\mathsf T}z}{\min_{x\in P_{\mathrm{cut}}}c^{\mathsf T}x},\]
over costs with positive finite denominator, using \(+\infty\) when the numerator is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The connectivity-cut gap compares the cheapest integral connectivity design with the cheapest fractional vector satisfying every required cut inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and \(r(S)\ge0\).
The cut requirements correctly encode necessary conditions for the intended connectivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed supremum is at least \(1\) whenever \(Z_{\mathrm{conn}}\subseteq P_{\mathrm{cut}}\).

notation.meaning: required capacity or edge count across cut S

children.title: Uncrossing Gaps
children.top_down_role: Losses or structural obstructions associated with insufficient uncrossing.

knowledge_statements.title: Uncrossing Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of standard pairwise uncrossing for cut-covering relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\), let \(r:2^V\to\mathbb{R}_{+}\), and consider \(x(\delta(S))\ge r(S)\) for every proper nonempty \(S\subset V\). Two sets \(A,B\) cross when all four regions determined by them are nonempty. If
\[
r(A)+r(B)>\max\{r(A\cap B)+r(A\cup B),\ r(A\setminus B)+r(B\setminus A)\},
\]
then neither canonical uncrossing pair preserves the aggregate right-hand side of the inequalities for \(A,B\). Consequently, submodularity and posimodularity of \(x(\delta(\cdot))\) alone do not justify replacing these crossing cuts by either canonical pair; an additional skew-supermodularity-type condition on \(r\) is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If both canonical replacement pairs have smaller total requirements than two crossing cuts, cut submodularity alone cannot uncross them without weakening the relaxation.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is an undirected graph and \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{E}\).
\(A,B\subset V\) are proper crossing sets.
All displayed cut inequalities belong to the relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A,B\) cannot be replaced by either canonical uncrossing pair while preserving their aggregate requirement.

notation.meaning: Edges with exactly one endpoint in S.
Sum of x-values over the edge set F.

children.title: Cut–Uncrossing Interaction
children.top_down_role: Dependence of cut-relaxation strength on laminar or uncrossed structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut–Uncrossing Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tight-cut uncrossing under a skew-supermodular requirement function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\ge0\) satisfy \(x(\delta(S))\ge r(S)\) for every proper nonempty \(S\subset V\), where \(r\) is skew-supermodular: for all crossing \(A,B\),
\[
r(A)+r(B)\le\max\{r(A\cap B)+r(A\cup B),\ r(A\setminus B)+r(B\setminus A)\}.
\]
If the inequalities for crossing sets \(A,B\) are tight, then at least one maximizing canonical pair consists entirely of tight cuts. Thus \(A,B\) may be replaced by either \(A\cap B,A\cup B\) or \(A\setminus B,B\setminus A\), according to the valid alternative, without changing the summed cut value or summed requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under skew-supermodular requirements, two tight crossing cuts can be replaced by a canonical tight pair without changing their total value.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is undirected and \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{E}\).
\(r\) is skew-supermodular on crossing sets.
\(x(\delta(A))=r(A)\) and \(x(\delta(B))=r(B)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At least one canonical uncrossing pair is tight and preserves the summed cut value.

children.title: Nonlaminar Obstruction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instances where crossing constraints resist useful laminar organization.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlaminar Obstruction Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise certificate obstructing canonical laminarization of a tight-cut family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal F\) be a family of tight cuts for \(x(\delta(S))\ge r(S)\). A crossing pair \(A,B\in\mathcal F\) is an uncrossing obstruction if
\[
r(A)+r(B)>r(A\cap B)+r(A\cup B)
\quad\text{and}\quad
r(A)+r(B)>r(A\setminus B)+r(B\setminus A).
\]
The pair \((A,B)\), together with these two verifiable strict inequalities, certifies that no standard canonical replacement of this pair preserves its summed requirement. If every crossing pair available during a pairwise laminarization procedure has this property, that procedure cannot reach a laminar family without weakening a requirement or introducing a noncanonical cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two strict requirement inequalities certify that a crossing tight-cut pair resists both standard uncrossing replacements and obstructs canonical laminarization.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is feasible for the stated undirected cut-covering system.
\(A,B\in\mathcal F\) cross and are tight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed pair is a locally verifiable obstruction to requirement-preserving canonical uncrossing.

knowledge_statements.title: Activation Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality gap of a fixed-charge multicommodity activation relaxation.

For a directed or undirected network, let \(y_e\) indicate whether edge \(e\) is activated, let \(U_e\ge0\) be its capacity, and let \(f_e^k\ge0\) be routed flow for commodity \(k\). The activation formulation imposes flow conservation and
\[
\sum_k f_e^k\le U_e y_e.
\]
With nonnegative activation costs \(a_e\), define \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}\) by \(y_e\in\{0,1\}\) and \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}\) by \(0\le y_e\le1\). The activation gap of an instance is \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}/z_{\mathrm{LP}}\), with value \(+\infty\) when \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}>0=z_{\mathrm{LP}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The activation gap is the ratio between binary fixed-charge routing cost and its relaxation allowing fractional edge activation.
assumptions_latex: Commodity demands and edge capacities are nonnegative.
The integer routing problem is feasible.
Both models use identical flow-conservation and demand constraints.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let edge \(e\) admit integer capacity modules \(x_e\in\mathbb Z_{+}\), each providing \(u_e>0\) units at cost \(c_e\ge0\). For commodity flows \(f_e^k\ge0\), impose
\[
\sum_k f_e^k\le u_e x_e
\]
together with flow conservation and demand satisfaction. Let \(z_{\mathrm{mod}}\) be the minimum cost \(\sum_e c_e x_e\) with integral modules and \(z_{\mathrm{frac}}\) the value obtained from \(x_e\ge0\). The capacity-linking gap is \(z_{\mathrm{mod}}/z_{\mathrm{frac}}\), using value \(+\infty\) if \(z_{\mathrm{mod}}>0=z_{\mathrm{frac}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The capacity-linking gap compares discrete capacity-module installation with the relaxation that permits fractional modules under the same routing constraints.

children.title: Activation–Capacity Coupling
children.top_down_role: Interaction between discrete activation decisions plus capacity installation.

knowledge_statements.title: Activation–Capacity Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local feasibility predicate linking activation, installed capacity, and routed load.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each edge \(e\), let \(y_e\in\{0,1\}\) be its activation state, \(x_e\ge0\) its installed capacity, \(U_e\ge0\) an activation upper bound, and \(\ell_e=\sum_k f_e^k\) its total load. Activation and capacity are correctly coupled when
\[
0\le \ell_e\le x_e\le U_e y_e.
\]
The continuous relaxation replaces \(y_e\in\{0,1\}\) by \(0\le y_e\le1\). Under the integer condition, \(y_e=0\) forces \(x_e=\ell_e=0\); under relaxation, positive load may be supported by proportionally fractional activation whenever the remaining network constraints permit it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inequalities load ≤ installed capacity ≤ maximum capacity times activation define the local activation–capacity coupling and expose fractional activation in the relaxation.
assumptions_latex: \(U_e\) is a valid upper bound on installable capacity.
All flows and installed capacities are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_e=0\Rightarrow x_e=\ell_e=0\) integrally, while fractional \(y_e\) can support positive \(x_e\) and \(\ell_e\) in the relaxation.

notation.meaning: Aggregate routed load on edge e.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically precise and the condition content kind fits the coupling leaf, but no citation is supplied. The standard-field rationale is sufficient only to retain candidate status, not to resolve this source review. A direct network-design formulation source is required.

children.title: Fractional-Installation Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Gap-producing regimes with dispersed fractional installation.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional-Installation Pathologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-edge family with an unbounded fixed-charge activation gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(U\ge1\), consider two vertices \(s,t\), one edge \(e=st\) of capacity \(U\), one unit of demand from \(s\) to \(t\), and activation cost one. The linking constraint is \(f_e\le Uy_e\), and demand satisfaction forces \(f_e=1\). With \(y_e\in\{0,1\}\), the unique feasible activation has \(y_e=1\), so \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}=1\). With \(0\le y_e\le1\), choosing \(y_e=1/U\) is feasible and optimal, so \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}=1/U\). Hence the activation integrality gap equals \(U\) and is unbounded as \(U\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unit demand on one capacity-U edge costs one integrally but only 1/U fractionally, giving an unbounded activation gap.
assumptions_latex: Activation is the only charged design decision.
The edge may carry the full unit demand after activation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}/z_{\mathrm{LP}}=U\), so no constant gap bound exists over this family.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-edge construction is internally correct and counterexample is the appropriate content kind: the integer optimum is 1 and the relaxed optimum is 1/U. However, the record supplies neither a source reference nor an explicit standard-field rationale, so it does not satisfy the evidence requirement.

children.title: Directed-Reachability Gaps
children.top_down_role: Relaxation losses arising from asymmetric reachability requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed-Reachability Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality gap of the rooted directed-reachability cut relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) have nonnegative arc costs, root \(r\), and terminals \(T\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}\). A directed reachability design selects arcs so that every \(t\in T\) is reachable from \(r\). Its cut relaxation is
\[
\min\sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a,
\qquad x(\delta^-(S))\ge1
\]
for every \(S\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}\) with \(S\cap T\ne\varnothing\), with \(0\le x_a\le1\). If \(z_{\mathrm{reach}}\) is the minimum integral design cost and \(z_{\mathrm{cut}}\) the relaxation value, the directed-reachability gap is \(z_{\mathrm{reach}}/z_{\mathrm{cut}}\), with the usual positive-over-zero value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directed-reachability gap compares a minimum rooted terminal-reaching subgraph with its incoming-cut linear relaxation.
assumptions_latex: Arc costs are nonnegative.
Every terminal is reachable from the root in the available digraph.
Integral and fractional models use the same terminal set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gap}_{\mathrm{reach}}=z_{\mathrm{reach}}/z_{\mathrm{cut}}\).

notation.meaning: Arcs entering S from its complement.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) have nonnegative arc costs. A strongly connected spanning design selects arcs making every ordered vertex pair mutually reachable. Its standard cut relaxation is
\[
\min\sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a,
\qquad x(\delta^-(S))\ge1,
\qquad x(\delta^+(S))\ge1
\]
for every proper nonempty \(S\subset V\), with \(0\le x_a\le1\). If \(z_{\mathrm{SC}}\) is the minimum integral strongly connected design cost and \(z_{\mathrm{BCR}}\) is the relaxation value, the directed-component gap is \(z_{\mathrm{SC}}/z_{\mathrm{BCR}}\), interpreted as \(+\infty\) when \(z_{\mathrm{SC}}>0=z_{\mathrm{BCR}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directed-component gap compares a minimum strongly connected spanning subgraph with the relaxation enforcing one entering and one leaving arc across every cut.

children.title: Reachability–Component Coupling
children.top_down_role: Interaction between directed reachability constraints plus component selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Reachability–Component Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence coupling strong connectivity to two rooted reachability systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a root \(r\) in a finite digraph \(D=(V,A)\). The digraph is strongly connected if and only if every vertex \(v\in V\) is reachable from \(r\) and \(r\) is reachable from every \(v\). Equivalently, for every nonempty \(S\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}\), both
\[
\delta^-(S)\ne\varnothing
\quad\text{and}\quad
\delta^+(S)\ne\varnothing.
\]
Thus a strong-component design can be represented as the simultaneous satisfaction of an outward rooted-reachability cut system and an inward rooted-reachability cut system sharing the same selected arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong connectivity is exactly the conjunction of root-to-vertex and vertex-to-root reachability, represented by entering and leaving cuts for every root-free set.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite digraph.
\(r\in V\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) is strongly connected exactly when both rooted reachability systems hold.

children.title: Asymmetric-Connectivity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where undirected component intuition fails under arc orientation.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymmetric-Connectivity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on transferring symmetric undirected-cut arguments to rooted directed connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a digraph, the entering-cut function satisfies \(\delta^-(S)\ne\delta^-(V\setminus S)\) in general; indeed \(\delta^-(V\setminus S)=\delta^+(S)\). A rooted outward-reachability relaxation imposes entering-cut constraints only on sets \(S\) excluding the root and containing a required terminal. Complementation sends such a set to one containing the root, normally outside that constraint family. Therefore any undirected argument that identifies complementary cuts, or uses complement closure to perform a symmetric uncrossing step, is invalid for this directed relaxation unless matching leaving-cut constraints or another explicit symmetry condition is added.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed entering cuts are not complement-symmetric, so rooted reachability constraints are not complement-closed and cannot inherit symmetric undirected uncrossing arguments automatically.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a digraph with fixed root \(r\).
The relaxation contains rooted entering-cut constraints but not necessarily corresponding leaving-cut constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complement-based symmetric cut arguments require additional bidirectional constraints and are otherwise inapplicable.

notation.meaning: Root excluded from constrained terminal cuts.
